title: Repair Notices: Tenant's Remedies and Deadlines
bodyText:
Arizona law does not set a deadline for a landlord to begin repairs. The day counts come from the tenant's remedies.

If the landlord materially fails to comply with the lease, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 10 days after the landlord receives it unless the breach is remedied within 10 days. If the landlord's failure to maintain the property materially affects health and safety, the period is 5 days. If the landlord remedies the breach in time, the lease does not end, and the tenant cannot terminate over a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused.

For a repair costing less than $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, the tenant may give written notice and, if the landlord does not comply within 10 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have a licensed contractor do the work and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent after giving the landlord an itemized statement and a lien waiver.

If the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, gas or electric service, hot water, heat, air-conditioning or cooling where installed, or other essential services, the tenant may give reasonable notice and then buy the service and deduct its cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that period (with limited recovery of any extra cost).

The tenant may also recover damages and obtain a court order for the landlord's noncompliance, and in an eviction for nonpayment may counterclaim, in which case the court may order rent paid into court.

title: Landlord's Maintenance Duties
Lease Terms Arizona Law Prohibits
bodyText: An Arizona lease may not require the tenant to waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; to pay the landlord's attorney fees (although a written lease may award fees to the prevailing party in a court action, and the winner of a contested eviction may get fees under general law even without such a clause); to accept any exculpation or limit on the landlord's liability arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord for that liability; to waive or limit anyone's right to call the police or other emergency assistance in an emergency; or to pay penalties for doing so. A prohibited term is unenforceable, and a landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing terms the landlord knows are prohibited owes the tenant actual damages plus up to two months' periodic rent. A lease also may not contain terms contrary to the utility-service rules, may not let rent be collected free of the landlord's duty to keep the unit fit, and may be refused enforcement by a court as unconscionable. Every duty under the Act carries an obligation of good faith. A written lease must have all blanks filled in, and each side must give the other a signed copy.

title: Self-Help Eviction and Other Prohibited Practices
bodyText: An Arizona landlord may not recover possession except through the courts, abandonment, surrender or as the Act permits: no lockouts, removal of the tenant's belongings, or willful interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential services. If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant or willfully cuts services, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the lease and recover the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, plus return of the deposit. A landlord may not cut off utilities it provides under the lease except to make repairs, and may not shift a utility it provides to the tenant after signing without the tenant's written consent; a violation allows damages, costs, attorney fees and an injunction. After a writ of restitution is executed, the landlord may disconnect landlord-provided utilities only the following day and only through a person the utility authorizes. A landlord who enters unlawfully, enters lawfully in an unreasonable manner, or makes repeated harassing demands for entry owes actual damages of at least one month's rent and may be enjoined, and the tenant may terminate. A landlord lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable, and distraint for rent is abolished.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: An Arizona landlord may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because the tenant complained to a government agency about a building or housing code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to the landlord about a failure to maintain the premises, organized or joined a tenants' union, or complained to an agency enforcing the wage-price stabilization act. A complaint within six months before the landlord's action creates a presumption of retaliation, unless the complaint came after notice of termination. The tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, and has a defense to eviction. The landlord may still evict if the code violation was caused primarily by the tenant's or household's lack of reasonable care, or if the tenant is behind on rent.

title: Eviction Notices and Process
bodyText: For unpaid rent, the landlord gives written notice of nonpayment and of the intent to terminate if rent is not paid within five days; if it is not paid, the landlord files a special detainer action. Before filing, the lease is reinstated if the tenant pays all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee stated in a written lease; after filing, only if the tenant also pays attorney fees and court costs; after judgment, reinstatement is the landlord's choice. For other material breaches (including material falsification of the rental application), the landlord gives a written notice that the lease will end at least 10 days after the tenant receives it unless the breach is remedied in 10 days; for a breach of the tenant's maintenance duties that materially affects health and safety, 5 days. If a remedied breach of the same or similar nature happens again during the term, the landlord may file 10 days after a written notice of the second breach, with no further cure. The Act defines the 'term of lease' as the initial term or any renewal or extension of the written rental agreement currently in effect, not counting a wrongful holdover; it does not say how that period runs in a month-to-month tenancy. False statements about criminal records, eviction history or current criminal activity cannot be cured. For a material and irreparable breach on the premises (such as illegal discharge of a weapon, homicide, prostitution, gang activity, drug manufacturing or sales, threats, assault, or acts that jeopardize the health, safety and welfare of the landlord, staff or other tenants or cause serious property damage), the landlord may give notice of immediate termination; trial is set within three days of filing and restitution ordered 12 to 24 hours after a finding for the landlord. Days in these notices are calendar days. The summons in a special detainer is returnable in three to six days. After judgment, a writ of restitution issues no sooner than five calendar days later; a tenant who stays or returns after being served with the writ commits criminal trespass. The Act's notices are received when hand-delivered or sent by registered or certified mail (deemed received on actual receipt or five days after mailing, whichever comes first).

title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: If an Arizona lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly and month-to-month in every other case. Either party may end a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 10 days before the termination date in the notice, and a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice. No reason is required, and Arizona has no statewide just-cause or rent-increase notice rule; a landlord who wants to change the rent on a month-to-month tenancy generally does so by giving the same 30-day notice. A fixed-term lease ends on its expiration date. If a landlord consents in writing to a tenant staying after the lease ends, the tenancy becomes month-to-month.

title: Abandonment and Property Left Behind
bodyText: A unit is abandoned in Arizona if the tenant has been absent without notice for at least seven days with rent unpaid for ten days and no reasonable evidence, other than the tenant's belongings, that the tenant is living there; or absent for at least five days with rent unpaid for five days and none of the tenant's belongings in the unit. The landlord then sends a notice of abandonment by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known and any alternate addresses, and posts it on the door or another conspicuous place for five days. Five days after it is both posted and mailed, the landlord may retake and rerent the unit if no belongings remain; the deposit is then forfeited and applied to accrued rent and reasonable costs. If belongings remain, the landlord inventories them, gives the same kind of notice of their location and storage cost, and holds them for 14 calendar days with reasonable care; perishables, contaminated items and plants may be disposed of. Abandoned animals may be released to a shelter or boarding facility once any person the tenant authorized to retrieve them has been notified and one calendar day has passed (keep a record of where each animal went); otherwise the landlord must give them reasonable care during the 14-day holding period or notify the county enforcement agent or animal control, and is not liable for good-faith actions in removing, releasing or caring for them. After 14 days the landlord may donate the property to a qualifying charity or sell it, applying proceeds to rent and costs and mailing any excess to the tenant, and must keep records and hold undeliverable excess for 12 months. Before disposal, a tenant who notifies the landlord in writing has five days to reclaim the property by paying removal and storage costs; clothing, work tools, and identification, financial, immigration, employment, public assistance and medical documents may be retrieved without paying. If the tenant returns the keys and leaves property behind, the landlord may remove and dispose of it immediately unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing. The landlord must use reasonable efforts to rerent an abandoned unit; the lease ends when a new tenancy begins or, if the landlord does not try to rerent, when the landlord learns of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the remaining term for this purpose is one month or one week. After an eviction writ is executed, the landlord must follow the same storage and disposal rules starting the next day.

title: Partial Payments and Waiver
bodyText:
An Arizona landlord does not have to accept a partial payment of rent or other charges. A landlord who accepts one keeps the right to proceed against the tenant only if the tenant agrees, in a writing made at the time of the payment, to the terms of the partial payment, including the date the balance is due. If the landlord already served a five-day nonpayment notice before the partial-payment agreement, no new notice is needed if the tenant breaks the agreement.

Accepting a housing assistance payment is not accepting a partial payment and does not waive the landlord's rights. Otherwise, accepting rent or any part of it with knowledge of a default, or accepting performance that differs from the lease or rules, waives the right to terminate the lease for that breach.

title: Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
Arizona caps all security, including prepaid rent, at one and one-half months' rent, though a tenant may voluntarily pay more rent in advance. The purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit must be stated in writing, and any fee not designated nonrefundable is refundable.

At move-in the landlord must give the tenant a signed copy of the lease, a move-in form for noting existing damage, and written notice that the tenant may attend the move-out inspection.

At the end of the tenancy the landlord may apply the deposit and prepaid rent to rent and, subject to the duty to mitigate, to charges stated in the lease and damages from the tenant's failure to maintain the unit.

Within 14 days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) after the tenancy ends, the tenant returns the keys and vacates, and the tenant asks for the deposit, the landlord must send an itemized list of deductions and any refund, by first class mail to the last known residence unless the tenant arranged otherwise in writing. If the tenant does not dispute the list within 60 days after mailing, it becomes final.

A landlord who does not comply owes the money due plus twice the amount wrongfully withheld. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound.

After a lawful abandonment retake, the deposit is forfeited and applied to accrued rent and costs. The Act has no interest requirement for deposits. You don't have to hold a joint move-out inspection with a tenant being evicted for a material and irreparable breach if you have reasonable cause to fear violence or intimidation.

title: Fair Housing
bodyText: Arizona's Fair Housing Act protects race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin and disability, the same classes as federal law. Familial status covers a person who is pregnant, lives with a child under 18 as parent or legal custodian (or with the custodian's written permission), or is obtaining custody. It is unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, publish discriminatory advertising, or intimidate a person exercising fair housing rights; for disability, it also covers refusing reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, refusing reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (the landlord may require restoration where reasonable), and failing to meet accessibility design rules for covered multifamily buildings. The Act does not require renting to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and does not bar refusing a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. It does not apply to a single-family house rented by an owner of no more than three houses without a real estate licensee or discriminatory advertising (one such rental in 24 months if the owner did not live there), or to rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units. Housing for older persons may exclude children. Separately, refusing to rent to a person because of children, or advertising a no-children restriction, is a petty offense and allows actual damages, a civil penalty of three times the monthly rent if intentional, and attorney fees; an occupancy limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable. Victims may sue within two years for actual and punitive damages and attorney fees. Some Arizona cities have their own fair housing ordinances that may add protections; check local law.

title: Assistance Animals in Arizona Rentals
bodyText:
Arizona's Fair Housing Act requires reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities, including allowing an assistance animal. Arizona defines an assistance animal as a trained or untrained animal that works, provides assistance, performs tasks, or provides therapeutic or emotional support for a person with a disability, so emotional support animals are covered by state law.

A service animal is a dog or miniature horse individually trained for a person with a disability.

A landlord is not liable for injuries or damage caused by a purported assistance animal or purported service animal that the landlord allows as a reasonable accommodation or modification on property the landlord controls; this does not reduce the tenant's disability rights.

Arizona's service-animal rules on permitted questions, fees and a $250 civil penalty for misrepresenting an animal apply to public places, not to rental housing. A leasing office or other area open to the public may be a public place, where those rules and the class 2 misdemeanor in A.R.S. § 11-1024(J) apply. A landlord may deny an animal whose presence would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property.

title: Rental Registration with the County Assessor
bodyText: Every Arizona owner of residential rental property must keep on file with the county assessor the owner's name, address and telephone number (and, for an entity, a named officer, partner, member or trustee), the property's street address and parcel number, and the year it was built, and must update the information within 10 days after a change. An owner who lives outside Arizona must designate a statutory agent in Arizona to accept legal service. The property may not be occupied unless this information is on file. If it is not, a tenant may give the landlord a written 10-day notice to comply, by certified mail or hand delivery; if the owner does not comply, the tenant may terminate the lease and must get back all prepaid rent within 10 days, and the deposit under the deposit statute. Cities and towns may impose civil penalties for failing to register ($1,000 plus $100 a month for newly acquired property, or $150 a day otherwise), dismissed if the owner complies within 10 days of the complaint or notice, and may inspect unregistered property or property designated a slum. The assessor may charge up to $10 per registration or change. If you own through an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation, it must also register with the Arizona Corporation Commission, naming an Arizona statutory agent, before doing business here, and until it does it may not maintain a lawsuit, including an eviction, in Arizona (A.R.S. §§ 10-1501(A), 10-1502(A), 29-3902(A), (B), 29-3903(A)(5)). Owning property, without more, is not doing business (A.R.S. §§ 10-1501(B)(9), 29-3905(A)(10)); whether renting it out is more is a case-law question, so register before filing (see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-az). Registering a trade name with the Secretary of State is optional in Arizona (A.R.S. § 44-1460(A)).

title: State Limits on Local Rent Regulation
bodyText: Arizona preempts rent control: cities and towns, including charter cities, have no power to control rents on private residential property, except property owned, financed, insured or subsidized by a state agency or a city or town. Cities, towns and counties may not adopt a residential rental licensing requirement or a residential rental registration requirement; a city may obtain rental registration information only from the county assessor. A city or county may adopt a citywide or countywide residential rental inspection program only after notice to registered owners, a public hearing and a supermajority council vote (majority of a county board), and may inspect the interior of an individual rental only in specified situations such as conditions materially affecting health and safety, a history of violations, a complaint or consent. Cities and counties may not charge for most initial inspections, such as a program's first annual inspection or an inspection the owner or tenant requests, but may charge a reasonable fee for later follow-up inspections. Since January 1, 2025, no city, town or other taxing jurisdiction may levy a transaction privilege or similar tax on renting residential property. Cities and counties may still inspect property whose owner has not registered with the county assessor, and slum-designated property, and local building, housing and health codes continue to bind landlords. Other local rules, such as fair housing and pool ordinances, vary by city and should be checked locally.

title: Sealed Eviction Records
bodyText: An Arizona court must seal all records of an eviction case if it dismisses the case before judgment or enters judgment for the tenant, and must also seal a case when the landlord and tenant file a written stipulation to set aside the eviction order and seal the file. Sealed records are available only to the parties and their attorneys, the court and the clerk, and may not be sold or released in bulk or individual record transfers to third parties. This covers summary eviction, forcible entry and detainer and special detainer records, including pleadings, findings, orders and exhibits. A court may also seal an eviction case when a landlord fails to respond within 15 days to a tenant's motion to compel satisfaction of a paid judgment. Sealed records are left out of the courts' public remote access.

title: Removing a Guest or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText:
In Arizona, a guest of a tenant who is not named on a written lease and who stays without the tenant's or landlord's permission is not a lawful tenant, and a law enforcement officer may remove a person who knowingly remains, at the request of the tenant or the landlord entitled to possession.

Separately, an owner of residential property may bring a forcible detainer action against an unauthorized person who entered while the property was not open to the public, is not a current or former tenant, had no agreement to live there with the owner, is not an immediate family member, and has refused the owner's request to leave, when no other litigation is pending between them; the writ issues immediately after judgment. This route does not apply to landlords and tenants.

title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText:
In Arizona, the holder of a dishonored check, draft, order or note may charge the maker a service fee of not more than $25 plus any actual charges the holder's financial institution assessed because of the dishonor.

Separately, a person who writes a check with intent to defraud, knowing there is no account or insufficient funds, is liable in a civil action for twice the amount of the check or $50, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees. Failure to pay within 12 days after notice of nonpayment (given in person, or in writing by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the address on the check) is prima facie evidence of intent to defraud.

title: Renting in a Condominium or HOA Community
bodyText:
An Arizona condominium or planned-community association may not require a renting owner to disclose anything about a tenant beyond the names and contact information of adult occupants, the lease period with start and end dates, and a description and license plate numbers of the tenants' vehicles (plus photo ID showing age in an age-restricted community).

The association or its manager may charge up to $25 per new tenancy (not for renewals) for that information, payable within 15 days, and no more than $15 for incomplete or late information; otherwise it may not treat rental units differently from owner-occupied units in fees, fines or requirements.

It may not demand the tenant's application, credit report or lease, or require the tenant to sign a waiver of due process rights. An owner may use a crime-free lease addendum, the association may enforce a restriction on registered level two and three sex offenders, and the owner of rental property must abate criminal activity.

title: Criminal Activity on Rental Property
bodyText: Arizona treats residential property regularly used to commit crimes as a nuisance. The attorney general, county or city attorney, a homeowners' or condominium association, or an affected resident may sue the owner or manager to abate it. An owner or manager who receives a government notice of documented criminal reports is deemed to know of the activity and must begin within five business days to take legally available action to abate it. If the owner fails to act, a government authority may abate the nuisance and the cost becomes a priority lien on the property. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act supports this: a landlord may give notice of immediate termination for a material and irreparable breach such as drug dealing, gang activity, prostitution, threats or assault on the premises. A city may require the owner of slum-designated or seriously substandard property to hire a licensed property manager and join the city's crime-free multihousing program.

title: What a Landlord Need Not Disclose
bodyText: Arizona bars any criminal, civil or administrative action against a lessor for failing to disclose that the property is or was the site of a natural death, suicide, homicide or other felony; was owned or occupied by a person with HIV, AIDS or another disease not known to spread through common occupancy; or is near a sex offender. Failing to disclose these facts is not grounds to terminate or rescind a lease.

title: Landlord's Remedies After a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: An Arizona landlord may recover all reasonable damages from the tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, court costs, reasonable attorney fees and all quantifiable damage the tenant caused to the property, and after termination may claim possession, rent and separate actual damages. The landlord must mitigate damages. If a tenant abandons, the landlord must make reasonable efforts to rerent at a fair rental; the lease ends when a new tenancy begins, or, if the landlord does not try to rerent or accepts the abandonment as a surrender, when the landlord learns of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the remaining term for this purpose is one month or one week. A tenant who willfully holds over in bad faith owes up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages. A tenant who ends a lease by falsely claiming domestic violence and is convicted owes treble damages, and the person named in the order or report who provoked the termination is liable to the landlord for the resulting economic losses.

title: Foreclosure Notices to Tenants
bodyText:
If an Arizona owner receives a notice of trustee's sale or other foreclosure notice after a tenant has signed a lease, the owner must give the tenant written notice of the possible foreclosure, in the statutory form, within five business days. This applies only to the first such notice received after the lease was signed, and does not apply to multifamily units of four or more connected units.

If the owner fails to give the notice (or the move-in notice required for a lease signed after foreclosure began), the tenant may give a notice of landlord noncompliance and recover damages and injunctive relief, and the deposit must be returned. If a foreclosure action began before the lease is signed, include the statutory notice with the lease; the lease's Notice of Possible Foreclosure clause carries its text.

title: Rules, Regulations and Lease Amendments
bodyText: An Arizona landlord's rules bind a tenant only if they promote tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abuse or fairly distribute services; are reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; are explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; do not evade the landlord's obligations; and the tenant had notice of them when signing. A rule adopted later binds the tenant on 30 days' notice if it does not substantially modify the lease. When a government adopts a new law affecting existing leases, the landlord may amend leases immediately to comply, with written notice describing the amendment and its effective date.

title: No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets no dollar cap on late fees or rental application fees. A late fee must be reasonable and stated in a written lease: only a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease can be required to reinstate a lease before an eviction is filed, and the eviction judgment includes late charges stated in the lease.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not require a landlord to hold security deposits in a separate or interest-bearing account or to pay interest on them. During the tenancy a landlord may use refundable deposits as any applicable property management agreement allows, but all refundable deposits must be refunded under the deposit statute at the end of the tenancy.

title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no rent-increase notice statute and no cap on increases, and local rent control is preempted. Rent is set by the lease; during a fixed term it cannot be changed without the tenant's agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord generally changes the rent by giving the 30-day written notice that would end the tenancy. A rent increase in retaliation for a code complaint, a repair complaint to the landlord, or tenant organizing is prohibited, and a complaint within six months before the increase creates a presumption of retaliation.

title: City Rental Tax Repealed: No Pass-Through
bodyText: Since January 1, 2025, no Arizona city, town or other taxing jurisdiction may levy a transaction privilege or similar tax on renting residential property. The law that repealed the tax also removed the landlord's former statutory right to adjust rent on 30 days' notice when a city changed its rental tax rate, so a lease clause invoking that right no longer has a legal basis. Through December 31, 2026, a landlord may not charge a tenant the amount of the repealed tax, and in any lawsuit the landlord must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that a challenged charge, assessment or other amount does not represent all or part of the repealed tax. Do not add a 'tax', 'fee' or other line item that replaces the old city rental tax.

title: No Drug-Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Arizona no longer has a statute requiring a residential landlord to disclose, post notice of, or refrain from renting a property that was used as a clandestine drug laboratory; the former law was repealed in 2016. A landlord's general duty to keep the property fit and habitable and to comply with building, housing and health codes still applies to any contamination.

title: Foreign Adversary Land Ownership and Lease Ban
bodyText: Since September 12, 2026, Arizona bars a foreign adversary nation or its agent from buying, leasing or otherwise obtaining a substantial interest in Arizona real property, directly or through an entity. The law targets foreign governments, state-owned or state-controlled companies, and entities tied to countries identified on federal national-security lists. It is enforced by the Attorney General, not by landlords. Whether it reaches an ordinary residential lease to an individual tenant is unsettled, and no official guidance exists. Do not screen applicants by citizenship or national origin: that exposes a landlord to fair-housing claims, and the statute itself says enforcement may not be based on race or national origin. If an applicant is a foreign government or a company it controls, get legal advice before signing.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A security deposit refund that a tenant never claims or cashes does not become the landlord's money. Under Arizona's unclaimed property law, a security deposit, refund or credit balance is property that is presumed abandoned three years after the owner's right to demand it or the landlord's obligation to pay it arises, and is then handled under the unclaimed property law administered by the Arizona Department of Revenue.

title: No Mold Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose mold or to remediate it as a separate duty. Mold in a rental is handled through the landlord's general duty to comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the premises fit and habitable.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not require a residential landlord to test for or disclose radon. The only statutory reference to radon zones in a real estate context is an optional third-party disclosure report a buyer or seller may order in a sale.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not give a residential tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental and do not require a landlord to allow one.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not require or forbid a residential landlord to ask about or verify a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. Federal and Arizona fair housing laws still bar discrimination based on national origin, so screening questions should be applied the same way to every applicant. A tenant whose belongings are held after an abandonment may retrieve identification and immigration documents without paying storage costs.

title: No Statewide Source-of-Income Rule
bodyText: Arizona state law does not prohibit a landlord from refusing a housing voucher or other lawful source of income. Some Arizona cities have adopted local ordinances that do; check local law before declining a voucher. Accepting a government housing assistance payment is not accepting a partial payment and does not waive the landlord's rights.

title: Servicemembers: Lease Protections
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act has no rule letting a servicemember end a lease of an apartment or house early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs that. Separately, Arizona law gives members of the National Guard and the armed forces reserves who are ordered to active duty or training by Arizona, another state or the United States the protections that federal servicemember civil-relief law gives people on federal active duty. That can reach Guard members serving on state orders, whom federal law alone may not cover. When a tenant presents military orders with a request to end the lease or pause an eviction, get legal advice before refusing it. Arizona's only military rule inside the landlord-tenant statutes is for mobile home park spaces.

title: Holding Deposits and Earnest Money
bodyText: Arizona statutes have no rule written for holding deposits, earnest money or other money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed. Two rules in the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bear on it. First, once the lease is signed, money applied to deposits or prepaid rent counts toward the limit on all security, however named, of one and one-half months' rent (a tenant may still choose to prepay more rent). Second, the landlord must state in writing the purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit, and any fee or deposit not designated nonrefundable is refundable. The statutes do not say whether that rule reaches money taken before a lease exists, so a landlord who means to keep a holding deposit if the applicant backs out should say so in writing, with the amount and purpose, before taking it. A real estate broker who takes earnest money on a lease must state in the lease or receipt what form it took (cash, check, promissory note or other item of value) and place it in the designated broker's care.

title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText:
Before a private towing company may remove a vehicle from an Arizona rental property without the vehicle owner's permission, the property owner or the owner's agent must authorize the tow in writing, either by signing each towing order or by a written towing contract that runs for a specific period. The towing company cannot act as the owner's agent, and a tow without that authorization (or a law enforcement request) is a crime for the towing company.

Inside a city or town, the owner is treated as allowing unrestricted public parking in any parking area unless signs, clearly visible and readable from anywhere in the parking area and at each entrance, state the parking restrictions, what happens to vehicles that violate them, the maximum cost to the vehicle's owner including storage and other charges, and the phone number and address where the vehicle can be found.

Cities and counties may cap private towing rates. Abandoned and junk vehicles follow separate motor-vehicle procedures. Check your city's towing rules before relying on the lease's towing clause.

title: Selling a Rented Property
bodyText: When an Arizona landlord sells a rented dwelling in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, the seller is released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after the seller gives the tenant written notice of the sale, unless the parties agreed otherwise. The seller stays liable to the tenant for the security deposit and prepaid rent the tenant is entitled to get back, and whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is also bound by the deposit-return rules. A property manager whose management ends is likewise released only after written notice to the tenant. The owner and manager disclosure given to the tenant must be kept current, and the new owner's information must be on file with the county assessor. Showing the unit to buyers requires at least two days' notice to the tenant unless it is impracticable.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease by at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and security, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If a person's failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover from that person up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages. If possession is delivered but the property isn't in the condition Arizona law requires, rent doesn't abate on that account; the tenant has the remedies for landlord noncompliance instead (A.R.S. 33-1362).

title: Domestic Violence or Sexual Assault: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence as A.R.S. 13-3601 defines it (a listed offense committed by, for example, a current or former spouse, household member, relative, co-parent or current or former romantic partner), or of sexual assault in the tenant's dwelling, may end the lease with written notice requesting release, a mutually agreed release date within 30 days, and either a copy of a protective order issued to the tenant or a written law enforcement report that the tenant reported being a victim, if the events happened within the 30 days before the notice (you may waive that limit) (A.R.S. 33-1318). You may ask in writing for the name and address of the person named in the order or report, if the tenant knows it. The tenant owes only rent through the termination date and earlier obligations, payable by move-out, and no future rent, penalty or fee; you may keep prepaid rent for the final month and may not withhold the deposit because of the early termination (only for damage from failure to maintain). If there are several tenants, all tenancies end, and non-victim tenants other than the named person may be released and allowed a new lease if they qualify. The victim may require a new lock at their cost; you may rekey or replace it, keep a key, and refuse a key to the named person, and may not let that person in to reclaim property after they've been served with an order of protection you've received, unless a law enforcement officer escorts them. A law enforcement officer protected by a recent harassment injunction may end the lease the same way after repaying lease concessions received. None of this limits your right to terminate for unrelated reasons.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText:
If fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the property, the tenant may move out immediately and tell you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value (A.R.S. 33-1366).

If the lease ends, return all recoverable security and account for rent as of the date the tenant vacated all or part of the property. This right states no exception for damage the tenant caused, and a lease cannot take it away; see Tenant-Caused Damage for what the landlord can recover.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: Arizona's Rules of Procedure for Eviction Actions put several duties on a landlord who files an eviction. The complaint must state the specific reason for the eviction and when and how the notice was served, attach the notice, and be verified. A money claim must state the rent, the due dates, how late fees are calculated, the amounts due and any rent concession claimed. A nonpayment complaint must tell the tenant how to reinstate before judgment, and the landlord must serve the lease provisions the eviction relies on and, in a nonpayment case, the last six months of the tenant's charges and payments. A landlord who accepted a partial payment must show the court the partial-payment agreement the tenant signed, or the case is dismissed. The court awards late fees and other periodic fees only if a written lease specifies them, and attorney fees only where a statute or written contract provides for them, never more than the landlord paid or agreed to pay. A property manager may not represent the owner in court unless the manager is a lawyer. After a default judgment the landlord must mail or deliver a copy to the tenant. The landlord has 45 days after a judgment for possession to apply for a writ without explaining the delay. If the landlord later concludes the eviction was not valid, it must promptly move to set the judgment aside. Once a judgment is paid in full, the landlord must file a satisfaction of judgment within 30 days under the court rule (the statutes say 40 days) and serve a copy on the tenant; a landlord who does not answer a tenant's motion to compel satisfaction within 15 days risks having the case sealed.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Arizona has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (10 days' notice for a week-to-week tenancy), with no reason required, and a fixed-term lease ends on its expiration date; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational: a landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint, repair complaint, or joining or organizing a tenants' union or similar organization (a complaint within the prior six months creates a presumption of retaliation); fair housing law applies; and the domestic-violence statute preserves eviction of a victim for actions unrelated to the violence. Arizona has no condominium-conversion notice for apartments and no rule barring eviction while rent is paid into court. Mobile home parks have their own termination rules.

title: Electronic Notices and Signatures
bodyText:
Arizona's Electronic Transactions Act lets an electronic record or signature satisfy a law that requires a writing or a signature, but only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and either party may refuse to do a later transaction electronically.

A notice the law requires in writing can be sent electronically only in a form the recipient can print and store; a record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing cannot be enforced against the recipient. Where a law sets a delivery method, the electronic record must still go by that method: an abandonment notice, for example, must be sent by certified mail and posted.

Arizona's landlord-tenant act treats a notice as received when it comes to the tenant's attention or is delivered in hand or mailed by registered or certified mail; email is not one of the listed methods, so an emailed notice rests on proof that it reached the tenant.

A lease signed on paper may authorize doing business electronically only through the tenant's separate and express agreement that says which parts will be electronic and how, gives an email address, and promises to report a change. The Act has no special exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage
bodyText: If a tenant, a family member or a guest damages the property, Arizona law makes the tenant responsible. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and the landlord may recover all reasonable damages from the breach and all quantifiable damage the tenant caused to the premises, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Where the damage materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, the landlord may give 14 days' written notice, then do the work and bill it as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. The tenant's own repair remedies do not apply to a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused: no termination for the landlord's breach, no repair-and-deduct, and no essential-services remedies. The fire and casualty section is different. It lets a tenant leave, or pay reduced rent for the part that can't be used, after damage that substantially impairs enjoyment, and it states no exception for damage the tenant caused; a lease cannot take that right away. Whether rent lost after a tenant leaves under that section counts as damages the landlord can recover is not settled by statute.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not regulate using algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Federal antitrust law and any city ordinance may still apply.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act defines rent as the payments made to the landlord in full consideration for the rented premises, so late fees and other charges are not rent unless a statute treats them that way. One does: if a tenant doesn't fix a maintenance problem after the landlord's 14-day notice, the landlord's repair cost can be billed as rent on the next rent due date. The 5-day nonpayment notice covers rent only, but to reinstate before an eviction is filed the tenant must also pay a reasonable late fee set out in a written lease. In an eviction, the court awards late charges only if a written lease specifies them, and other periodic charges (such as extra-person, pet, storage, signage or common-area fees) only if a written lease specifies them and they are collected periodically with rent; anything else must be sued for separately. A partial payment of rent or other charges keeps the landlord's eviction rights only with the tenant's contemporaneous signed agreement.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to keep up the unit materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, an Arizona landlord may give written notice that describes the problem and asks the tenant to fix it within 14 days, or as promptly as an emergency requires. If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and bill the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value, as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. This is one of the few entries the access statute allows without the tenant's consent. No lease clause is needed for this right.

title: Complete, Signed Lease Copies
bodyText: A written Arizona lease must have every blank space completed, and the landlord must give the tenant a signed copy, with the tenant returning one fully signed copy, within a reasonable time after it is signed. Failing to do either is a material noncompliance with the lease by whichever party failed. Before signing, make sure every blank, bracket and placeholder in the lease is filled in or struck.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Enjoyment Covenant
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession. It protects possession in other ways: a landlord may not lock out a tenant, remove belongings or cut essential services, and owes the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages for an unlawful ouster; an unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages of at least one month's rent. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in an Arizona lease is a question of case law.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Arizona prescribes few forms for residential landlords. The one lease form is the foreclosure notice: a lease signed after a foreclosure action has started must include a notice substantially in the statute's words, and the same notice goes to existing tenants within five business days after the owner receives a first notice of trustee's sale (not for buildings of four or more connected units). The pool safety notice is a Department of Health Services document, not statutory text. No form is required for eviction notices: courts and agencies may not require a mandatory or technical form, and a notice that meets the statute's content requirements is enough. In court, the eviction summons must include the Arizona Supreme Court's Residential Eviction Information Sheet on a separate page.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Arizona statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern.

title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act makes deception, false promises, misrepresentation and concealment of material facts in the sale or advertisement of merchandise unlawful. Merchandise includes real estate, and a sale expressly includes leases and rentals of real estate subject to a deed restriction imposed in an earlier sale; whether the Act reaches other residential leases depends on case law. The Act has no list of specific lease practices such as blanks filled in after signing. Arizona's landlord-tenant act covers those directly by requiring a completed lease and a signed copy. Arizona has no plain-language statute for leases.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Arizona makes counties, and cities and towns of more than 75,000 people, allow accessory dwelling units (ADUs). Each must allow at least one attached and one detached ADU as a permitted use on any lot where a single-family home is allowed. Neither may forbid you to use or advertise the main home or the ADU as separately leased long-term rental housing (a lease of 90 days or longer, or month to month). Neither may require the ADU's occupant to be related to, married to or employed by the owner or occupant of the main home. These rules don't apply on tribal land or on some land near military and public airports, and they don't override building, fire and health codes. Short-term rentals are different: a city, town or county may require you to live on the property if you rent it as a vacation or short-term rental and it has an ADU whose certificate of occupancy, certificate of completion or similar final approval was issued on or after September 14, 2024. An ADU rented as a home is a dwelling unit, so the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to it in full. It counts as a single family residence only if it has direct access to a street and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility with the main home; that matters for which repair tasks a tenant may take on in writing. A smaller city's own zoning rules still decide what it allows; check them before you build or rent.

title: Foreclosure and Other Claims Against the Property
bodyText: In Arizona the notice duty on a foreclosure runs from you to the tenant. If a foreclosure action on the property began before the lease is signed, you must include the statutory notice of possible foreclosure with the rental agreement (the Notice of Possible Foreclosure clause carries its form). If you receive a notice of trustee's sale or other notice of foreclosure after the tenant has signed, you must give the tenant that written notice within five business days after you receive it; this applies only to the first such notice after the lease was signed. If you don't give a required notice, the tenant may give you a written notice of noncompliance under the landlord-tenant act and recover damages and get an injunction, and the security deposit must be returned. These rules don't apply to multifamily rental units of four or more connected units. A trustee also posts the notice of sale on the property at least 20 days before the sale, so a tenant may see it. Going the other way, we found no Arizona statute that requires a tenant to tell you about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property, or that voids a tenant's agreement to hold the property under a rival claimant. If you want the tenant to pass such papers on to you, the lease must say so; the shared clause on notice of proceedings against the property does that.

title: Substitute Housing When Essential Services Fail
bodyText: Arizona gives the tenant a substitute-housing remedy; it does not make you find or pay for other housing on your own. If, contrary to the rental agreement or your duty to keep the unit fit, you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, gas or electric service, reasonable hot water, heat, air-conditioning or cooling where installed and offered, or essential services, the tenant may give you reasonable notice of the breach and choose one remedy. One choice is to move to reasonable substitute housing while the failure lasts. The tenant then owes no rent for that period. If the substitute housing costs more than the rent, the tenant may recover the excess, on proof of payment, up to 25% of the rent excused. If your failure was deliberate, the tenant may also recover the reasonable cost or value of the substitute housing, up to one period's rent. The tenant who chooses this remedy can't also use the termination notice or repair-and-deduct remedy for the same breach (except for damages before choosing), and the right doesn't arise until the tenant gives you notice, or at all if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent. A lease can't contain terms contrary to these rules. We found no Arizona statute that requires you to provide or pay for alternate housing or relocation during repairs, after a fire or casualty, or after a code order. After a fire or casualty, the tenant's options are to end the lease or pay reduced rent for the usable part.

title: A Tenant's Animal Left Without Care
bodyText:
Arizona gives you a way to deal with a tenant's animal in two situations and limits your entry otherwise.

First, if the tenant dies or is otherwise incapacitated: you may ask the tenant to name, and keep updated, a person authorized to enter and retrieve the tenant's property, including an animal (the optional Authorized Person clause records this).

That person must show you government-issued identification before removing anything. If you can't reach the person at the address and phone number given, or the person doesn't respond within one day after your first written contact, you may treat the animal as abandoned and release it to an animal shelter or boarding facility. You may release the animal to a relative of the tenant if no authorized person was named, the contact information is no longer valid, or you can't reach the authorized person after one calendar day.

Second, if the tenant has abandoned the unit: once you retake it, you don't have to store the tenant's animals. After notifying any authorized person and waiting one calendar day without a retrieval, you may remove and release the animals to a shelter or boarding facility; keep a record of its name and location. If you don't release them, you must give them reasonable care for the 14-day holding period, or, if you can't or won't, notify the county enforcement agent or an animal control officer so the animals can be seized. You aren't liable for good-faith actions in removing, releasing, seizing or caring for abandoned animals under these rules.

Outside these cases, the act gives you no right to enter just to care for an animal: your access rests on the tenant's consent, an emergency, a court order, abandonment or surrender, or the act's repair remedy, and except in an emergency you must give at least two days' notice.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText:
Arizona makes you keep in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply. You aren't required to supply a particular appliance, and an appliance the tenant brings is the tenant's.

But the act doesn't say what "supplied" means for an item you leave in the unit, and it defines the premises to include the existing facilities and appurtenances in the unit. A lease can't excuse or limit your liability arising under law. So a clause saying you leave an appliance but won't repair it may not protect you. The safe course is to remove anything you won't maintain before the tenancy starts, and to list in the lease the appliances you do supply.

Heat, running water, hot water and air-conditioning or cooling where installed and offered must be supplied unless they come from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own direct utility connection, or the building isn't required by law to have them.

If you want the tenant to take over upkeep of an appliance, use a written tenant-maintenance agreement that meets the act's conditions: for a single family residence, a written agreement supported by adequate consideration and made in good faith; for any other unit, a separate signed writing, also supported by adequate consideration and made in good faith, that doesn't affect your duties to other tenants. Neither kind of agreement may cover work needed to meet the building code or keep the unit fit and habitable.

We found no Arizona statute that presumes an appliance left in the unit is supplied, or that sets its own rule for excluding appliances.

title: No Duty to Disclose Association Documents in the Lease
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a planned community to disclose the association's rules or obligations, or to give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules. Arizona's association statutes regulate what the association may ask of you when you rent. You may rent your unit unless the declaration prohibits it, and you must follow the declaration's rental time period restrictions. The association may require only the names and contact information of adult occupants, the lease period with its start and end dates, and a description and the license plate numbers of the tenants' vehicles (and photo identification showing age in an age-restricted community). It may not demand the tenant's application, credit report or lease, or make the tenant sign a waiver of due process rights. You may designate an agent in writing to handle association matters for the rental. If your lease makes the tenant follow association rules, give the tenant a current copy of them at signing so the tenant knows what they are; the law doesn't require it, but a tenant can't easily follow rules the tenant has never seen.

title: No Automatic-Renewal Rule for Leases
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that regulates an automatic-renewal clause in a residential lease: none requires special type, a separate signature or a reminder notice before the lease renews, and Arizona's held consumer statutes have no general automatic-renewal law that reaches leases. The general rules apply. A lease may include terms not prohibited by the landlord-tenant act or other law, including the term of the agreement. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly). The act's definition of the term of a lease includes any renewal or extension of the written rental agreement. Once a renewal runs month to month, either party may end it by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice. If the tenant stays after the term ends and you consent in writing, the tenancy becomes month-to-month unless you fix a new term. Every duty under the act must be performed in good faith, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. If you use a renewal clause, say plainly how long each renewal lasts, how and when either party can opt out, and what rent applies; a reminder before the opt-out deadline is good practice but not required by statute.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to inspect balconies, decks, stairways or other exterior elevated elements on a set schedule, or to report on them. Arizona's statutes mention balconies only in the condominium act, which treats a balcony serving one unit as a limited common element allocated to that unit unless the declaration says otherwise. Your general duties still cover them: you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable, and keep all common areas clean and safe. Check balconies, railings and stairs yourself at turnover and after storms, fix what you find, and check your city's building and property maintenance codes, which this research did not cover.

title: No Alarm-Tampering Fee Rule: Charge Your Actual Cost
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that sets, allows or forbids a fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm.

What Arizona does say: where a smoke detector was installed under the state smoke detector law (in a new unit, or when a sleeping area is remodeled under a local permit), the tenant must maintain it and keep it working unless the tenant tells you in writing that it is malfunctioning, and then you must repair it. You must give the tenant written notice of those responsibilities (the Smoke Detectors clause does this). A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage, impair or remove any part of the premises.

You may recover all reasonable damages resulting from the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or those duties, and all quantifiable damage the tenant causes to the premises.

The safe course is to charge the documented cost of repairing or replacing a tampered alarm, not a flat penalty; a fixed charge for a breach raises the questions covered under the liquidated-damages topic. A disabled alarm may also be a noncompliance materially affecting health and safety, for which the act allows a five-day notice to remedy.

title: Marijuana in Arizona Rentals
bodyText:
Arizona has two marijuana laws, and they treat landlords differently.

Adult use: adults 21 and over may possess up to one ounce, and may grow up to six plants at their primary residence (no more than 12 where two or more adults live) in a locked, enclosed area not visible from public view. That law does not restrict a private person or business that owns or controls property from prohibiting or regulating that conduct on the property. So your lease may ban adult-use smoking, vaping, growing or possession on your property.

Medical use: you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for being a registered cardholder, unless not doing so would cost you a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations. The medical law says nothing requires a person in lawful possession of property to let a guest, client, customer or other visitor use marijuana there, but it says nothing of the kind about a tenant, and the adult-use law expressly doesn't limit a qualifying patient's rights. Neither law lets anyone smoke marijuana in a public place.

Before you ban a cardholder's non-smoked medical use or possession inside the unit, or treat lawful marijuana as a drug-related breach, get legal advice; no statute settles those questions.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your lease can't take away the tenant's casualty rights or your duty to mitigate, because both are in Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and a lease may not make the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the act. Casualty: if fire or casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out at once and give written notice within 14 days ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if staying is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; if the lease ends you must return all recoverable security. Mitigation: under the act the injured party must mitigate damages, and if a tenant abandons the unit you must make reasonable efforts to rerent it at a fair rental. A lease term that says otherwise is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a prohibited term the tenant may recover actual damages and up to two months' rent. A lease may add rights for you that don't cut into the tenant's, such as an optional right to end the lease after a casualty you didn't cause.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to show or give a tenant a certificate of occupancy, or that makes a lease void or rent uncollectible because a unit lacks one. Arizona's statutes treat certificates of occupancy as part of city and county permitting, development fees and taxes. What does reach you: you must comply with applicable building codes materially affecting health and safety, and the state list of such conditions includes improper occupancy, meaning space occupied for living, sleeping, cooking or dining that wasn't designed and permitted for that use, or occupied beyond the maximum occupancy the building code or state law allows. So don't rent a garage, shed or other conversion as a home unless it was permitted for living. Where a city or town finds an interior inspection reasonably necessary under its rental inspection rules and the tenant has moved out, it may require another inspection and its approval before a new occupancy. Check your city or county code for any local certificate or inspection requirement.

title: Children and Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Arizona doesn't require a lease to say anything about children, but it limits what you may do about them. Under the landlord-tenant act, knowingly refusing to rent a dwelling to someone because they have children, or advertising a no-children restriction, is a petty offense, and the person harmed may sue for an injunction, actual damages, a civil penalty of three times the monthly rent if the violation was intentional, and court costs and attorney fees. Under the Arizona Fair Housing Act you may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, conditions or privileges, because of familial status, which covers a person who is pregnant, lives with a child under 18 as parent or legal custodian (or with the custodian's written permission), or is getting legal custody of a child. That protection doesn't end once the lease is signed, so don't treat a new baby or a child joining the household as a breach in itself. You may limit occupancy by reasonable standards that apply to people of all ages and that you adopted and published before the situation arose; a limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable. Housing for older persons may exclude children, and if your property qualifies you must not rent it to people with children living with them; a valid restrictive covenant against people with children binds you only in a building of four or fewer units where the owner lives in one of them. Some small landlords are exempt from the Fair Housing Act's rental rules, but not from the landlord-tenant act's children rule.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacating Notice Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a tenant to give you notice before moving out or leaving the unit empty in cold weather, or that sets any freeze-protection duty for a vacating tenant. The general rules apply. The tenant must use the heating and plumbing in a reasonable manner and must promptly notify you in writing of any situation that requires you to make repairs. You must supply reasonable heat when seasonal weather requires it, where the building is required to have it, unless the heat comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own direct utility connection. If you want advance notice of a winter move-out or a long absence, or want the tenant to leave the heat on at a set level, put that in the lease; for property left after an abandonment, follow the act's abandonment procedure.

title: No Specific Common-Area Lighting Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets a lighting standard for hallways, stairways, parking areas or other common areas of a rental, or that addresses charging a tenant for common-area lights wired to the tenant's electric service. The general rules apply. You must keep all common areas clean and safe, and you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety; the state list of such conditions includes a lack of required adequate electricity and lighting as required by the building code. Keep common-area lights working and fix outages promptly. If any common-area light runs through a tenant's meter, say so in the lease and handle it under the utility-billing rules covered by the utility topics; never shift a landlord-provided utility to the tenant mid-lease without the tenant's written consent.

title: No Rent Bar Tied to Condemnation
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that bars you from collecting rent once a government agency condemns, placards or orders the vacating of a rental unit. The tenant's other remedies do the work instead. If fire or casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If your noncompliance with your maintenance duties materially affects health and safety, the tenant may give a five-day written notice and end the lease if you don't fix it. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply essential services, the tenant may move to substitute housing and owes no rent while the failure lasts. And in a suit for rent or possession the tenant may counterclaim for what you owe under the act. An older general landlord-tenant statute says a tenant whose building is destroyed or so damaged, without the tenant's fault, as to be untenantable owes no further rent unless a written agreement expressly says otherwise and may quit the premises; for a dwelling unit, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs where the two conflict. Where a government order makes the unit unlawful to occupy, expect the tenant to use these remedies, and don't count on rent for that period.

title: Habitability: What Arizona Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Arizona compares on habitability features found in other states. Present: (1) a statutory duty to comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain supplied facilities and appliances, provide trash receptacles and removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat and cooling where installed and offered, with a state list of conditions that materially affect health and safety; (2) a non-waiver rule: a lease can't make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act, though for a single family residence, and in a separate signed writing for other units, the tenant may take on specified tasks in good faith for adequate consideration, never the code and fitness duties; (3) termination after written notice: five days for a health-and-safety noncompliance, ten days for other material noncompliance, plus damages and an injunction; (4) repair-and-deduct for minor defects costing less than the greater of $300 or half a month's rent, after written notice and ten days, by a licensed contractor with an itemized statement and lien waiver; (5) essential-services remedies: buy the service and deduct it, damages for lost rental value, or substitute housing with no rent owed; (6) a counterclaim in a rent or possession case, with the court able to order rent paid into court. The termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies don't apply to a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent. Absent: (7) no right for the tenant to withhold rent on the tenant's own; the act forbids withholding not authorized by the act; (8) no numeric indoor heat or cooling temperature standard; (9) no mold, radon, asbestos or carbon monoxide alarm statute for landlords; (10) no balcony inspection or specific common-area lighting rule. The absences rest on the statutes and searches described in each topic's own row.

title: Other Rules Arizona Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some other states for which we found no Arizona statute. (1) Rent reporting: no Arizona statute requires, limits or sets notice for reporting a tenant's rent payments to a credit bureau; Arizona's credit-reporting statutes deal with security freezes, report corrections and permissible uses, and one bars a rental-purchase lessor of goods from certain reporting, which doesn't reach a home lease. (2) Government shutdowns and delayed benefits: no Arizona statute gives a tenant extra time or a defense when a paycheck or government benefit is delayed by a shutdown or furlough; the usual nonpayment rules apply. Each of these is also absent and explained in its own row: no rule letting the lease add a notice method; no duty on the tenant to tell you about claims against the property; no alarm-tampering fee rule; no asbestos rule; no automatic-renewal rule; no balcony inspection rule; no duty to disclose association documents; no certificate of occupancy disclosure; no cold-weather vacating notice; no specific common-area lighting rule; no lease-arbitration statute; no state approval for leases of tribal land; and no rent bar tied to condemnation.

title: No Agreed Notice Method: Use the Statute's Delivery Rules
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets you and the tenant agree in the lease on an extra way of giving notice, such as a text message or email, that then counts as delivery of a notice the law requires. The landlord-tenant act's own notice rule controls. You give notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the tenant in the ordinary course. The tenant receives it when it comes to the tenant's attention, or when it is delivered in hand or sent by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has named for notices (or, if none, the tenant's last known residence). Notice sent by registered or certified mail counts as received on the day it actually arrives or five days after mailing, whichever is first. Where a statute names a method for a particular notice, use that method. Arizona's Electronic Transactions Act lets an electronic record meet a writing requirement only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, and it doesn't replace a delivery method another law prescribes. Federal law adds a limit of its own: the general rule of the federal electronic-signatures law (15 U.S.C. § 7001) doesn't apply to a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a tenant's primary residence. A text or email is a useful extra copy, but for a notice that starts a deadline, deliver it in hand or by registered or certified mail and keep proof. Your lease may name the address where each party takes notices.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Arizona Leases
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that deals specifically with arbitration clauses in residential leases or with arbitrating eviction cases. Arizona's Revised Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, except on a ground that exists at law or in equity for revoking a contract. Before a dispute arises, a party can't give up the right to be represented by a lawyer in the arbitration. The landlord-tenant act adds two limits that matter here. A lease can't make the tenant waive or give up rights or remedies under the act, and a prohibited term is unenforceable; if you knowingly use one, the tenant may recover actual damages and up to two months' rent. And the act's rights are enforceable by action, which it defines to include any proceeding in which rights are determined, including an action for possession. Federal law also makes a written arbitration provision in a contract evidencing a transaction involving commerce valid, irrevocable and enforceable, except on grounds that exist for revoking any contract. Whether a lease arbitration clause is a forbidden waiver of the act's remedies, and whether the federal rule reaches a residential lease and overrides that bar, are questions no statute answers. The cautious course is not to put a binding arbitration clause in a residential lease, and this library does not offer one for Arizona. If you want one anyway, have a lawyer draft it, keep it mutual, and leave eviction (possession) cases and the tenant's statutory remedies in court.

title: No Asbestos Rule for Landlords
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to test for asbestos, tell a tenant or applicant about it, or remove it. Arizona's asbestos statutes deal with injury lawsuits, disease reporting, waste handling and an educational pamphlet for contractors. Your general duties still apply: you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, and make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable. If you know of damaged or crumbling material that may contain asbestos, have it assessed and handled by qualified people, and don't let repairs or renovations disturb it without proper precautions. Federal asbestos rules for demolition and renovation don't cover residential buildings with four or fewer dwelling units (unless the building has a loft used as a dwelling or was covered by the rules before). For a larger building, whoever owns, leases or controls the building or the work must, before a demolition or renovation starts, have the affected part thoroughly inspected for asbestos. If the work is a demolition, or a renovation that disturbs at least 260 linear feet of the regulated asbestos material on pipes, 160 square feet on other parts of the building or 35 cubic feet off them, the owner or operator must also give written notice of the work to the federal environmental regulator and follow the rule's other requirements. The rest of the federal rule and any state or county asbestos rules weren't researched here.
