title: Leases on Tribal Land
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a state officer to approve a lease of tribal, communal or Native-owned land before it is valid. The reason is constitutional: in the Arizona Constitution the people of the state disclaim all right and title to lands owned or held by any Indian or Indian tribe whose title came through or from the United States or a prior sovereign, and those lands remain under the absolute jurisdiction and control of Congress until that title is extinguished. Leasing on tribal land is therefore a matter of federal and tribal law. Federal law lets restricted Indian lands, whether owned by a tribe or by an individual, be leased by the Indian owners for residential and other purposes with the approval of the Secretary of the Interior, under the terms and regulations the Secretary prescribes. Those regulations and tribal law weren't researched here. Arizona's accessory-dwelling-unit rules expressly don't apply on tribal land. If you are renting a home on a reservation or on land held in trust, find out before signing what federal and tribal approvals, forms and eviction procedures apply.

title: Checked Across the Whole Arizona Code
bodyText: Three things landlords ask about, checked outside the landlord-tenant act. (1) Squatters: Arizona has a specific remedy. A property owner, or the owner's authorized agent, may bring a forcible detainer case against an unauthorized person unlawfully occupying residential property who refuses a reasonable request to leave, if the property was not open to the public when the person entered, the person is not a current or former tenant there, had no prior agreement to live there with the owner, is not an immediate family member of the owner, and no other case is pending between them. The writ of restitution issues immediately after the court signs a judgment. This route doesn't apply to landlords and tenants under the landlord-tenant act. Separately, a guest of your tenant who isn't named on a written lease and who knowingly stays without your or the tenant's permission may be removed by a law enforcement officer at your or the tenant's request (see the unauthorized-occupant removal row). (2) Rent receipts: see the rent receipts row. (3) Registration before an eviction: we found no Arizona statute that makes registration of the rental with the county assessor a condition of filing an eviction or winning a judgment for possession. Registration is still required: residential rental property may not be occupied unless your information is on file with the assessor, a tenant may end the lease after a ten-day notice to comply that you don't meet and get back all prepaid rent, and cities and towns may impose civil penalties (see the rental registration row). Keep your registration current. One other registration can stop an eviction: an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation doing business in Arizona may not maintain a lawsuit, including an eviction, in an Arizona court until it registers with the Arizona Corporation Commission (A.R.S. §§ 10-1502(A), 29-3902(B)); owning property, without more, is not doing business, but whether renting it out is more is a case-law question (A.R.S. §§ 10-1501(B)(9), 29-3905(A)(10); see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-az). The missing registration doesn't void the lease or stop the company from defending a suit (A.R.S. §§ 10-1502(E), 29-3902(C)). Trade-name registration is optional in Arizona, and we found no rule barring a suit by an unregistered trade-name user (A.R.S. § 44-1460).

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Arizona's mechanics' lien law gives everyone who labors or furnishes professional services, materials, machinery, fixtures or tools in building, altering or repairing a building a lien on that building, whether the work was done at the request of the owner or the owner's agent. Every contractor or other person in charge of the work is treated as the owner's agent, and the owner is liable for the reasonable value of labor or materials furnished to that agent.

For the preliminary twenty-day notice that most lien claimants must serve, the owner includes a lessee who causes the work to be done.

We found no Arizona statute that says when work your tenant orders binds your own interest, that treats your consent to a tenant's alteration as consent to a lien, or that lets a lease clause or a posted or recorded notice keep your interest free of liens for tenant work; Arizona's "no lien" notice is only for owners of mines worked under a lease.

A lease term can't protect you against the contractors themselves: an owner can't, by any term of a contract, waive or impair other people's lien claims. The protection for owner-occupied homes doesn't help either, because it covers only an owner who lives in the home and doesn't intend to sell or lease it.

If you receive a preliminary twenty-day notice for your tenant's work, read it: it warns that unpaid bills can lead to a lien and foreclosure, and you have ten days to correct any wrong information in it or lose that defense.

Practical steps: require your written consent before any tenant work, require the tenant to pay its contractors and collect lien waivers and releases in the statutory forms, and require the tenant to get any lien released at its own expense (see the optional no-liens clause).

title: No Condominium Conversion Notice for Tenants
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to notify tenants before converting a rental building to condominiums or a cooperative, gives tenants a right to buy their units, limits evictions during a conversion, requires a conversion statement in the lease, or bars converting rental housing to hotel or short-term use. What Arizona requires is disclosure to buyers: if a condominium is a conversion from multifamily rental, the declaration must say so and give the date original construction was completed, the original owner, builder, developer and general contractor, and each later owner, and the notice filed with the state real estate commissioner for the subdivision must say it is a conversion and give the construction date. Ending current tenancies for a conversion follows the ordinary rules, with no conversion exception: a month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date, a week-to-week tenancy on 10 days' written notice, and a lease for a definite term can be ended early only as the lease and the act allow. Mobile home parks are different: a park landlord must give the state housing director and every tenant written notice at least 180 days before a change in use.

title: Cure Periods and No-Cure Breaches
bodyText:
Arizona sets the notice periods for a tenant's breach.

Unpaid rent: a written notice of nonpayment and of your intent to end the lease if rent isn't paid within five days.

Other material noncompliance with the lease, including material falsification of the rental application: a written notice naming the acts and omissions that make up the breach and saying the lease will end at least 10 days after the tenant receives it unless the breach is remedied in 10 days.

A breach of the tenant's statutory maintenance duties that materially affects health and safety: the same kind of notice with 5 days.

No cure is owed for: a second noncompliance of the same or a similar nature during the lease term after the first was remedied (you may file a special detainer 10 days after a written notice of the second one); false information on the application about criminal records, prior evictions or current criminal activity; and a breach on the premises that is both material and irreparable (notice of immediate termination).

Days are calendar days. Your lease may give the tenant longer than these periods, but it can't give less, because a lease can't make the tenant waive rights under the act. Deliver the notice by a method the act recognizes (in hand, or registered or certified mail).

The act doesn't define material noncompliance and doesn't say whether a lease can decide which terms are material; apart from the listed kinds of application falsification, a label in the lease may not bind the court. Naming important rules in the lease still helps show the tenant knew of them.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to tell a tenant or applicant about defective or corrosive drywall, or to test for it. The only Arizona statute on drywall deals with cracks in new manufactured homes, which the dealer or manufacturer repairs for the buyer. Your general duties still apply: you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable. If you know of drywall that is corroding wiring or plumbing or giving off fumes, treat it as a repair problem and fix it.

title: Who Does a Tenant's Repair-and-Deduct Work
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets a lease name the person or firm who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. The act sets the rule itself. If you fail to comply with your duty to keep the premises fit, the repair costs less than $300 or half a month's rent (whichever is greater), and you don't fix it within 10 days after the tenant's written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), the tenant may have the work done by a licensed contractor and, after giving you an itemized statement and a waiver of lien, deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, up to that limit. The essential-services remedy doesn't include a right to repair. Because a lease can't make the tenant waive rights under the act, a clause that limits the tenant to your chosen repairer, beyond the licensed-contractor requirement, risks being unenforceable. You may ask tenants to send repair requests to you and use your own contractors for the repairs you make.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, wildfire or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, limits how long such a stay may last, or says when a displaced person staying in a hotel or other lodging becomes a tenant. The ordinary rules apply. Arizona's landlord-tenant act does not cover transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or recreational lodging, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act. For your own rentals, the lease's guest and occupancy terms govern. A rule you adopt after the tenant signs binds the tenant only after 30 days' notice, and only if it doesn't substantially modify the rental agreement. A guest who isn't named on a written lease and stays without the tenant's or your permission is not a lawful tenant, and a law enforcement officer may remove a person who knowingly stays on without that permission, at the request of the tenant or the landlord entitled to possession. If a tenant asks to take in displaced family or friends, consider a written, temporary consent with an end date, and apply any limit the same way to every tenant.

title: No Disaster Rule; Casualty Rule Applies
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that ends a tenancy, suspends or limits rent, or pauses evictions because the governor or a local government has declared a disaster or emergency. The fire-or-casualty rule decides what happens to the lease. If fire or casualty damages or destroys the unit so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out at once and give you written notice within 14 days of ending the lease, which ends on the day the tenant moved out. Or, if continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate the unusable part, and the rent goes down in proportion to the drop in the unit's fair rental value. If the lease ends, you must return all recoverable security, and rent is accounted for as of the day the tenant vacated (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options). During a declared state of emergency the governor may exercise the state's police power in the affected area, so check for emergency orders before you act; those orders weren't researched here. A state fund may pay housing assistance, including payments to prevent eviction, only after the governor declares a state of emergency. During a declared public health pandemic emergency, a property owner, manager or lessor who acts in good faith to protect tenants from the pandemic is not liable for failing to protect them unless wilful misconduct or gross negligence is proven by clear and convincing evidence.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that forbids letting the same room or unit to two tenants, or that suspends rent as a penalty when you do. The rule on delivering possession decides what happens instead. At the start of the term you must deliver possession to the tenant as the lease requires. If you don't, because someone else is in the unit or for any other reason, rent abates until you deliver it, and the tenant may either end the lease by at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and security, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If the failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater. You may sue anyone wrongfully in possession. So don't sign a second lease for a unit until the first tenancy has ended and the unit is vacant (see If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time).

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Addenda
bodyText:
Arizona has no statute that prescribes a drug-free housing addendum or its wording. The condominium and planned-community statutes do say that an owner may use a crime free addendum as part of a lease agreement. The library's optional Crime-Free Lease Addendum covers drug-related criminal activity, so use that clause rather than a separate drug-free addendum.

Even without an addendum, the unlawful manufacturing, selling, transferring, possessing, using or storing of a controlled substance on the premises is among the breaches Arizona lists as possibly material and irreparable. For a material and irreparable breach that occurs on the premises, you may give a written notice of immediate termination and must then proceed by special detainer.

Other drug-related breaches go through the ordinary 10-day notice for material noncompliance. A rental property owner must also abate criminal activity as the nuisance-abatement statute authorizes.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: A lease may not make a tenant waive or limit the tenant's right, or anyone else's right, to call a peace officer or other emergency assistance in an emergency. It also may not make the tenant pay a monetary penalty, or otherwise penalize the tenant, because the tenant or anyone else called for that help. Such a term is unenforceable. If you knowingly use a lease with a prohibited term, the tenant can recover actual damages and up to two months' periodic rent. This doesn't limit your right to evict a tenant for a breach of the lease under the ordinary notice rules. Arizona gives the tenant no presumed defense when an eviction follows a call for help, and calling police isn't one of the tenant acts listed in the retaliation statute. We found no such rule. Still, base any notice on the tenant's own conduct, never on the call itself, and keep crime-free and nuisance terms clear of any penalty for calling for help (see Lease Terms Arizona Law Prohibits).

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number, requires a tenant to name an emergency contact, or requires the lease to carry a management website or a social-services hotline.

What Arizona does require is that, at or before the start of the tenancy, you disclose in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the property and of an owner or the owner's agent for service of process and notices, keep that information current and give it again on request (see Owner, Manager and Landlord-Tenant Act Disclosure). You may also ask the tenant, who may choose to provide it, for the contact details of a person authorized to retrieve the tenant's belongings and animal if the tenant dies or is incapacitated (see the library's authorized-person clause).

Beyond that, giving tenants an emergency repair number is good practice, and you may ask in the lease for a tenant's emergency contact (the library's optional emergency contact clause). Fill in every blank in a written lease, because Arizona requires a written rental agreement to have all blank spaces completed.

title: Eminent Domain and the Lease
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that ends a residential lease, abates or apportions rent, or divides the award between you and the tenant when the property is taken by eminent domain. So the lease decides, and the library's optional Condemnation clause covers it.

In the condemnation case, the court or jury values each separate estate or interest in the property, which can include the tenant's lease, and anyone occupying or claiming an interest in the property may appear and defend even if not named. Before filing, the condemning body must send its written offer and appraisal to the owner of record and, as a courtesy, to the sole lessee of record.

A tenant who has to move because of a public project may be entitled to relocation advisory services and payment of moving expenses from the agency doing the project; those payments belong to the tenant.

title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires, or specially permits, a residential landlord or management company to run background checks on apartment managers, maintenance workers or other staff who may enter tenants' homes. Screening is your choice. Two statutes bear on it. First, an employer, including a premises owner, is not liable just for hiring an employee or contractor who was previously convicted of a criminal offense other than a violent or sexual offense. In most other negligent-hiring cases that conviction can't be used as evidence, but the protection doesn't apply in some cases, such as misuse of others' money or property by a worker who handles it and had a prior fraud conviction, or violence by a security guard. In a claim for failing to supervise, the conviction may be used if you knew of it, or were grossly negligent in not knowing, and it directly related to the work and the harm. Second, anyone applying for an Arizona real estate licence must first obtain a valid fingerprint clearance card. If you screen, apply the same criteria to every applicant and follow federal consumer-report rules when you use a screening company; those rules weren't researched here.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets, or requires, a lease to authorize the release of a tenant's energy usage data to you for benchmarking. Arizona instead bars cities, towns and counties from requiring an owner, operator or tenant of a multifamily housing property to measure and report energy usage, including energy benchmarking, so no local benchmarking mandate can apply to you. If you want a tenant's utility information anyway, get the tenant's written authorization first. No one may knowingly obtain a utility customer record of an Arizona resident (which includes the customer's name, address, length of service, payment method and other personal identifying information) without the customer's authorization, and a utility may disclose its records with the customer's lawful consent. Whether a particular utility accepts a lease term as that consent, or requires its own form, depends on its procedures and the Corporation Commission's rules, which weren't researched here.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord in Court
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that says who may appear in an eviction or other court case for a landlord that is a corporation, LLC, partnership or other entity, or that lets a property manager or other non-lawyer agent do so. Who may represent you is decided by the Arizona Supreme Court's rules, including the Rules of Procedure for Eviction Actions, which this review didn't hold. The library's eviction court-rules row says a property manager may not represent the owner in court unless the manager is a lawyer (see Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties). Until you have confirmed the current court rule, have an Arizona lawyer file and appear for an entity landlord, and don't let a manager or leasing agent sign pleadings or argue for the owner.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives you, or lets a lease give you, a right to end a residential lease because of an environmental event such as contamination, a toxic release or a public health hazard. The statute that does apply is the fire-or-casualty rule, and it gives the right to the tenant, not to you: if fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease, or stay in the usable part at reduced rent (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options). A lease may include terms the law doesn't prohibit, and the library's optional landlord casualty clause lets you end the lease after a fire or casualty. A broader term letting you end the lease for an environmental event that hasn't damaged the unit has no statute behind it either way, so a court could refuse to enforce it if it was unconscionable when made. Whatever the lease says, you may recover possession only through the court process or the tenant's surrender or abandonment, and the lease can't take away the tenant's own rights.

title: EV Charging: What Arizona Law Sets
bodyText:
Arizona gives a tenant no right to install an electric vehicle charger and doesn't require you to provide one (see No Tenant EV Charging Right). If you agree to a charger, the library's optional EV charger installation clause sets the terms.

Two statutes bear on charging for the electricity. First, a business that offers charging equipment and sells electricity to charge electric vehicles by the kilowatt hour or megajoule isn't a public service corporation for doing so, and it may also charge for other services by time, a fixed fee or both.

Second, if you charge a tenant separately for electricity through a submeter or an allocation method, you may recover only what the utility charges you plus an administrative fee for your actual administrative costs, with no other charges. The lease must list the utilities charged separately and the administrative fee, and must describe any allocation method. Each bill must show the charges and, for a submeter, the opening and closing readings and their dates.

We haven't settled whether a landlord's pay-per-use charger is a separately charged utility or a charging business, so until that is settled, bill a tenant only for the electricity used, at cost, under the utility-charge rule.

We found no Arizona statute that sets meter-accuracy, registration or price-posting rules for chargers.

title: EV Chargers When the Lease Ends
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that says whether a tenant must remove an electric vehicle charger the tenant installed, may take it, or must leave it when the lease ends, or who pays to restore the space. Arizona gives tenants no right to install a charger in the first place, so the lease decides. The library's optional EV charger installation clause makes you choose at signing: the tenant removes the system and repairs any damage, or leaves it in place and it becomes yours. Make that choice in writing before installation. If a tenant abandons the unit and leaves belongings behind, the abandonment rules for personal property apply; whether a wired-in charger counts as the tenant's personal property wasn't researched.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to provide electric vehicle chargers in shared or common parking, gives a tenant a right to install one there, or sets rules for chargers in a condominium's or planned community's common areas. If you provide shared chargers, set their use through your rules. A rule on how tenants use shared facilities binds a tenant only if it makes a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for tenants generally or serves another purpose the statute allows, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies to all tenants fairly, is explicit enough to tell tenants what to do, and the tenant had notice of it when signing; a rule adopted later needs 30 days' notice and mustn't substantially modify the lease. If you bill tenants for the electricity, see EV Charging: What Arizona Law Sets. In an association-governed property, check the association's own rules before installing anything in common areas.

title: No Hardship Stay of an Eviction
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets a court stay or delay an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, such as age, illness, disability, children, the school year or the weather. The delays the statutes do allow are these. The trial in a special detainer case may be postponed for good cause shown by affidavit, for up to three days in justice court or five in superior court. No writ of restitution may issue until five calendar days after judgment, and a motion to set aside the judgment doesn't delay the writ unless a judge finds good cause. A party who appeals from justice court may stay the judgment for possession by filing a supersedeas bond for the rent accruing until the next rental date, plus costs and any attorney fees, and the tenant must then pay rent into the court on each due date; if the tenant misses a payment, you may move to lift the stay, and the court must hear it within five court days, or within three days after a finding of a material and irreparable breach. Court rules weren't reviewed here (see Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties).

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets a lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. The statute sets how the tenant is served in a special detainer case: the summons is deemed received three days after mailing if personal service is attempted, and within one day after the summons issues a copy is conspicuously posted on the main entrance of the tenant's residence and the same day sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address. So don't rely on a lease-named agent; follow that statute and the court's rules, which weren't reviewed here. Going the other way, you must disclose in writing the name and address of an owner or agent authorized to receive service of process and notices for you (see Owner, Manager and Landlord-Tenant Act Disclosure). If a tenant is a participant in the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program for victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses or stalking, the participant may be served by registered or certified mail at the program's substitute address, unless a court rule provides otherwise; this is one way to serve, not necessarily the required way.

title: Fast-Track Eviction for Serious Breaches
bodyText:
Arizona has a faster eviction track for a breach that is both material and irreparable and occurs on the premises. The statute's examples include illegal discharge of a weapon, homicide, prostitution, criminal street gang activity, unlawfully manufacturing, selling, transferring, possessing, using or storing a controlled substance, threatening or intimidating, assault, acts found to be a nuisance, and any other breach that jeopardizes the health, safety and welfare of you, your agent or another tenant or involves imminent or actual serious property damage; the list isn't exhaustive.

For such a breach you may give a written notice of immediate termination and must then file a special detainer action. The court sets trial no later than the third day after you file, and if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the breach happened, it orders restitution of the premises 12 to 24 hours later. If the tenant appeals and stays the judgment, the court must treat your motion to lift the stay as an emergency and hear it within three days.

The tenant answers for a guest's violation if the tenant could reasonably be expected to know it might happen and didn't try to prevent it. Conduct off the premises doesn't qualify for this track; use the ordinary 10-day notice for material noncompliance instead (see Eviction Notices and Process).

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets up a special procedure, election or fee for an early or expedited disposition of a security deposit. None is needed, because Arizona's deadline is an outer limit: within 14 days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant asks for the deposit, you must give the tenant an itemized list of all deductions with the amount due, by first-class mail to the tenant's last known residence unless the tenant arranges otherwise in writing. You may do it sooner. If you don't comply, the tenant may recover what is due plus damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld. No statute provides a fee for early processing, and the library offers no Arizona clause for one; a fee not designated nonrefundable in writing is refundable (see Security Deposit Rules).

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, or that gives you a right to enter during one. A lease may require that notice, and the library's extended absence clause does.

Notice matters for abandonment. Arizona treats a unit as abandoned when the tenant has been absent without notice to you for at least seven days, rent has been unpaid for ten days and there is no reasonable evidence other than the tenant's belongings that the tenant is living there, or when the tenant has been absent for at least five days, rent has been unpaid for five days and none of the tenant's belongings are in the unit. A tenant who tells you about an absence isn't absent without notice under the first test.

An absence alone doesn't widen your access: apart from emergencies, you may enter only on at least two days' notice, at reasonable times, for the purposes the statute lists, or by court order, or after abandonment or surrender.

title: Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to let a tenant run a family child care home in a rental, that bars you from prohibiting it, or that sets conditions such as insurance or liability waivers when you allow it. So the lease decides, through its use and occupancy terms. A tenant who cares for children for pay may also need state approval: a child care group home must be certified by the Department of Health Services, and the state certifies child care home providers who care for four or fewer children paid for with state child care assistance. If you allow child care, put your consent and any conditions in writing, and ask for proof of the certification or licence the tenant holds. Remember that a lease can't make the tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant act or limit your own liability arising under law.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: Arizona's State Fire Marshal adopts a state fire code by rule. It sets minimum standards for fire safety, including fire escapes, fire alarm systems, smoke detectors and fire extinguishing equipment, and the means and adequacy of fire protection and exits in places where numbers of people work, live or congregate, but that last standard excludes family dwellings with fewer than five residential dwelling units. The State Fire Marshal enforces the state code throughout Arizona, except in a city of 100,000 or more people that has a nationally recognized fire code in effect and has passed an ordinance taking over that jurisdiction; its routine inspections also exclude family dwellings with fewer than five units. A county may adopt a national fire prevention code that is as stringent as the state fire code. Which edition of a model code the state rule or your city adopts is set in the administrative code and local ordinances, which this review didn't hold, so check with the State Fire Marshal or your city. As a landlord you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety. Those conditions include fire hazards, missing fire-resistive construction or fire extinguishing systems the building code requires, inadequate fire detection systems required by law, and inadequate exits.

title: No Fire Sprinkler Retrofit Duty
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in an existing rental. For single family detached homes and buildings with no more than two dwelling units, the choice is the owner's: a city, town or county may not adopt a code that takes away the choice to install sprinklers or not, or fine anyone for it, except under a city or town code requiring them that was adopted before December 31, 2009. Cities, towns and counties also may not require an accessory dwelling unit, and cities and towns may not require the structures in required middle housing, to contain a fire sprinkler. For larger buildings, sprinklers depend on the building and fire codes that applied when the building was built or changed. Your duty as a landlord is to comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, which include fire extinguishing systems the building code requires, maintained in relation to any increase in occupant load, alteration, addition or change in occupancy. Sprinkler installation and repair must be done by a licensed contractor; routine work by an apartment or condominium complex employee that is incidental to the fire safety equipment isn't treated as fire safety maintenance and repair.

title: Firearms Rules for Rentals
bodyText:
A property owner may not have or enforce a policy or rule that prohibits a person from lawfully transporting or storing a firearm in the person's locked, privately owned motor vehicle, or in a locked compartment on the person's privately owned motorcycle, if the firearm can't be seen from outside. A rule that does so is null and void.

The rule doesn't apply where possession is illegal, where the parking is on an owner-occupied or tenant-occupied single family detached residence, where you provide a parking area that is fenced or otherwise physically secured, has access limited by a guard or other security measure and offers monitored, temporary and secure firearm storage, where you provide alternative parking reasonably close by at no extra fee for people who want to keep a firearm in their vehicle, or in a few other listed cases.

We found no Arizona statute that bars a residential lease from limiting firearms inside the unit or in common areas, or that protects permit holders from such a term.

An illegal discharge of a weapon on the premises is among the breaches that may be material and irreparable, allowing a notice of immediate termination. The library's optional firearm discharge and storage clause fits Arizona law.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to tell a tenant that the property is in a flood zone or has flooded before, or that gives a tenant a remedy for a missing flood notice. Arizona's flood statements are for sales, not rentals: a seller of five or fewer unsubdivided parcels in an unincorporated area must give the buyer a disclosure affidavit that says whether the property is in a FEMA designated regulatory floodplain, and a buyer or seller may order a third-party report that covers special flood hazard areas. Neither applies to a lease. The disclosures the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does require at or before the start of a tenancy are the names and addresses of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for service and notices, and a written statement that the Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website. If you choose to tell a tenant about flood risk, make sure what you say is accurate.

title: Paying to Reinstate After a Rent Notice
bodyText: Arizona lets a tenant who is behind on rent save the rental agreement by paying, in three stages. After your written five-day notice of nonpayment runs out, you may end the rental agreement only by filing a special detainer action. Before you file, the rental agreement is reinstated if the tenant tenders all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee set out in a written rental agreement. After you file, it is reinstated only if the tenant pays all past-due rent, reasonable late fees set out in a written rental agreement, attorney fees and court costs. After a judgment for you, reinstatement is up to you alone. A lease clause can't take away the before-filing and after-filing rights, because a tenant can't waive rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Late fees count toward reinstatement only if they are reasonable and in a written rental agreement. See the eviction process row for the notices and timing.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act doesn't fix a building code at a named edition. You must comply with applicable building codes materially affecting health and safety, as listed in the state's rental inspection chapter, and that list measures most conditions against "the building code" of the place where the rental is. Building codes are local. A city or town may adopt a code by reference in an ordinance and amend it the same way. A county may adopt, for its zoned unincorporated areas, a building, electrical, plumbing or mechanical code issued by a national code organization or adopted by the largest city in the county; if it adopts the city's code, it must adopt each change within 90 days after notice of it or drop the code. So the edition that binds you is the one your city, town or county has adopted, not the newest national edition. Older buildings get some protection: a building that conformed with all applicable building code laws isn't treated as lacking required fire-resistive construction or fire extinguishing systems if they have been adequately maintained and improved for any increase in occupant load, alteration, addition or change in occupancy. The state disability standards for public entities, public accommodations and commercial facilities that are built into building codes apply to new construction and alterations, not to existing buildings that don't meet them. For covered multifamily dwellings, following HUD's fair housing accessibility guidelines satisfies the state's adaptive-design requirement; the statute names no edition. When an Arizona statute refers to another statute, it means that statute as later amended. Check with your local building department which code edition applies to your building and to any work you do on it.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that allows or forbids a residential landlord to pass a government fee, such as a rental registration, licensing or inspection fee, on to a tenant. But a lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for any liability of yours arising under law, or for the costs connected with it, and a fee a city or county charges you for renting reads, on the statute's words, as exactly that kind of liability (A.R.S. § 33-1315(A)(3)); no Arizona case was read on the point. So the library offers no clause making the tenant reimburse a government fee. The safe way to recover it is to build it into the rent: set the Monthly Rent, at signing or renewal, high enough to cover the fees you expect (for example, a $120 yearly fee is about $10 a month). Don't raise one month's rent by the amount of a fee when it comes due: during a fixed term you can't change the rent unless the lease already provides for it, and a term tying the rent to the fee is the same pass-through under another name. Never pass on fines or civil penalties against you, such as the city penalties for failing to register the rental with the county assessor, or inspection fees a city or county charges because of a code violation or your failure to fix one. The government fees themselves are limited: the county assessor may charge no more than $10 for each initial registration and each change of information, and a city, town or county may not charge for initial inspections and may charge a reasonable fee only for follow-up inspections after a citation or when an owner fails to correct a violation. From January 1, 2025, a city or town may not levy a transaction privilege tax or similar tax or fee on renting residential property, so there is no city rental tax to pass on. How a pass-through charge is treated in an eviction is covered in the fees-as-rent row.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that bars a residential landlord from passing a government fine or abatement charge on to a tenant who caused it, or that makes the tenant liable to you for such a charge unless the lease says otherwise.

The general rules decide it. You may recover all reasonable damages that result from a tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or with the tenant's statutory duties, such as keeping the unit clean and safe and disposing of garbage properly. A tenant is responsible for guests' violations of the lease or your rules only if the tenant could reasonably be expected to be aware they might happen and didn't try to prevent them. A lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for a liability of yours arising under law, so a fine for a condition you are responsible for stays with you.

Some government orders can reach the tenant directly: a city or county rubbish and weed ordinance must compel the owner, lessee or occupant to remove hazardous rubbish, trash, weeds or debris, and a health officer orders the owner or occupant to remove a nuisance at the owner's or occupant's expense. For a rental of four or fewer units that had a tenant during the removal, a city or town may not require the owner to pay its rubbish removal assessment. The library's optional Arizona clause on fines caused by the tenant follows these limits.

title: Lease Guarantors and Renewals
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that limits a residential lease guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, or otherwise sets special rules for lease guaranties. So the guaranty's own words decide whether it covers a renewal, an extension or a month-to-month continuation; say so expressly.

Three general rules apply. A promise to answer for another person's debt can't be enforced unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor.

A person bound as surety on a contract to pay money may, once the right to sue has accrued, give the creditor written notice to sue; if the creditor doesn't bring the action within 60 days and prosecute it to judgment and execution, that surety is discharged. Whether a lease guarantor counts as a surety for this rule, and whether a guaranty can waive it, is for the courts, so be ready to sue promptly if a guarantor sends that notice.

Any money a guarantor gives you as security counts toward the limit of one and one-half month's rent on security, however it is labeled.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that gives a residential tenant's guests, visitors or suppliers a right of access to the building, that bars a lease or rule from limiting guests, or that limits guest fees for houses and apartments.

Your guest rules are governed by the general rules on rules and regulations: a rule is enforceable only if it promotes the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property from abusive use or fairly distributes services and facilities, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies to all tenants fairly, is explicit enough to tell tenants what to do, isn't meant to evade your obligations, and the tenant had notice of it when signing; a rule adopted later needs 30 days' notice and can't substantially modify the lease.

A tenant is responsible for guests' violations of the lease or your rules if the tenant could reasonably be expected to be aware they might happen and didn't try to prevent them. A guest not named on a written lease who stays without your or the tenant's permission is not a tenant and can be removed by police. Mobile home parks and long-term recreational vehicle spaces have their own guest-fee rules under separate acts.

title: When a Defect Is Serious Enough
bodyText: Arizona sets different thresholds for different tenant remedies. To end the lease for your breach, the tenant needs a material noncompliance with the rental agreement (10-day notice) or a failure to maintain the premises that materially affects health and safety (5-day notice); the statute doesn't otherwise define "material", except that material falsification includes false written statements about the unit's availability, its condition, current and future services and utilities, and who pays for utilities. For the code-compliance part of your maintenance duty, the conditions that materially affect health and safety are the ones listed in the state's rental inspection chapter, such as lack of hot and cold running water, lack of adequate heating and cooling, infestation, structural hazards, and hazardous wiring or plumbing. Other remedies have lower or different thresholds. A tenant may recover damages and get a court order for any noncompliance, with no materiality requirement. Repair-and-deduct is available only if the condition breaches the fit and habitable condition of the premises. The essential-services remedies require a deliberate or negligent failure to supply water, gas or electricity, hot water, heat, air-conditioning or cooling where installed, or essential services. In an eviction for nonpayment, the tenant may counterclaim if you are not in compliance with the lease or the Act. The termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies are not available for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member or a person there with the tenant's consent. Whether a particular defect is material is decided by the courts case by case (we searched no case law).

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that presumes a rental is habitable, or uninhabitable, because of a code inspection, a certificate, a code violation or anything else, and none that shifts the burden of proof on habitability. Whether your unit meets the maintenance duty is proved like any other fact. The one presumption tied to repair complaints is about retaliation: if a tenant complained to a code enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or complained to you about your maintenance duties, within six months before you raise the rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction, the court must presume your action was retaliation until evidence is introduced that would support a finding that it wasn't. The presumption doesn't arise if the tenant complained after a notice of termination. You may still bring an eviction if the code violation was caused mainly by the tenant's or the household's or guests' lack of reasonable care, or if the tenant is behind on rent.

title: No Habitability Statement Required
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. You don't need one, because the duty applies by statute whatever the lease says: you must comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain the facilities and appliances you supply, provide waste receptacles and removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and, where installed and offered, reasonable heat and cooling when the season requires. The written disclosures Arizona does require at or before the start of the tenancy are the manager's and owner's (or owner's agent's) names and addresses and a statement that the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website. The library doesn't restate the maintenance duty as a lease clause.

title: Environmental Use Restrictions in Leases
bodyText:
If a remediated property has a recorded "declaration of environmental use restriction" (a restrictive covenant recorded when contamination is left above residential standards or an engineering or institutional control is used), each party to that declaration must incorporate its terms, in full or by reference, into any lease, license or other agreement the party signs that grants a right in the restricted property. The declaration runs with the land and binds the owner's heirs, successors and assigns.

If you own or rent out property subject to one, put its terms in the lease; the library's optional environmental use restriction clause does that. Check the county records and the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality's repository before leasing a property that was remediated.

Apart from that, we found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to tell a tenant that the property is or was contaminated, is a brownfield or is near a Superfund site. The written notice of soil remediation that Arizona requires is from a seller to a purchaser, not from a landlord to a tenant.

The incorporation duty is written for each party to the declaration; because the declaration runs with the land, including its terms whenever the property is subject to one is the cautious course even if you are not a party.

title: No Health District Rental Rules
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets health district rules for rental housing, requires a landlord to give tenants a copy of health regulations on request, or sends tenants to a health district for rental complaints. Health agencies still reach rental property in general ways. When a nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness exists on private property, the county board of health, local health department, county environmental department or public health services district must order the owner or occupant to remove it within 24 hours at the owner's or occupant's expense. A tenant may also complain to the agency that enforces the building or housing code, and you may not retaliate against a tenant for complaining about a violation materially affecting health and safety. The conditions that count as materially affecting health and safety, such as lack of hot and cold running water, inadequate heating and cooling, and infestation, are listed in the state rental inspection chapter.

title: Heat and Cooling
bodyText: You must supply reasonable heat, and reasonable air-conditioning or cooling where such units are installed and offered, when seasonal weather requires, along with running water and reasonable hot water at all times. The duty doesn't apply where the building isn't required by law to be equipped for heat or cooling, or where the unit is built so that the heat, cooling or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Arizona sets no temperature. Shifting the duty is limited: for a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, for adequate consideration and in good faith, that the tenant supplies heat and cooling; for other units the statute allows a separate signed writing only for specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and never for work needed to keep the unit up to code and habitable. After the lease is signed you may not transfer payment for utility services provided as part of the rental agreement to the tenant without the tenant's written consent, and a lease may not contain terms contrary to that rule. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, cooling or hot water, the tenant may, after reasonable notice, buy the service and deduct its reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that time; the tenant has no right to make the repair under this remedy. Lack of adequate heating and cooling is one of the conditions that materially affect health and safety. Some cities set their own cooling standards; check local law.

title: Home Businesses in Rentals
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a tenant a right to run a business from a rental home or that limits a lease term restricting home businesses. The one home-business statute limits county zoning, not leases: in unincorporated areas, a county zoning ordinance may not stop the owner of a licensed home-based business, which can be a business run by the tenant of the residential property, from making improvements such as doors, shelving or display racks, displaying a small temporary sign during business hours, selling goods, generating traffic that doesn't congest the street, having more than one client at a time, or employing residents, immediate family and one or two others; the county may still impose reasonable operating requirements. We found no matching statute for cities and towns. A lease may include terms the law doesn't prohibit, so you may limit or bar business use in the lease, and the library's residential-use-only clause does that. If you allow a home business, say what is allowed, since the county rule doesn't give the tenant permission to make improvements to your property.

title: No Exemption Waivers in Arizona Leases
bodyText: Start with the default: a tenant who owes you a judgment keeps Arizona's exemptions from collection. The personal property exemptions include household furniture, furnishings, goods, electronics and appliances used by the debtor or a dependent, up to an aggregate fair market value of $15,000, along with the other listed items. The homestead exemption protects up to $400,000 (adjusted yearly for cost of living) of a resident's interest in the real property, condominium, cooperative or other shelter where the person lives; whether a tenant's lease interest can be a homestead isn't settled by statute. A lease can't take these away. A waiver of the personal property exemption rights is void and unenforceable notwithstanding any agreement, except as the statute allows for enforcing a security interest or pledge or recovering leased property, and except when done with notice. Apart from a transfer of the property or permanently moving away, a homestead is given up only by a declaration of abandonment or waiver that the person signs and acknowledges, and the declaration takes effect only when recorded with the county recorder, so a lease clause won't do it. In any case, a landlord lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods isn't enforceable under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and distraint for rent is abolished. The library offers no exemption-waiver clause for Arizona.

title: No Termination Right for Illness or Death
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that ends a residential tenancy when a tenant dies or becomes incapacitated, or that lets a tenant end a lease early to move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care because of age, illness or disability. The Act's only early-termination rights are for victims of domestic violence or sexual assault and for law enforcement officers protected by a recent injunction against harassment. Otherwise the ordinary rules apply: a month-to-month tenancy ends on written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date stated in the notice, and if a fixed-term tenant leaves early you must mitigate your damages, for example by trying to re-rent. If a tenant dies or is incapacitated, the lease may name a person the tenant authorizes to enter and retrieve the tenant's property and animals, and the statute sets the steps and time limits for that. A request tied to a disability may also raise a reasonable-accommodation question under fair housing law. You may agree to an early release, and you may offer one in the lease.

title: No Code-Order Disclosure Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to tell a tenant or applicant about an outstanding inspection order, code violation, slum property designation or condemnation order. These orders still matter. A city, town, county or the state may inspect a rental whose owner hasn't registered it with the county assessor, or one designated a slum property, which it may inspect yearly for three years; it must ask an occupying tenant's consent before entering the interior, and the owner pays the inspection cost. What you do tell a tenant in writing must be true: a material falsification of written information about the condition of the premises lets the tenant give a 10-day notice to end the lease. And if a building is destroyed or so damaged that it is unfit for occupancy without the tenant's fault, a tenant under the older landlord-tenant chapter owes no further rent unless a written agreement says otherwise and may move out.

title: Penalty for Entry Without Proper Notice
bodyText:
Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give the tenant at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times, and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

If you enter unlawfully, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that, though otherwise lawful, unreasonably harass the tenant, the tenant may get a court order to stop it from happening again or may terminate the rental agreement. Either way, the tenant may recover actual damages of not less than one month's rent. A lease can't waive these rights.

The rule cuts both ways: if the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages. A tenant's written maintenance request is permission to enter for that request alone, without a separate notice. The library's right-of-entry clause states the Arizona notice rule.

title: No Key Control Mandate
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord or apartment complex to adopt a key control policy, to limit or log employee access to unit keys, or to run background checks on employees who have access to units. The key rules that do apply are these. A tenant delivers possession by returning the unit keys and vacating. Your staff's entries are your entries, so they need the two days' notice and reasonable times the access rule requires, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault may require you to install a new lock at the tenant's cost, as the domestic violence row explains. A written key policy and limited key access are still good practice. The library's keys clause covers key receipts, return and re-keying.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: A lease term that Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prohibits is unenforceable. If you deliberately use a rental agreement containing terms you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover the actual damages the tenant suffered and up to two months' periodic rent. The prohibited terms are those making the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act; pay your attorney fees (a written prevailing-party fee clause is allowed); accept an exculpation or limit on your liability arising under law, or indemnify you for it; waive or limit anyone's right to call the police or other emergency help in an emergency; or pay a penalty for doing so. The utility-service section separately says a lease may not contain terms contrary to it; a term that takes away a tenant's rights under that section is also a waiver of rights under the Act. The rule doesn't limit your right to evict for the tenant's noncompliance. The penalty turns on knowing, deliberate use, so review your lease form against the prohibited-terms row before you use it.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: Arizona gives tenants a set of remedies for a landlord's breach, and a lease can't take them away. For a material breach of the lease, the tenant may give written notice that the lease ends at least 10 days after you receive it unless you remedy the breach within 10 days; for a failure to maintain the premises that materially affects health and safety, 5 days. The tenant may also recover damages and get a court order for any noncompliance with the lease or your maintenance duties. For a repair costing less than $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, the tenant may give written notice and, if you don't act within 10 days (or sooner in an emergency), have a licensed contractor do it and deduct the cost after giving you an itemized statement and a lien waiver. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply water, gas or electricity, hot water, heat or cooling where installed, or essential services, the tenant may buy the service and deduct its cost, recover damages for reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that time. If you fail to deliver possession at the start, rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on five days' written notice or sue for possession; a willful failure costs up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. If fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days or, where occupancy is lawful, stop using the damaged part and pay reduced rent. If you unlawfully remove or lock out the tenant or willfully interrupt essential services, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; the same remedies apply to retaliation. Unlawful or harassing entry allows an injunction or termination and at least one month's rent in damages. In an eviction for nonpayment, the tenant may counterclaim for these amounts. The termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies don't apply to a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent, and the tenant must mitigate damages.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Farmland
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that says whether the tenant of rented farm or ranch land gets hunting or fishing rights, or may let others hunt there, unless the owner grants them in writing. The game law lets both landowners and lessees of private land close it: landowners or lessees who want to prohibit hunting, fishing, trapping or guiding on their land without their permission must post it with notices or signboards. Each sign must be at least 8 by 11 inches, with plainly legible capital, bold-faced lettering at least one inch high, and must say "no trespassing", "no hunting", "no trapping", "no fishing" or "no guiding" (alone or combined). Signs go at all points of vehicular access, at all property or fence corners and at least every quarter mile along the boundary; between corners and access points, a post with at least 100 square inches of orange paint, covering its whole aboveground surface facing outward and on both sides, may serve instead. State or federal land, even if leased, may be posted only with the Game and Fish Commission's consent. Entering to take wildlife is criminal trespass only if the land is posted this way and the signs also say "no trespassing", or if the person knowingly stays after a reasonable request to leave from a law enforcement officer acting for the owner, the owner or anyone else with lawful control of the land, or knowingly disregards reasonable notice prohibiting entry. It is also unlawful to discharge a firearm while taking wildlife within a quarter mile of an occupied farmhouse or other residence, cabin, lodge or building without the permission of the owner or resident. An owner, lessee, tenant or occupant of agricultural or range land isn't liable to someone allowed to hunt or fish there without paying, except for wilful, malicious or grossly negligent conduct, and the hunter is liable for any damage to the land, livestock or crops. Because both owner and lessee may post, say in the farm lease, expressly, who holds hunting and fishing rights, who may give permission and who may post the land. Arizona's residential landlord-tenant act covers dwelling units, not farmland.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Arizona's Fair Housing Act makes it discrimination to refuse reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. It is also discrimination to refuse to let a tenant with a disability make reasonable modifications to the premises at the tenant's own expense when they may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. Where it is reasonable to do so, you may condition your permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its condition before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Federal fair housing law has the same two rules. We found no Arizona statute that requires the restoration condition to appear in the lease or that addresses a restoration escrow. The federal fair housing rule adds three points. You may not increase the customary security deposit for a person with a disability. Where it is necessary to make reasonably certain that money will be there to pay for the restoration at the end of the tenancy, you may negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, for the tenant to pay into an interest-bearing escrow account, over a reasonable period, a reasonable amount not more than the cost of the restoration, with the interest going to the tenant. And you may condition permission on a reasonable description of the proposed modification and reasonable assurances that the work will be done in a workmanlike manner and that any required building permits will be obtained. Whether such an escrow counts toward Arizona's limit of one and one-half month's rent on security isn't settled, so keep the deposit and any escrow together within that limit. Because the restoration condition is allowed only where it is reasonable, decide it case by case and put it in your written approval of each modification rather than in every lease. The Act doesn't require renting to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Assistance animals are covered in their own row.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to file proof of insurance with a city, county or state office, or to tell tenants whether you are insured. The rental registration you keep with the county assessor asks for owner, agent and property details, not insurance. One narrow exception: if you rent a home as a vacation rental or short-term rental, a city, town or county may require liability insurance of at least $500,000 in the aggregate, or that you list the rental through an online lodging marketplace that provides equal or greater coverage. Transient occupancy of that kind is outside the residential landlord and tenant act. Insurance is still wise for a long-term rental. Your lease can't limit your liability arising under law or make the tenant indemnify you for it; such a clause is unenforceable. Your lender, your association or your property management agreement may also require coverage.

title: No Lien on a Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: In a residential rental you can't hold or seize a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Under the residential landlord and tenant act, a lien or security interest of yours in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable (only one perfected before the act took effect could be), and distraint for rent, seizing a tenant's goods to force payment, is abolished. An older general landlord and tenant chapter still gives landlords a lien on a tenant's non-exempt property on the premises and a right to seize and sell it, but where it conflicts with the residential act, the residential act governs. The residential act also bars you from taking possession by removing the tenant's possessions, except after abandonment, surrender or as the act permits. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. A lease clause giving you a lien or a right to seize belongings is not a safe substitute, and a waiver of the tenant's legal exemptions from creditors is void, except as the exemption law allows and with notice. Collect unpaid rent through a court judgment instead. You may deal with belongings left behind through the abandonment procedure, or after a writ of restitution is executed, under the same storage and sale rules; if the tenant returns the keys and leaves property behind, you may remove and dispose of it at once unless you and the tenant agreed in writing to other treatment, and a deceased or incapacitated tenant's authorized person may retrieve it as A.R.S. 33-1314 provides.

title: Possession, Rent and Damages
bodyText: When a lease ends because of the tenant's breach, you may claim possession and rent, and you have a separate claim for your actual damages for the breach. While the lease is still running, you may recover all reasonable damages from the tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's legal duties, plus court costs, reasonable attorney fees and all measurable damage the tenant caused to the property. In an eviction case the court may give you possession, the late charges stated in the lease, costs and, if you choose, all rent due and unpaid through the current rental period. Other losses, such as rent for the rest of a fixed term, belong in your separate damages claim. If personal service was attempted and the summons was then posted and sent by certified mail as the statute allows, that service counts as personal service for a money judgment. You must take reasonable steps to limit your losses, including trying to rerent at a fair rental. Which court hears a money claim alone, and whether a small claims route fits, is set by the court statutes and rules, which this library hasn't read; check them before you file. The row on remedies after a breach covers mitigation and abandonment.

title: Police Calls and Cooperation
bodyText: Your lease can't waive or limit the tenant's or anyone else's right to call the police or other emergency help in an emergency, and it can't charge a penalty or otherwise penalize the tenant because the tenant or anyone else made that call. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it lets the tenant recover actual damages and up to two months' rent. A few other rules connect you to the police. If a court orders the interception of communications, the order may direct landlords to give the officers the information, facilities and technical help needed to carry it out. A tenant's guest who isn't named on the written lease and stays without your or the tenant's permission isn't a tenant, and a law enforcement officer may remove that person at your request or the tenant's. You may use a crime-free lease addendum, and a homeowners' or condominium association can't stop you. A city may require the owner of a property designated a slum, or with violations that materially affect occupants' health and safety, to join its crime-free multihousing program. Apart from the death-reporting duty below, we found no Arizona statute that otherwise requires you or your tenants to cooperate with police, to report tenants, or to give police tenant information or access to a unit. One general duty does reach you: anyone who knows of a death that must be reported, including a death of someone not under a health care provider's current care, a violent, unexpected or unexplained death, or a death in a suspicious, unusual or nonnatural manner, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must promptly give the nearest peace officer all the information the person has about it, and a person who knows of the body and knowingly fails to notify police as soon as possible, without good reason to believe they have already been told, is guilty of a class 2 misdemeanor (A.R.S. § 11-593(A), (B), (D)). Arizona's child-abuse and vulnerable-adult reporting duties bind listed professionals and people responsible for the child's or adult's care, not a landlord as such; anyone else may report to a peace officer, the Department of Child Safety or adult protective services, and retaliating against a person who reports vulnerable-adult abuse in good faith is prohibited (A.R.S. §§ 13-3620(A), (H), 46-454(A), (E), (L)). Entry without the tenant's consent still follows the access rules.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a lead-safe or lead-free certificate, a lead inspection or clearance, or a lead registry listing for a rental unit, or that requires you to attach any lead certificate to the lease. Arizona's own lead law is a health program: it lets the state health department run lead poisoning prevention programs, and it makes it a misdemeanor to apply lead-based paint to interior surfaces of housing, or to exterior surfaces and porches that young children can reach. Federal law still applies to housing built before 1978: before the tenant is bound by the lease, you must give the federal lead pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint or lead hazards, and hand over any lead reports you have. The library's lead-based paint disclosure clause covers those federal steps. If you renovate or repaint a pre-1978 unit, check the federal renovation rules first.

title: No State Lead Notices
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that requires a landlord to give tenants any lead notice, pamphlet, certificate or packet of its own, beyond the federal lead disclosure.

The federal disclosure is what you must give for housing built before 1978, unless an exception applies (housing for the elderly or people with disabilities, or a studio or other 0-bedroom unit, when no child under 6 lives or is expected to live there). Before the tenant is bound by the lease, give the federal lead pamphlet, disclose any lead-based paint or lead hazards you know of, and provide any lead report you have. If an agent leases the unit for you, the agent must also make sure this is done. The library's lead-based paint disclosure clause carries the federal statement and acknowledgments.

Arizona's own lead law doesn't add a tenant notice; it bans applying lead-based paint to interior surfaces of housing, and to exterior surfaces and porches that young children can reach.

title: What an Arizona Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Arizona lets you and the tenant set the lease terms, so long as no law prohibits them, and it has no list of terms every lease must contain. We found no Arizona statute that requires the start and end dates, or any other term, to appear on the first page. A few things must be in writing, in the lease or given with it. At or before the start of the tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name and address of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices and service, and tell the tenant in writing that the residential landlord and tenant act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website. Fill in every blank in a written lease, and exchange signed copies. State in writing the purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit; any fee not designated nonrefundable is refundable. At move-in, give the tenant a signed copy of the lease, a move-in form for listing existing damage, and written notice that the tenant may be present at the move-out inspection. If you charge separately for utilities, the lease must list those utilities and state any administrative fee, and a ratio billing method must be described. If the lease is signed after a foreclosure action began, include the written foreclosure notice the statute prescribes (not required for buildings of four or more connected units). A late fee counts in a reinstatement only if it is set forth in a written lease. If the unit has a pool, give the tenant the state-approved pool safety notice, and, except in a single family residence, give tenants bedbug educational materials. Each item has its own row in this library.

title: Signed Lease Copies
bodyText:
If the lease is in writing, you must give the tenant a signed copy, and the tenant must sign and return one fully signed copy to you, within a reasonable time after the lease is signed. Every blank space must be filled in.

At move-in you must also give the tenant a signed copy of the lease, with the move-in form and the notice about the move-out inspection. A failure by either side counts as a material noncompliance with the lease by that side, so the other side may use the remedies for a material breach, such as a written notice to fix the problem within 10 days or the lease ends. The statute doesn't say that a missing copy makes the lease unenforceable.

Give the tenant your written rules at signing too, because a rule binds the tenant only if the tenant had notice of it when entering the lease, or if it was adopted later on 30 days' notice and doesn't substantially change the lease. The library's lease-copy receipt clause records both.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a tenant to initial particular lease clauses, such as a notice requirement longer than the statute's, or that makes a residential lease term enforceable only if it is initialed, separately signed or printed in conspicuous type. The tenant's signature on the lease binds the tenant to its lawful terms, and a real estate broker isn't required to review and initial a fully signed residential lease. Notice periods in the lease must still meet the statute, and a lease can't waive the tenant's rights under the residential landlord and tenant act. What Arizona does require at the start of a tenancy is written notice of the manager's and an owner's or agent's names and addresses, and of where to find the residential landlord and tenant act; the library's disclosure clause gives both. Asking for initials beside the terms that matter most is still good practice, because it helps show the tenant saw them.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
