bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that bars terms more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or the reverse, or that limits how much more rent you may charge for a month-to-month tenancy than for a longer lease. You may set rent and other terms for each kind of tenancy, so long as no law prohibits them. A tenancy without a definite term is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly), and either side may end it by written notice at least 30 days before the rental date named in the notice (10 days for week-to-week). The general limits still apply: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, every duty and remedy carries an obligation of good faith, and a difference in terms can't be based on a protected class under fair housing law. Rent increases follow the rent increase row.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets a minimum type size for a printed residential lease, or that makes a lease, or any part of it, unenforceable or inadmissible because the print is too small. Type-size rules in Arizona law apply to other contracts, such as self-storage rental agreements and solar energy system agreements, not to leases of homes and apartments. Use a readable type size anyway. A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term, and a term the tenant could not reasonably read invites that argument. Every blank in a written lease must still be filled in.

title: Deadlines to Sue a Tenant
bodyText: Arizona sets these time limits, each counted from when the claim arises. A suit for a debt founded on a written contract signed in Arizona, such as unpaid rent under a written lease, must be brought within six years. A debt not based on a written contract, such as rent under an oral lease, has three years. A claim for injury to your property has two years, and so does a forcible entry or forcible detainer action, counted from when the entry or detainer begins. A claim on a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture, has one year, and claims with no other limit have four years. Which period fits a particular claim is a legal question, and the statutes don't answer every case, so sue well inside the shortest period that might apply. Time the tenant spends outside Arizona isn't counted. Once a claim is barred, the tenant's later acknowledgment that the debt is owed revives it only if the acknowledgment is in writing and signed by the tenant. The statutes don't say whether a partial payment restarts a period; get a signed written acknowledgment instead of relying on one.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText:
Arizona lets you shift some maintenance to the tenant, on conditions that depend on the kind of home.

For a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, for adequate consideration, that the tenant will handle trash receptacles and removal, supply water, hot water, heat and cooling, and do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling.

For any other dwelling unit, the tenant may take on only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and the agreement must be in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by adequate consideration, and must not reduce your obligations to other tenants.

Either way, the agreement must be made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and it can't cover work needed to meet building codes materially affecting health and safety or to put and keep the home fit and habitable; that work stays yours.

The statute doesn't say the consideration must be a rent reduction, only that it be adequate. A single family residence here means a home used as one dwelling unit; a unit sharing walls counts if it has direct street access and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility.

The tenant's own statutory duties, such as keeping the unit clean and disposing of garbage, apply without any agreement. The library's tenant maintenance agreement is written for these rules.

title: No Military Zone Lease Disclosure
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a landlord to tell a tenant that a rental is near a military airport, under a military training route or in a noise or accident potential zone, or that gives a tenant a right to end the lease over it. Arizona's military airport disclosure rules reach other transactions: the state real estate public report for new subdivided or unsubdivided land, reservation documents and conditional sales contracts before that report issues, and a seller of residential real estate, who must disclose in writing before title transfers. The state real estate commissioner also records a notice in the county records for land in the vicinity of a military airport, saying it may be subject to increased noise and accident potential. If you are a developer offering subdivided lands for lease, the public report rules can reach you; check them separately. For an ordinary rental, telling the tenant voluntarily is a sound practice where the location is in a military airport vicinity.

title: Renting to Minors
bodyText: In Arizona an adult is a person who has turned 18, and a minor is anyone under 18. We found no Arizona statute that lets a person under 18 contract to lease a home, says whether a lease signed by a minor binds the minor, or limits naming a minor as a defendant in an eviction case. One rule is clear. A court may emancipate a minor who is at least 16, lives in Arizona and is financially self-sufficient, and an emancipation order recognizes the minor as an adult for entering into a binding contract, suing and being sued, establishing a legal residence and incurring debts. Whether an unemancipated minor's lease can be enforced against the minor is left to case law, which this library hasn't searched. The cautious course: have the lease signed by an adult, or by an emancipated minor who shows you the court order. If a minor will live in the unit with a parent or guardian, have that adult sign as the tenant. Who must be named and served in an eviction is set by the court rules, which this library hasn't read.

title: Utility Liens and Tenant Bills
bodyText: A city or town may file a lien on your property for sewer user fees more than 90 days delinquent, after giving you at least 30 days' written notice with a chance for a hearing, and a county that runs a sewage system may do the same for its sewer user fees. Neither may file that lien on residential property occupied by a tenant who is responsible for paying the fees, and the city, town or county must check whether the property is leased before filing. For residential property of four or fewer units, a city water or wastewater service, a city sewer service, a private water company and a sewer corporation may not make anyone pay a past-due bill except the person who contracted for the service, lived at the property and received it, and a city can't refuse service to a new occupant because of the old occupant's unpaid water or wastewater bill. You may choose to put the service in your own name, and then you must pay it. The payment and refusal-of-service protections don't cover buildings of five or more units (the sewer-lien exception for tenant-paid fees has no unit limit), and we found no Arizona statute that creates a lien on your property for a tenant's unpaid electric, gas or garbage bill, or that makes you answer for a tenant's account in your tenant's name. To keep the protections, have the tenant contract for the service in the tenant's own name and state in the lease that the tenant pays it.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential landlord of a house or apartment to have good cause to end or not renew a tenancy, to state a reason in a termination or nonrenewal notice, or to tell tenants whether a good-cause rule covers their unit. You may end a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 10 days before the termination date stated in the notice, and a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date stated in the notice, without giving a reason. A notice for a tenant's breach is different: it must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach. Mobile home parks and long-term recreational vehicle spaces are under separate acts that do require good cause and a written statement of the reasons with specific facts, so these rules don't carry over to them. If the unit is in the federal Housing Choice Voucher program, federal rules limit the grounds on which you may end the tenancy during the lease term, and to end it during the term you must give the tenant a written notice that specifies the grounds, at or before the start of the eviction case. That notice may be part of, or combined with, your eviction notice, and you must give the housing agency a copy of any eviction notice. Ending a tenancy is still unlawful if it is retaliation or discrimination.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets a maximum term for a residential lease. Without a definite term, a tenancy is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly). A lease for longer than one year must be in writing: no court action can be brought on an agreement to lease for longer than one year unless the agreement, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against or that party's authorized agent, and if an agent signs, the agent's authority must also be in writing and signed. A lease term of more than one year in land can be conveyed only by a written instrument signed and delivered by the owner or the owner's agent authorized in writing. The deed statute also requires every deed or conveyance of real property to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other officer; the statutes don't say whether a long lease counts as a conveyance, so for a lease longer than one year the cautious course is to have the owner's signature acknowledged. If the property is community property, see the spouses row.

title: Spouses and Long Leases
bodyText: If the rental property is the community property of a married owner, Arizona requires both spouses to join in any lease of one year or more: either spouse may manage community property alone, except that both must join in any transaction disposing of or encumbering an interest in real property other than a lease of less than one year. So a standard 12-month lease of community property needs both spouses' signatures; a lease shorter than one year (for example month-to-month or six months) may be signed by either spouse. Either spouse may authorize the other by a power of attorney signed and acknowledged like a deed. A separate statute says a conveyance or encumbrance of community property is valid only if both spouses execute and acknowledge it; the statutes don't say whether a lease is a conveyance for that purpose, so for a lease longer than one year the cautious course is to have both spouses' signatures acknowledged before a notary. A spouse's separate property is managed by that spouse alone.

title: Five-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
If rent is unpaid when due, give the tenant written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within five days. If the tenant does not pay within five days after the notice, you may terminate by filing a special detainer action.

The days are calendar days. Arizona's statute prescribes no wording, form or type size for the notice, and no move-in acknowledgment. Deliver it in hand or by registered or certified mail; a notice sent by registered or certified mail is received when the tenant actually gets it or five days after mailing, whichever comes first. To be safe, count the five days from the date the tenant receives the notice.

Before you file, the rental agreement is reinstated if the tenant tenders all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee set forth in a written rental agreement; after you file, the tenant must also pay attorney fees and court costs; after judgment in your favor, reinstatement is your choice. The statute sets no limit on how often a tenant may reinstate this way.

The notice comes after the rent is unpaid, so the lease cannot serve as it, and a lease term that waives the notice or shortens the five days is unenforceable, because a rental agreement may not waive the tenant's rights under the Act. The older general landlord-tenant rule that no notice is needed for nonpayment under a month-to-month lease does not apply to a dwelling unit under the Act, because the Act governs any conflict.

If the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate also applies. The court rules for eviction actions may add requirements; we did not hold them.

title: Out-of-State Owners Must Record an Arizona Agent
bodyText: If you own residential rental property in Arizona and live outside the state, you must designate and record with the county assessor a statutory agent who lives in Arizona and will accept legal service for you, giving the agent's name, address and telephone number. The agent goes on file with the assessor registration every rental owner must keep (see edu-rental-registration-az). The property may not be occupied unless the registration is on file; if it is not, a tenant may give a written 10-day notice to comply and, if you do not comply, terminate and get back all prepaid rent. Separately, at or before move-in you must tell the tenant in writing the name and address of an owner, or of a person authorized to act for the owner to accept service of process and to receive and receipt for notices and demands (see landlord-disclosure-az). If that disclosure is not made, the person who fails to make it becomes your agent for service, notices and your duties as landlord. The statutes do not make you name the assessor-recorded agent in every lease beyond that disclosure. If you own through an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation, the company must also register with the Arizona Corporation Commission before doing business here, naming an Arizona statutory agent, and until it does it may not maintain a lawsuit, including an eviction, in an Arizona court; owning property, without more, is not doing business, but whether renting it out is more is a case-law question, so register before filing (A.R.S. §§ 10-1501, 10-1502(A), 29-3902(A), (B), 29-3903(A)(5), 29-3905(A)(10)). If a foreign corporation fails to appoint or keep a statutory agent, the Commission becomes its agent for service (A.R.S. § 10-1510(B)). We found no Arizona statute that requires a tenant to withhold income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner. The income tax title (Title 43) is held as headings only, and none of its withholding headings mentions rent; ask your tax adviser about your own Arizona filing duties.

title: No Rule on Move-Out Forms or Work During a Notice
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a warning on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign when the form adds terms not in the lease, or that bars alterations or work that make the unit hard to live in while a notice to vacate is pending. Keep any such form to the move-out date and a forwarding address. The Act treats all agreements, written or oral, as part of the rental agreement, so a signed form can add terms, but a term in it that waives the tenant's rights under the Act is unenforceable. Until the tenancy ends, your duties continue: keep the premises fit and habitable and keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities you supply in good and safe working order. If you willfully interrupt electric, gas, water or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate and recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater.

title: Where Arizona Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Arizona lets a lease include any term not prohibited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other law. Several rules give way only to what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the default. (1) Rent: due without demand or notice at the time and place you agree; if the lease is silent, at the unit, at the start of a term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month, apportioned day by day. (2) Term: without a definite term, the tenancy is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly). (3) Use: the tenant may use the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise (residential-use-only). (4) Late fees: only a reasonable late fee set forth in a written rental agreement is part of what a tenant pays to reinstate, and the court awards late charges stated in the rental agreement (late-fee-az). (5) Attorney fees: a written agreement may award fees only to the prevailing party in court; a one-way clause for your fees is prohibited. (6) Deposit: at the end of the tenancy the deposit may be applied to rent and to charges specified in the signed lease or allowed by the Act; state the purpose of every nonrefundable fee in writing, or it is refundable (nonrefundable-fees-az). (7) Repairs: in a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, for adequate consideration, that the tenant handles garbage removal and the water, heat and cooling supply duties, and specified repairs or maintenance; in other units, specified tasks need a separate signed writing (maintenance-allocation-az). Neither may cover work needed to meet building codes or keep the unit fit and habitable. (8) Utilities: billing utilities separately requires a lease disclosure, and starting a submeter or ratio billing during the term requires a lease term allowing it plus notice (utility-billing-disclosure-az). (9) Sale: unless otherwise agreed, a selling landlord or departing manager is released from later events after written notice to the tenant (edu-selling-rented-property-az). (10) Contacts: you may ask the tenant to name a person authorized to retrieve the tenant's property and animal if the tenant dies or is incapacitated. A lease with an option to purchase: we found no Arizona statute that requires you to give the tenant a seller's disclosure statement before signing such a lease. Note that occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale is outside the Act.

title: Facilities You Must Supply and Maintain
bodyText: Beyond the general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and to follow building codes that materially affect health and safety, Arizona's Act names these facilities. Keep all common areas clean and safe. Keep in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facility and every other facility and appliance, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply; a garage door opener, laundry machine or other appliance you supply falls under this duty. Provide and maintain receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for their removal. Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat and reasonable air-conditioning or cooling where those units are installed and offered, when seasonal weather requires; this does not apply where the building is not required by law to have them, or where the heat, cooling or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own utility connection. In a single family residence the tenant may take over the waste and the water, heat and cooling duties by a written agreement (maintenance-allocation-az). See edu-landlord-maintenance-az for the full repair duty, smoke-detector-duty-az for smoke detectors and pool-safety-notice-az for pools. We found no Arizona statute that adds a landlord duty for other building facilities, such as automatic garage door openers, telephone jacks or wiring, window screens or mail receptacles. Elevator safety rules sit in the labor title, which we hold as headings only, and local building codes may add requirements.

title: Giving Tenants Your Parking Rules
bodyText:
Arizona has no statute written for tenant parking rules. We found none that sets when you must hand them over, prescribes a heading, limits mid-term changes beyond the general rules statute, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term.

Parking rules are rules under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so the general test decides whether they bind the tenant. A rule is enforceable only if it promotes the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property or fairly distributes facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants fairly; is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; is not meant to evade your duties; and the tenant had notice of it when entering the rental agreement. A rule adopted later binds the tenant only if you give 30 days' notice of its adoption and it is not a substantial modification of the lease.

So give the parking rules with the lease, and give 30 days' written notice of any new rule.

Towing is separate: inside a city or town, the parking area must carry the statutory signs, or you are treated as allowing unrestricted public parking, and a towing company may tow only with your written authorization or a law enforcement request.

title: Scheduled Services Still Need Two Days' Notice
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that lets you enter for regularly scheduled services, such as pest treatment or filter changes, without notice, even if the lease says so.

The ordinary access rule applies: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to supply necessary or agreed services, and, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. A lease term that drops the notice is unenforceable, because a rental agreement may not waive the tenant's rights under the Act.

One exception helps: when the tenant asks in writing for maintenance or a service, the request is permission to enter for that purpose and the tenant waives a separate notice.

If you enter unlawfully or unreasonably, or make repeated harassing demands for entry, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages of at least one month's rent.

You may list recurring services in the lease as agreed services (scheduled-services-entry-az) and give notice before each visit (landlords-access-az).

title: No Pesticide Notice Rule for Rentals
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to notify tenants before pesticides are applied or pest control is done in or around a rental. Arizona's pesticide-notice statutes we found cover child care facilities and schools. The pest management chapter (Title 3) is held as headings only, and none of its headings mentions residential or tenant notice; the pest management rules in the Arizona Administrative Code were not held, and your pest control company may have its own duties under them. Two rules do apply. To treat inside a unit, give the tenant at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable (landlords-access-az). For any rental other than a single family residence, you must give existing and new tenants bedbug educational materials and may not lease a unit you know has a current bedbug infestation, and a tenant who knows of bedbugs must notify you in writing or electronically (bedbug-obligations-az). Cities, towns and counties may not add their own landlord-tenant bedbug control rules, except on disposing of infested items.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or other notice about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat. What Arizona does say about a tenant's animals when a tenancy ends: after you retake an abandoned unit, and on the day after a writ of restitution is executed, you need not store the tenant's animals. Once you have notified any person the tenant authorized to retrieve the animal and no one retrieves it within one calendar day, you may release the animal to a shelter or boarding facility and must keep a record of where it went. If you keep the animal instead, you must give it reasonable care, and if you cannot or will not, you must notify county or city animal control. You are not liable for good-faith actions in removing, releasing or caring for the animal. You may ask the tenant at move-in to name a person authorized to retrieve the tenant's animal (authorized-person-contact-az). See edu-abandoned-property-az and pet-policy-az.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential lease to meet a plain-language or readability test, to be divided into captioned sections, or to follow consumer-contract drafting rules. Arizona's plain-English rules we found cover other contracts, such as senior residential entrance-fee contracts. What does apply to the form of your lease: a written lease must have every blank completed, and you and the tenant must each deliver a signed copy to the other within a reasonable time; failing to do so is a material noncompliance (edu-lease-completeness-az). At or before move-in you must tell the tenant in writing that the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website (landlord-disclosure-az). Whether the Consumer Fraud Act reaches an ordinary lease turns on case law we did not review (edu-consumer-fraud-act-az). Clear wording still matters: prohibited terms are unenforceable (edu-prohibited-lease-terms-az).

title: No Front-Page Consumer Statement Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a residential lease to carry a front-page statement listing the terms that limit the tenant's rights, to pass a readability test, or to be preapproved by the Attorney General, and no plain-language law with a dollar threshold that reaches leases. Because Arizona has no such statement, there is nothing to list. What protects the tenant instead is the Act's list of prohibited terms: a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act, agree to pay your attorney fees (except a written prevailing-party clause), agree to excuse or limit your legal liability or indemnify you for it, or waive or be penalized for calling police or emergency help. Such a term is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with terms you know are prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages and up to two months' periodic rent (edu-prohibited-lease-terms-az). See also edu-no-plain-language-rule-az.

title: No Political Access Rule for Landlords
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to let political candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators into an apartment building or complex, to set aside an area for voter information, or to let a tenant display political signs despite a lease rule. The election title (Title 16) is held as headings only, and none of its headings mentions access to residential property. Related rules: if your rental is in a condominium or planned community, the association may not prohibit door-to-door political activity or the circulation of political petitions on property normally open to visitors, though it may bar the activity from sunset to sunrise, require identification tags, and keep out anyone not accompanied by a resident where access to the community is restricted. The association statutes that protect political signs and flags protect a unit owner or member on that owner's property; they do not mention tenants. You may not retaliate against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization by raising rent, cutting services or bringing or threatening an eviction. Any rule you adopt on signs or solicitation must meet the Act's test for rules (see edu-parking-rules-notice-az for the test).

title: No Tenant Right to Install Cooling Units
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a tenant of a house or apartment a right to install a portable or window cooling device, or that requires a lease restricting window units to say so. Arizona gave a cooling right only to park tenants: a mobile home park landlord may not prohibit a tenant from installing reasonably necessary commercial cooling methods on the tenant's mobile home (since 2024), and a long-term RV park landlord may not do so for certain recreational vehicles (since 2025). Those acts do not reach a dwelling unit you rent under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. What does apply to you: where air-conditioning or cooling units are installed and offered, you must supply reasonable cooling when seasonal weather requires and keep the equipment in good and safe working order; and the building-code conditions your repair duty points to include lack of adequate heating and cooling. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply cooling you have installed and offered, the tenant may give notice and use the statutory remedies, including damages for the reduced rental value or substitute housing. A rule limiting window or portable units must meet the Act's test for rules, and the tenant must not damage the premises in installing one. City codes may add cooling standards.

title: Tenant Solar Devices and Lease Bans
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a tenant a specific right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, or that lets a tenant connect one without utility approval. But a general Arizona statute may reach your lease. Any covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract or other instrument affecting the transfer or sale of, or any interest in, real property that effectively prohibits installing or using a solar energy device is void and unenforceable. A lease is a contract that gives the tenant an interest in real property, and nothing we read limits the rule to sales. A solar energy device is a system designed primarily to provide heating, cooling, electrical or mechanical power or daylighting from solar energy, used primarily to serve on-site demand at a residential dwelling unit or multifamily structure. So do not put a flat ban on tenant solar devices in an Arizona lease. Use conditions that do not effectively prohibit one: placement, safe installation by the rules that apply, no damage to the premises, and removal and repair at move-out. The tenant must not damage the premises, and the shared alterations clause yields to any installation the law entitles the tenant to make (no-alterations). In a planned community, the association also may not prohibit solar devices and may adopt only reasonable placement rules.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets you require a tenant to post a bond, or sign a confessed judgment, to secure giving up possession when the lease ends. Do not add one. Money or property a tenant gives to assure performance of the lease is security under the Act, however it is named, so a possession bond counts toward the limit on all security (the deposit cap is answered under the security-deposit-cap topic). A lease term in which the tenant agrees in advance to a judgment for possession would waive the tenant's rights and defenses under the Act, which a rental agreement may not do (the confession-of-judgment topic answers that term). If a tenant stays after the term ends without your consent, bring an action for possession; for a willful holdover not in good faith you may also recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice your actual damages, whichever is greater. The bonds Arizona law does know arise inside an eviction case: a party appealing a justice court judgment files a bond for costs, and a tenant who wants to stay the judgment for possession during the appeal must post a supersedeas bond covering rent to the next rental date, plus costs and attorney fees, and pay each period's rent into the court as it falls due.

title: Tenant Property After an Eviction Writ
bodyText: On the day after a writ of restitution is executed, you must handle the tenant's belongings under the abandonment rules (edu-abandoned-property-az). Prepare an inventory and send the tenant notice of where the property is and what storage costs, by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the last known and any alternate addresses, and post it on the door or another conspicuous place. You may store the property in the vacated unit, another available unit, your own storage space or off the premises. Perishables and plants may be disposed of, and items that are contaminated, may be a biohazard or pose a health and safety risk may be removed and disposed of. Animals: you need not store them; once you have notified any person the tenant authorized to retrieve an animal and no one comes within one calendar day, you may release it to a shelter or boarding facility and must record where it went; if you keep it, give it reasonable care, and if you cannot, notify county or city animal control. Hold the rest for 14 calendar days with reasonable care. If the tenant notifies you in writing before you dispose of it, the tenant has five days to reclaim it by paying removal and storage costs, and may take clothing, work tools and personal documents without paying. After 14 days you may donate it to a qualifying charity or sell it, applying the proceeds to rent and costs and mailing any excess to the tenant, and keep records for 12 months. If you follow these rules, you are not liable for loss from moving, storing or donating the property; you are not liable for good-faith actions in handling animals. If the tenant returned the keys, you may dispose of what is left at once unless you agreed otherwise in writing. You may also discontinue utilities you provide on the day after the writ is executed, using only a person the utility authorizes. The writ may not issue until five calendar days after judgment, and a tenant served with it who stays or comes back without permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule for Rentals
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to test a private well serving a rental or to give tenants the test results. The groundwater code (Title 45) is held as headings only; its well headings cover registration, construction, drilling, capping and inspection for cross-contamination, and none mentions testing for tenants. Environmental quality and health department rules were not held. What does apply: you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, and keep the premises fit and habitable, so water from a well you supply has to be fit to use. If you have test results showing a problem, deal with it as a repair. If the tenant is responsible for the well under a written agreement for a single family residence, that agreement cannot cover work needed to meet code or keep the unit habitable (maintenance-allocation-az).

title: Written Promises About Repairs and Condition
bodyText: Arizona has no rule that a promise to clean, repair or improve the unit must be in writing with a completion date, or given before the lease is signed; we found none. But what you put in writing binds you. A material falsification of the written information you give the tenant is a material noncompliance with the rental agreement, and it includes false information about the condition of the premises and current services as you represented them in writing, and any representation about future services or future changes to the condition of the premises. The tenant may then give a written notice that the lease will end at least ten days after receipt unless you remedy the breach within ten days, and may recover damages and get an injunction. The rental agreement also includes oral agreements, so a spoken promise can become a term too. Put any repair or improvement you agree to make in writing, describe it plainly, give a realistic completion date, and keep it. Your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable applies whatever you promise (edu-landlord-maintenance-az).

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute like California's Proposition 65 that requires you to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm at a rental property. Arizona's chemical warning statutes we found are product-label and sales rules (for example marijuana product labels and vapor-releasing substances), not landlord duties. Federal disclosures still apply where they reach your property, such as the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 (lead-based-paint). Your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable also applies.

title: Rules That Turn on Property Size or Type
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no small-landlord exemption: it applies to every rental of a dwelling unit, and its exclusions turn on the kind of arrangement (for example a hotel stay or a buyer under a contract of sale), not on how many units you own. A few rules do turn on your portfolio or the type of property. (1) Fair housing: the state fair housing sections on sales and rentals do not apply to a single family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three single family houses at a time (counting any interest in the proceeds of more than three), but only if the owner rents it without a licensed broker or agent and without a discriminatory notice or advertisement; both limbs must be met, and if the owner was not the most recent resident, the exemption covers only one rental in 24 months. They also do not apply to rooms or units in a building for no more than four families when the owner lives in one of them. The federal Fair Housing Act has the same two exemptions in close to the same words, with two differences. First, even an exempt rental stays under the federal ban on any notice, statement or advertisement that shows a preference, limitation or discrimination, so never advertise a preference, even for a room or unit in a building of four or fewer units you live in. Second, the federal single-house exemption is lost if you rent through a broker or agent or through anyone in the business of renting dwellings, which includes anyone who in the past 12 months took part as principal in three or more sales or rentals of a dwelling, or who owns a dwelling for five or more families (see edu-fair-housing-az). (2) Foreclosure notice: the duty to tell tenants about a foreclosure does not apply to multifamily rental units of four or more connected units (foreclosure-notice-az). (3) Bedbugs: the bedbug duties do not apply to a single family residence (bedbug-obligations-az). (4) Repairs and services: in a single family residence the tenant may take over specified duties by a written agreement; in any other unit, specified tasks need a separate signed writing (maintenance-allocation-az). (5) Waste service: a multifamily property with five or more rental dwelling units must give its city or town at least 60 calendar days' notice to end recycling or solid waste service. The county assessor registration applies to every owner of residential rental property, whatever the size (edu-rental-registration-az). We found no other Arizona landlord duty tiered by the number of units you own.

title: Property Tax Share of Rent Statement on Request
bodyText: If a tenant asks, you must give the tenant a written statement of the percentage of the rent payments that goes to property tax. The duty applies to the owner or lessor of property rented solely for residential purposes. The statement supports Arizona's income tax credit for property taxes or rent paid, a credit for certain residents 65 or older: a renter counts the gross rent paid for the right to occupy the renter's homestead (the principal dwelling, which can include a mobile home and its land), and space rent paid to a landlord to park a mobile home counts too. The state will not allow the credit if it finds the rent was paid solely to get the credit. The parts of the statute we hold set no form, deadline or penalty for the statement, so answer a request promptly, in writing, and keep a copy. Rent itself is what the lease says (edu-fees-as-rent-az); for the end of city taxes on residential rent, see edu-rental-tax-az.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance or munitions site near the property, about a demolition permit you have applied for, or that the tenant's gas or electric meter also serves common areas or other units. Arizona's military disclosures are for sales: the Real Estate Commissioner records a notice for land near a military airport, and a subdivision public report must say when property is under a military training route or in a military range or influence area. The military airport disclosure for residential property in the transportation title binds only public reports, sale reservation documents and sellers of residential real estate; it puts no duty on a landlord or a lease. If you bill a utility separately through a submeter or ratio billing, the lease must list the utilities billed separately and the administrative fee (utility-billing-disclosure-az). If you plan to demolish, end a periodic tenancy with the notice the Act requires (edu-periodic-tenancy-termination-az).

title: Criminal Use Does Not Void the Lease by Itself
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that makes a lease void, or annuls it, just because the tenant uses the home for a crime or another prohibited purpose. The lease stays in force until you end it. What Arizona does instead: (1) You may end the lease. For a material and irreparable breach on the premises, such as an illegal discharge of a weapon, prostitution, criminal street gang activity, making, selling or storing illegal drugs, threats, assault, or acts a court has found to be a crime nuisance, you may deliver a written notice of immediate termination and file a special detainer action; other material breaches need a 10-day notice to cure (edu-eviction-process-az). (2) Others can sue you. Residential property regularly used to commit a crime is a nuisance. Once you have notice from a government authority of documented criminal reports, you must take reasonable, legally available steps to stop it, or a court can order an injunction, costs, a civil penalty of up to $10,000, a receiver (who may renew, end or change existing leases) or the closing of the unit, and can make you refund deposits and pay moving help to innocent tenants ordered out (edu-crime-nuisance-abatement-az). A building used for lewdness, assignation or prostitution is also a nuisance, and a judgment can close it to all use for one year. (3) Acting helps: a restraining order based only on a tenant's criminal activity ends if you bring an eviction action against that tenant, unless the court finds you brought it in bad faith.

title: No Duty to Tell Tenants How to Recycle
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to tell tenants where or how to recycle at the property, or to provide recycling for them. Two related state rules: (1) Every city and town must give its residents an opportunity to recycle, so your tenants may already have a city program; check local rules. (2) If your property has five or more dwelling units rented under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, it counts as a multifamily residential property, and you must give the city or town at least 60 calendar days' notice before ending recycling or solid waste service; a city may not bar a private hauler from serving you (edu-portfolio-thresholds-az). If you do offer recycling, telling tenants where the bins are and what goes in them is good practice, not a legal duty.

title: Tenant's Right to Reinstate After Nonpayment
bodyText: Arizona lets a tenant behind on rent save the tenancy, in three stages. (1) Before you file a special detainer (eviction) action, the lease is reinstated if the tenant pays all past-due rent plus a reasonable late fee set out in a written lease. (2) After you file, the lease is reinstated only if the tenant pays all past-due rent, reasonable late fees set out in a written lease, attorney fees and court costs. (3) After a judgment for you, reinstatement is up to you. You do not have to accept a partial payment. If you do accept one and want to keep your right to evict, have the tenant sign, at the time of payment, a written agreement on the terms of the partial payment that states the date the balance is due; otherwise, accepting rent while knowing of the default waives your right to terminate for that breach. A housing assistance payment is not a partial payment and does not waive your rights. A writ of restitution cannot issue until five calendar days after judgment. Court rules on what the eviction complaint must say about reinstatement were not checked (edu-eviction-court-rules-az); the overall process is in edu-eviction-process-az.

title: No Specific Religious Display Right
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives tenants a specific right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame or a religious symbol on a door, or that limits what a landlord may say about them in a lease. Your rules on what tenants may attach to doors, walls and common areas are ordinary rental agreement terms. Two limits still apply. Arizona's fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion or national origin, so a rule that singles out religious or cultural items, or that you enforce against one faith or culture and not others, invites a fair housing claim (edu-fair-housing-az). And under the Act, a rule binds tenants only if it serves tenant convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property from abusive use or fairly shares facilities, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies to all tenants fairly, and the tenant had notice of it on signing (or 30 days' notice of a later rule that is not a substantial change). The safest course: write any decoration rule in neutral terms (for example, about size, damage and fire safety), apply it the same way to everyone, and consider allowing small door-frame items that cause no damage.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit with Code Violations
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or from serving a nonpayment notice, because the unit has code violations, has been cited by an inspector, or has been designated slum property. The tenant also may not withhold rent for any reason the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not authorize. But you cannot collect rent free of your duty to keep the unit fit: no lease or other instrument may allow that, and unrepaired conditions cut into what you are owed in specific ways. Rent abates if you fail to deliver physical possession at the start of the tenancy, though not merely because the unit is out of repair. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply water, gas, electricity, hot water, heat or cooling where installed, or essential services, the tenant may buy the service and deduct its cost, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent while the failure lasts. After fire or casualty the tenant may pay reduced rent for the part still usable. And in your eviction or rent case the tenant may counterclaim for what you owe; the court may order rent paid into court, and if no rent remains due after the counterclaim, the tenant wins the possession case. Separately, a rental whose owner information is not on file with the county assessor may not be occupied, and the tenant may end the lease after a ten-day notice (edu-rental-registration-az). For a condemned or vacated unit, see edu-no-condemned-rent-bar-az. Fix reported conditions promptly and keep records; that protects your right to the full rent.

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
Arizona lets you and the tenant agree when and where rent is paid, so a lease may split the monthly rent into scheduled installments (for example, half on the 1st and half on the 15th); use the optional clause rent-installments-or and state each amount and due date.

If the lease says nothing, rent is due at the unit, at the start of a term of one month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month.

We found no Arizona statute that says whether a scheduled installment is a partial payment. Writing the schedule into the lease settles it: an installment paid in full on its date is the rent then due.

That matters because you do not have to accept a partial payment, and accepting one keeps your right to proceed against the tenant only if the tenant signs a contemporaneous written agreement on its terms, with the date the balance is due.

Paying more than once a month does not by itself make the tenancy week-to-week: absent a definite term, only a roomer who pays weekly rent has a week-to-week tenancy; everyone else is month-to-month. Treat each installment as rent due on its own date for your five-day nonpayment notice and for any late fee your written lease sets.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In an Arizona eviction for nonpayment, or a suit for rent while the tenant still lives in the unit, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount the tenant can recover under the lease or the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, such as damages for repairs you failed to make. After notice and a hearing, the court may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the undisputed rent already accrued and the rent as it comes due, and then decides what each side owes; whoever is owed a net amount is paid first from that money and the rest by the other side. If no rent remains due after the counterclaim, or the tenant is found to have acted in good faith and pays a rent judgment entered for you, the tenant wins the possession case. A tenant who has moved out may still counterclaim in your suit for rent but does not have to pay rent into court. We found no Arizona statute that makes the counterclaim mandatory, that requires the tenant to pay rent into court before raising a defense, or that ties a rent deposit to a trial postponement, which is limited to three days in justice court or five in superior court for good cause shown by affidavit. On an appeal from justice court, a tenant who wants to stop the judgment for possession must post a bond and pay the rent to the justice court clerk on each rent due date; if the tenant raised habitability as a defense or counterclaim, the court holds that money until final judgment. The Rules of Procedure for Eviction Actions also govern counterclaims and are not covered here (edu-eviction-court-rules-az). If a counterclaim is filed, ask the court for a rent-into-court order early, and keep your repair records ready.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting, that creates a state rent-reporting program, that lets or stops a tenant opting out of one, or that requires you to notify the tenant before reporting late rent to a credit bureau. Whether to report rent payments is your choice, and the lease may say what you will report. If you do report, report accurately. Under Arizona's consumer reporting law, a source of information that is grossly negligent in the use or preparation of a consumer report, or that acts wilfully and maliciously with intent to harm a consumer, is liable for actual damages, punitive damages, attorney fees and court costs. Federal credit reporting law also sets duties for anyone who furnishes information to a credit bureau; check them before you start (FEDERAL, not read in this pass). Report only rent and charges the tenant actually owes, correct errors promptly, and keep the payment records that back up each report.

title: No Renter's Insurance Statute
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute on requiring renter's insurance in a dwelling lease.

No statute says the tenant must be free to choose the insurer, regulates buying a policy for a tenant who fails to and charging the tenant for it, caps an administrative fee, or requires you to tell the tenant in writing that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings.

So you may require renter's insurance as an ordinary lease term; the library's clause tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca, tagged for Arizona, does this and also tells the tenant your insurance does not cover the tenant's property.

Two limits apply. First, a lease may not make the tenant agree to the exculpation or limitation of your liability, or to indemnify you for it; an insurance term written as a release of your own liability is unenforceable, and deliberately using a provision you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages and up to two months' rent.

Second, apply the requirement to every tenant the same way, because fair housing law bars different terms because of a protected class.

If you want to buy a policy for a tenant who doesn't and charge for it, check Arizona's insurance code (Title 20, which we hold by section heading only) on who may sell or place insurance before you do.

title: No Right to End the Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets you refuse a repair and end the lease because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and none that gives the tenant such a right. Your duty to make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable has no cost limit, and no lease may let you collect rent free of it. Your ways out are the ordinary ones. A fixed-term lease runs to its end date. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date the notice names (10 days for week-to-week), but not in retaliation: a notice served within six months after the tenant complained to a code agency or to you about your maintenance duties is presumed retaliatory. After fire or casualty, the statute gives the tenant, not you, the right to end the lease or pay reduced rent; the optional clause casualty-landlord-termination-az adds a landlord right for casualty damage only. The one cost figure in Arizona's landlord-tenant act runs the other way: a tenant may have a minor defect fixed by a licensed contractor and deduct the cost when it is less than $300 or half a month's rent, whichever is greater, after written notice and ten days. If a repair truly isn't worth making, plan the exit with the notice rules above and keep the unit fit until the tenancy ends.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption From Repair Remedies
bodyText: Some states let tenants pay rent into an escrow account while repairs are outstanding, and let a landlord with few units opt out by giving the tenant a notice. Arizona has neither: we found no Arizona rent-escrow procedure for repairs and no notice or other procedure that excuses a landlord with few units, or an owner who lives on site, from the tenant's repair remedies. The tenant's rights to end the lease after written notice, recover damages, repair and deduct for minor defects, use the essential-services remedies, act after fire or casualty, and counterclaim in your rent or eviction case apply however few units you own. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act leaves out only listed kinds of occupancy, such as transient hotel or motel stays, employee-manager housing, occupancy under a contract of sale and public housing, and none of these exclusions applies if the arrangement was created to avoid the Act. A lease term claiming an exemption would be a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act, which is unenforceable, and deliberately using a provision you know is prohibited can cost you actual damages and up to two months' rent. Do not copy another state's exemption notice into an Arizona lease. The nearest Arizona tool is the court's power to order rent paid into court when a tenant counterclaims (edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-az).

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice
bodyText: Arizona makes written repair notice the tenant's duty: the tenant must promptly notify you in writing of anything that needs maintenance or repair or otherwise requires you to act under your repair duties (the library's tenant-maintenance and landlord-maintenance clauses, both tagged for Arizona, say so). The tenant's remedies then turn on different kinds of notice. To end the lease for your breach, the tenant must give you a written notice describing it. To repair and deduct for a minor defect, the tenant must notify you in writing. But for a failure of water, gas, electricity, hot water, heat, cooling or essential services, the statute asks only for reasonable notice, not writing, except that a tenant who will pay your delinquent utility bill must first give you written notice of that intent. And under the Act you have notice of a fact you actually know, were told, or had reason to know from the facts and circumstances, so a phone call, text or portal ticket that reaches you can count. A lease term making a written request the only way to give you notice can't cut off a remedy the statute doesn't tie to writing; that would be a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act, which is unenforceable. We found no Arizona statute that says a lease inviting phone or verbal repair requests gives up the written notice the statute requires for termination or repair and deduct. The safe course: accept and log every request however it arrives, say in the lease that urgent problems may be phoned in but must also be put in writing, and act on what you know. A tenant's maintenance request also counts as permission to enter for that repair under your access rules (landlords-access-az).

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to tell tenants about a housing, health or building code variance or exception granted for your rental, or to attach one to the rental agreement. Arizona has no statewide housing or sanitary code for private rentals in its statutes; your code duty is to comply with the applicable building codes materially affecting health and safety, and the statutes list the conditions that count, while the codes themselves are local. If a local code official grants a variance, the local code may attach its own conditions, including notice; check it, because local codes were not searched. A variance from a code does not by itself change your separate statutory duty to make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable. If you hold a variance that affects what a tenant will experience, such as room size, ventilation or exits, telling the tenant in writing before signing avoids a later claim that you misrepresented the unit's condition.

title: What the Arizona Landlord and Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: The Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (A.R.S. title 33, chapter 10) governs the rental of dwelling units located in Arizona, wherever the rental agreement was made. A dwelling unit is a structure, or part of one, used as a home, residence or sleeping place by one household. Where the Act conflicts with Arizona's general landlord-tenant chapter (chapter 3) or the lien chapter (chapter 7), the Act controls, and chapter 3 does not govern the rental of dwelling units. Seven arrangements are outside the Act, unless they were created to avoid it: residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, educational, counseling, religious or social services; occupancy under a contract to buy the unit; housing run for a fraternal or social organization's members; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or recreational lodging; an employee manager or custodian whose right to occupy depends on that job; occupancy by a condominium owner or a cooperative's proprietary lessee; and public housing under Arizona's public housing law or federal law. Other acts govern other rentals: a mobile home space in a mobile home park is under the Mobile Home Parks Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (chapter 11), though a mobile home the landlord itself rents out is a dwelling unit under chapter 10; and a recreational vehicle space rented to the same tenant for more than 180 consecutive days in an RV or mobile home park is under chapter 19. Some rules inside the Act have their own limits, such as the bedbug rules (not for a single family residence), the foreclosure notice (not for four or more connected units) and the rules on shifting repair tasks to the tenant, which differ for a single family residence. We found no Arizona exclusion for farm tenancies, for leases of five years or more, or by county population or city. The Act doesn't define recreational lodging, so whether a vacation or short-term rental is transient occupancy is not settled by statute. For a lease of tribal trust land, see edu-no-communal-land-lease-approval-az.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Rules
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that creates a seasonal or winter-visitor tenancy, shortens notices for one, or exempts one from the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease of a house or apartment for a season to someone who lives there is an ordinary tenancy with the usual deposit, disclosure, repair and eviction rules. Write in exact start and end dates: a lease that fixes a definite term ends on its last day, while a rental with no definite term is month-to-month (week-to-week only for a roomer paying weekly) and needs a 30-day (or 10-day) written termination notice. If the tenant stays on after the end date without your consent, you may bring an action for possession, and a willful, bad-faith holdover can cost the tenant up to two months' rent or twice your actual damages; if you consent in writing to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes month-to-month. Two other regimes matter for seasonal stays. Transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or recreational lodging is outside the Act, though the Act doesn't define recreational lodging, so a vacation rental's status is not settled by statute. And an RV space rented to the same tenant for more than 180 consecutive days falls under the Recreational Vehicle Long-Term Rental Space Act (chapter 19); a mobile home space in a park falls under the mobile home act (chapter 11).

title: No Lock or Rekey Statute
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to provide particular locks, deadbolts, door viewers or other security devices in a rental, to rekey between tenants, or that sets a statutory duty of care for locks and keys. Your general duties still reach doors and windows. You must comply with applicable building codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable, and the statutory list of conditions that materially affect health and safety includes broken or missing windows or doors that create a hazardous condition or a potential attraction to trespassers. Two specific lock rules exist. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault may require a new lock at the tenant's cost; you may rekey a lock in good working condition or replace it with one of equal or better quality, keep a key, and refuse a key to the person named in the protection order or report (topic dv-lockchange). And where the house itself forms part of a required pool enclosure, ground-level doors with direct access to the pool need self-latching devices, and some windows need latches or limits, unless another listed barrier option is used (pool-safety-notice-az). Rekeying between tenants is not required by statute but is good practice; the library's keys clause covers lost keys and rekeying at the tenant's cost.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: Arizona bars self-help eviction. You may not recover or take possession of the unit, by action or otherwise, including by forcibly removing the tenant or the tenant's belongings or by willfully interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, except after abandonment or surrender or as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act permits, which means a court judgment and writ. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, or willfully interrupt an essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and, either way, recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; if the lease ends, you must return recoverable security. Cutting off a utility you provide under the lease, except to make needed repairs or on the day after a writ of restitution is executed, is a separate violation: the tenant may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees and get an injunction. Abusive entry has its own floor: an unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages of at least one month's rent. The full rules are in edu-prohibited-practices-az; for unpaid rent, see edu-lockout-for-rent-delinquency-az.

title: No Work-Card Rule for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires employees of 55-and-older or other senior rental housing to hold a work card, fingerprint clearance card or background check because of where they work. Arizona's fair housing law recognizes housing for older persons (for example, housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit, under Attorney General rules), but that exemption concerns familial status and says nothing about staff screening. Licensed care settings, such as assisted living facilities, have their own licensing rules and are not ordinary rental housing; and a person who manages property for others for compensation may need a real estate license, a separate matter. If you screen staff who will have keys or access to residents' units, follow the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's rules for employment background checks (FEDERAL, not read in this pass) and apply your policy consistently.

title: Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal: No Housing Penalty
bodyText: Arizona's penalty for misrepresenting a service animal does not reach housing. It bars fraudulently misrepresenting an animal as a service animal, or one in training, to a person or entity that operates a public place, with a civil penalty of up to $250 for each violation; a public place is an office or place of business or recreation to which the general public is invited, and the rule doesn't name dwellings. We found no Arizona statute that penalizes a tenant or applicant for misrepresenting an assistance or emotional support animal to a landlord, or that sets what documentation a landlord may require. Two rules help you instead. A material falsification on a rental application, including untrue or misleading information about pets, is a material noncompliance: you may serve a written notice that the lease will end in ten days unless the breach is remedied. And you are not liable for injuries or damage caused by a purported assistance or service animal you allow as a reasonable accommodation. Handle a doubtful request through the accommodation process, not by accusing the tenant: under fair housing law you may deny an animal whose presence would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and a wrongful denial is disability discrimination (edu-assistance-animals-az).

title: No Duty to Disclose Nearby Sex Offenders
bodyText: You don't have to tell a tenant that the rental is near a sex offender. Arizona bars any criminal, civil or administrative action against a lessor, or a real estate licensee, for failing to disclose that leased property is located in the vicinity of a sex offender, and failing to disclose it is not grounds to end or rescind the lease. We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease notice about the sex offender registry or its website. The same section covers deaths, felonies and certain diseases on the property (edu-disclosure-immunity-az). The immunity covers silence, not false statements: if a tenant asks, don't misstate what you know, and you may point the tenant to the state's public sex offender website.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Font Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a single-family home lease to carry an occupancy or anti-squatter notice, to put any disclosure at the top of the first page or in larger type than the rest of the lease, or to be notarized or signed by a licensed manager to prove the tenant's right to occupy. Arizona deals with people living in a home without right through the courts instead. If someone who is not a current or former tenant, not a cohabitant by prior agreement and not an immediate family member unlawfully occupies a residential property that wasn't open to the public, and refuses the owner's or authorized agent's reasonable request to leave, the owner may bring a forcible detainer action, and a writ of restitution issues immediately after the court signs a judgment against that person; the Supreme Court is to adopt rules for fast resolution. That route does not change the rules between you and your tenants: a tenant or former tenant is removed only through the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's eviction process (edu-eviction-process-az). A clear written lease, signed by both sides with all blanks completed and copies exchanged, is your best proof of who has the right to occupy.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease of a home on a lake, river or other waterfront to disclose public access rights to the shore or water, or any shoreline condition. If the rental includes a swimming pool or similar contained body of water, the pool safety notice applies instead (pool-safety-notice-az). Water rights and access to Arizona's rivers and lakes are governed by Title 45, which we hold by section heading only and did not read, so if your lease grants or limits the tenant's use of a dock, beach or water, describe exactly what is included and don't promise access you don't control.

title: No Government Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that delays rent, bars late fees or stays an eviction for a tenant who is a federal, state or local government worker furloughed or unpaid during a government shutdown. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due without demand at the time the lease sets, and if it goes unpaid you may serve the five-day nonpayment notice. Before you file an eviction, the tenant reinstates the lease by paying all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee set in the written lease. You may choose to help: you don't have to accept a partial payment, but if you do, you keep your right to proceed only if the tenant signs a written agreement at the time of the payment stating its terms and the date the balance is due (edu-partial-payments-az). A written payment plan of that kind is the practical tool for a tenant caught by a shutdown.

title: No State Limit on Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that limits renting a home in a single-family zone unless the owner lives on the lot, and no state lot-split program with an owner-occupancy or tenant-protection condition. Arizona's recent housing laws point the other way. A city or town of more than 75,000 people, and a county, may not prohibit using or advertising the main house or an accessory dwelling unit on the same lot as separately leased long-term rental housing (a lease of 90 days or longer, or month-to-month), and may not require a family, marital, employment or other preexisting relationship between the occupants of the house and the accessory unit. A larger city that must allow duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and townhomes in certain single-family areas may not require owner occupancy of any structure on the lot. Private restrictions are different: those state limits don't stop private covenants, and in a planned community you may rent your home unless the declaration prohibits it, following any rental-period limits in the declaration. Before you buy or lease a home in an association, read its documents. Short-term vacation rentals have their own state rules; local zoning was not searched, so check local codes as well (state limits on local rules: edu-local-preemption-az).

title: No Criminal Penalty for Denying an Assistance Animal in Housing
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that makes it a crime for a landlord to refuse a tenant's service or assistance animal in rental housing, or that requires a landlord to waive a lease's animal rules under a guide-dog or hearing-dog law. Arizona's criminal service-animal rule, a class 2 misdemeanor, binds anyone who operates a public place, defined as an office or place of business or recreation to which the general public is invited; it doesn't name dwellings or tenants' units. A leasing office or other area you open to the public may be a public place, so treat a visitor's service dog there under that rule. In housing, the duty is civil and it is real: refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services that a person with a disability may need, including an assistance animal, is disability discrimination under Arizona's fair housing law. A court may award actual and punitive damages, attorney fees and an injunction, and in an Attorney General pattern-or-practice case, a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for a later one. You may deny an animal whose presence would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Separately, it is a crime to knowingly interfere with or harm a service animal. See edu-assistance-animals-az.

title: Rent Changes During a Lease Term
bodyText:
Arizona has no statute written for rent escalation clauses.

Rent is a term you and the tenant set in the rental agreement, so a fixed-term lease may schedule rent changes (set amounts and dates, or a formula tied to a published index) or let you raise rent on written notice, as the optional clauses rent-escalation-la and rent-increase-midterm-ky do. Without such a term, the rent stated for the term holds until the term ends.

Cities and towns may not control rents on private housing.

Arizona's retaliation rule has no safe harbor that depends on an escalation clause. You may not retaliate by raising rent after a tenant complains to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, complains to you about a violation of your maintenance duties, or organizes or joins a tenants' union, and a complaint within six months before the increase creates a presumption of retaliation (not if the tenant complained after a notice of termination). The statute does not say whether an increase the lease already scheduled before the complaint is covered.

Write any escalation term plainly, with the dates, amounts or formula and the notice you will give: a court may refuse to enforce a provision it finds unconscionable when made.

title: No Special District Statement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease to state, or a landlord to represent, that the property lies in a special district, such as a community facilities district, improvement district or other special taxing or assessment district, or to have the tenant acknowledge a district's charges or plans. Arizona's district-debt disclosure is a subdivider's duty, not a landlord's: a subdivider offering lots for sale or lease must report to the real estate commissioner any special district debt to be repaid by taxes or assessments on the subdivision, but leasehold offerings of one year or less, and the leasing of apartments and similar space in an apartment building, are outside the subdivision rules. So nothing has to go in your lease. If you want the tenant to bear any part of a district tax or assessment, the lease must say so, because rent and other charges are terms you and the tenant agree on.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, when it was last inspected, or that it has none, and no state grant or loan program for sprinkler retrofits in rental housing. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a building and fire code question (see edu-no-fire-sprinkler-duty-az and edu-fire-code-standard-az). For a single family detached home or a building with no more than two dwelling units, a city, town or county may not take away the owner's choice to install sprinklers or not, except under a code requiring them adopted before December 31, 2009. Your duty is to comply with building codes materially affecting health and safety, which include fire extinguishing systems the building code requires. If the building has a sprinkler system, you may say so in the lease and tell tenants not to hang items from, paint, cover or tamper with the heads.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Arizona, a lease for longer than one year must be in writing. No court action can be brought on an agreement to lease for longer than one year unless the agreement, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against, and if an agent signs, the agent's authority must be in writing signed by that party. A term of more than one year in land also can be conveyed only by a written instrument signed and delivered by the landlord or an agent authorized in writing. A lease of one year or less may be oral: the Landlord and Tenant Act treats written, oral and implied agreements alike, and a tenancy with no definite term is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly). If you do use a written lease, you must give the tenant a signed copy and the tenant must sign and return one fully executed copy within a reasonable time, with every blank filled in; failing to do so is a material noncompliance. Recording is a separate matter: Arizona does not require a lease to be recorded, and a lease is recorded only for priority against later buyers and lenders (see edu-lease-registration-az). The statutes do not say whether an assignment, extension or early surrender of a long lease must be in writing; put each one in a writing both sides sign.

title: Arizona Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Arizona sets few dollar limits for residential rentals. The limits that apply, whatever the lease says: Security: all security, however named and including prepaid rent, may not exceed one and one-half months' rent, though a tenant may choose to pay more rent in advance (edu-security-deposit-cap-az). Wrongly withholding a deposit costs twice the amount withheld. Nonrefundable fees: no cap, but you must state each one's purpose in writing or it is refundable. Late fees and application fees: no cap; a late fee must be reasonable and in a written lease (edu-late-fee-limit-az, edu-application-fees-az).
