Returned checks: a service fee of no more than $25 plus your bank's actual charges; a check written with intent to defraud costs the writer twice its amount or $50, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney fees. Separately billed utilities: only the provider's charges plus an administrative fee for actual administrative costs, with no other charges. Rent: no cap, and cities and towns may not control rents on private housing. Attorney fees: only a prevailing-party clause is allowed. Statutory damages: a tenant you unlawfully exclude, whose essential services you wilfully cut off, or against whom you retaliate may recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; deliberately using a lease term you know is prohibited costs actual damages and up to two months' rent; an unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages of at least one month's rent. Your own recovery against a tenant who holds over wilfully and not in good faith is up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to install steam radiator covers, offer them on request, or attach a radiator rider to the lease. The general rules apply to any heating system you supply: keep it in good and safe working order, and supply reasonable heat when seasonal weather requires it, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for heat or the tenant controls the heating installation and its direct utility connection. The tenant must use the heating facilities in a reasonable manner. If a building has exposed steam radiators and young children live there, covering them is a sensible step even though no Arizona statute requires it.

title: No State Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to supply a stove or a refrigerator in a rental. Whether appliances come with the unit is a lease term, so list in the lease the appliances you supply. If you supply them, you must keep them in good and safe working order, and a lease can't excuse you from that; see edu-appliances-excluded-az before leaving an appliance in the unit that you don't intend to maintain. A required kitchen sink is part of the code conditions that materially affect health and safety, and local housing codes may require cooking or refrigeration equipment. A unit without its own refrigerator, stove or sink, where one is shared with other units, makes the occupant a roomer under the Landlord and Tenant Act. If you take an old refrigerator or freezer out of service, remove its doors, lids or latches before leaving it anywhere children can reach on property you control: leaving it intact is a misdemeanor.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: Arizona has no licence, certification or special set of rules for renting to students. Its one student-related rule is an exemption: the Landlord and Tenant Act does not cover residence at a public or private institution if it is incidental to the institution's educational services, nor occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the part of a building operated for the organization's benefit, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the Act. A private apartment or house you rent to students is an ordinary dwelling unit, and the Act applies in full. The statute does not say whether privately owned or master-leased student buildings tied to a school count as residence at an institution, so treat them as covered by the Act. Student status is not a protected class under Arizona's fair housing law, but you may not treat a student differently because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability (edu-fair-housing-az). If a parent or other person guarantees a student's rent, get the guarantee in writing signed by the guarantor: a promise to answer for another person's debt can't be enforced in court otherwise. Whether roommates are jointly liable is a lease term (joint-liability).

title: Slum Property Designation and Receivership
bodyText: A city, town, county or the state may designate residential rental property as slum property if it has deteriorated or is in disrepair and shows conditions dangerous to public health or safety: structurally unsound exterior surfaces, roof, walls, doors, floors, stairwells, porches or railings; no potable water or adequate sanitation, water or waste pipe connections; hazardous electrical systems or gas connections; no safe, rapid egress; or accumulated waste, hazardous materials or drug paraphernalia. The agency must give you an administrative appeal, and you may then seek judicial review. A designated property may be inspected every year for three consecutive years at your cost, and an unpaid inspection cost or penalty can become a priority lien. The state, city, town or county may also ask the superior court to appoint a temporary receiver, for no more than one year, to manage the property. The receiver, a property-management licensee or real estate attorney, may take control, collect the rents, make the repairs needed to meet statutes and ordinances, restore utilities, and renew, end or enter into leases as the law allows, but may not sell the property. The receiver's costs come first from the property's income after taxes and mortgages, and the party that pays them gets a recorded lien ahead of most others. The receivership ends once all violations are cured. A court may also appoint a temporary receiver to abate a residential nuisance (edu-crime-nuisance-abatement-az), and a lender may seek a receiver for rental homes under the commercial real estate receivership act. Unregistered rental property may also be inspected (edu-rental-registration-az). Keep the property out of these conditions and answer code notices promptly; city repair orders come from local codes.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText:
Arizona has no statute written for passing property tax or insurance increases on to a residential tenant.

There is no required statement of the tenant's share and no required refund of an abatement. Rent and other charges are terms you and the tenant agree on, so a pass-through works only if the lease provides for it, as the optional clause tax-insurance-escalation-la does: state the tenant's percentage, give the bill and your calculation, and credit any later reduction or refund. Without such a term, a tax increase is yours until the lease ends. A share the lease specifies is a charge you may deduct from the deposit at the end of the tenancy.

Two Arizona rules matter here. Cities may no longer tax residential rents, and a 2023 session law also limits charging tenants the amount of the repealed city rental tax, so don't use a tax clause to recover it. And if a tenant asks, you must give a written statement of the percentage of the rent that goes to property tax.

You may not raise rent to retaliate against a protected complaint, and the statute does not say whether an increase the lease already provides for is covered.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to let a cable, satellite or internet provider wire a residential building, gives residential tenants a choice of provider, or bars a different rent for tenants who subscribe to a particular service. Arizona's building-access rule is for commercial buildings only: on a prospective tenant's request, the owner must name the telecommunications providers already in place, and the state may not force a commercial owner to accept a provider. Separately, a city, town or special district may not unreasonably delay, prevent or raise the cost of a small antenna (one meter or less, for wireless or broadband radio video service, not satellite) on property in the user's exclusive use or control, including leased property; that rule limits local governments, not landlords. Federal rules on tenants' antennas and satellite dishes and on exclusive building contracts may apply. In the lease, say which services you provide and any charge for them: a charge you require is a lease term, and a term limiting dishes or antennas should allow for the federal rules.

title: No Tenancy at Will for a Dwelling
bodyText: The Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no tenancy at will. A rental agreement, written, oral or implied, that does not fix a definite term creates a week-to-week tenancy for a roomer who pays weekly rent and a month-to-month tenancy in every other case. Either side may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice given at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice, and a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 10 days before the termination date (edu-periodic-tenancy-termination-az). If a tenant stays after the term ends or the tenancy is terminated, without your consent, you may bring an action for possession, and for a wilful holdover not in good faith you may also recover up to two months' rent or twice your actual damages, whichever is greater. If you consent in writing to the tenant staying on, the tenancy becomes month-to-month. Older Arizona rules that speak of tenants at will or by sufferance, with shorter notices, apply only to rentals that are not dwelling units; the Landlord and Tenant Act governs dwellings and controls any conflict. The forcible detainer statute still names tenants at will and by sufferance, but it does not change the Act's rights and remedies.

title: Flags and Signs: No Tenant Display Statute
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a residential tenant a right to display a flag, political sign or other item despite a lease term or landlord rule, or that lets a tenant, as the person in possession, authorize a sign on the property. Arizona's flag and political-sign protections bind homeowners' and condominium associations, not landlords: an association may not ban the American flag, service flags, the Arizona flag and certain other listed flags, or political signs within set election periods, but the statutes protect an association member or unit owner on that owner's property and do not mention tenants. So whether your tenant may display a flag or sign is a matter for your lease and rules. Any rule you adopt binds the tenant only if it meets the Act's test for rules: a proper purpose, reasonably related to it, applied fairly to all tenants, clear enough to tell the tenant what to do, and given to the tenant at signing (or adopted later on 30 days' notice without substantially changing the bargain). Write sign and flag rules in neutral terms, such as size, placement and damage, and apply them the same way to everyone: a rule that singles out religious or national-origin displays invites a fair housing claim. If the home is in an association, your lease should also require the tenant to follow the association's rules (hoa-compliance). See also edu-no-political-access-rule-az and edu-no-religious-display-rule-az.

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: The Landlord and Tenant Act does not cover occupancy by your employee as a manager or custodian whose right to occupy depends on working in and about the premises, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the Act. Any other employee you house, such as a worker who rents a unit at a discount or lives in a home you own elsewhere, is an ordinary tenant, and the Act applies in full: a definite term or 30 days' notice for a month-to-month tenancy, and the Act's eviction rules. We found no Arizona statute that requires a signed disclosure of an employee's occupancy and vacating terms, requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, or makes a sponsor answer for a worker's rent. For an excluded manager or custodian, removal after the job ends falls under the general forcible detainer statute, which reaches a person whose tenancy has been terminated who keeps possession after a written demand; how it applies to a former employee is case law we did not search. The safe course: put the housing terms in a separate written agreement signed at hiring, saying the occupancy is tied to the job, how much time the employee has to leave when it ends, and what happens to rent or wages; and if the person pays rent or the unit is not tied to the job, treat the arrangement as a tenancy under the Act. A city or town may not require an employment or family relationship between the owner and the occupant of an accessory dwelling unit.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute on whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance, or may file a claim against the tenant's policy yourself. The insurance code, Title 20, is held only as headings and was not read. Three Landlord and Tenant Act rules set the limits. Your repair and habitability duties stay with you: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep supplied systems and appliances in working order, and only a qualifying written agreement can shift specified tasks to a tenant, never work needed to meet the building code or keep the unit habitable. A lease may not make the tenant agree to the exculpation or limitation of your liability or to indemnify you for it, so a term making the tenant's insurance pay for your duties or your own fault is unenforceable, and deliberately using one costs actual damages and up to two months' rent. And a tenant who deliberately or negligently damages the premises is liable for it, so you may recover that damage from the tenant, who may choose to claim on the tenant's own policy. Don't make repairs wait on a tenant's insurance claim, and don't claim on a tenant's policy without the tenant's written consent.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute written for online tenant portals: nothing bars you from requiring rent to be paid through one, regulates portal convenience fees, or sets rules for portal signatures. Rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree, so the lease may name a portal as a payment method (acceptable-payment-methods). Any fee you charge for using it should be stated in the lease (edu-required-fees-az). Signatures and documents are different. Arizona's Electronic Transactions Act applies only between parties who have each agreed to do business electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to do later transactions electronically; a lease can't waive that right. So keep a paper way to sign renewals and addenda for a tenant who asks. Notices are different again: a notice reaches the tenant when it comes to the tenant's attention, is delivered in hand, or is sent by registered or certified mail. Posting a notice in a portal relies on proof the tenant saw it, so serve important notices by those methods too (edu-electronic-transactions-az). Watch partial payments: if your portal accepts less than the full rent, accepting it keeps your right to proceed against the tenant only if the tenant signs a written partial-payment agreement at the time, so set the portal to refuse partial payments or to collect that agreement.

title: No Separate Ban on Protected-Class Questions
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that, in its own words, bars you from asking a rental applicant about, or keeping a record of, race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability. That does not make such questions safe. Arizona forbids refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status or national origin, and the same for disability. You also may not make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination on any of those grounds. So the answer to a question about a protected trait can never lawfully be used to decide whether or on what terms you rent. The practical course: leave these traits off your application and out of interviews, and ask every applicant the same questions about rent, income, rental history and the number of occupants. Federal fair housing rules go further for disability: you may not ask whether an applicant, a person who will live in the unit, or anyone associated with them has a disability, or ask about its nature or severity. You may ask every applicant, whether or not they have a disability, about their ability to meet the requirements of the tenancy, whether they qualify for housing or a priority available only to people with disabilities, whether they currently illegally use or are addicted to a controlled substance, and whether they have been convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. If an applicant asks for a disability accommodation, see edu-assistance-animals-az. Fair housing generally: edu-fair-housing-az.

title: Tenant Repair Remedies and Rent Paid into Court
bodyText: Arizona gives a tenant several remedies when you don't make repairs, and the details are in two other rows: repair notices and deadlines (habitability-timeline-az) and remedies for a landlord's breach (edu-landlord-breach-remedy-az). In short: a written notice ending the lease unless you remedy the breach within 10 days, or 5 days for a failure to maintain the unit that materially affects health and safety; damages and a court order; repair and deduct, through a licensed contractor, for a repair costing less than $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater; and, if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply water, gas or electricity, hot water, heat, cooling or other essential services, buying the service and deducting its cost, damages for lost rental value, or substitute housing. The tenant's right to pay your unpaid utility bill and deduct it is covered in edu-utility-landlord-account-az. We found no Arizona statute that lets a tenant pay rent into escrow while a unit is certified unfit, or that suspends rent on a housing agency's finding. A tenant may not withhold rent for any reason the Landlord and Tenant Act does not authorize. Rent is paid into court in two situations. First, when a tenant counterclaims for your noncompliance in a nonpayment eviction or a suit for rent, the court may, after notice and a hearing, order the tenant to pay into court the undisputed rent accrued and the rent as it comes due; the court decides what each side is owed and pays the net amount first from that money. Second, when a tenant appeals an eviction judgment and stays it, the tenant pays each month's rent to the justice court, which pays it to you as it accrues; if the tenant raised habitability as a defense or counterclaim, the court keeps the money until final judgment. If the tenant misses a payment during the appeal, you may ask the court to lift the stay and release the money held, and it must hear that within five court days. No statute sets a separate release procedure or makes a tenant liable for a bad-faith deposit. Termination, repair and deduct, and the essential-services remedies don't apply to a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: You may not retaliate against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization by raising the rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening to bring an eviction. A tenant you retaliate against has a defense to the eviction and may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. The statute ties its six-month presumption of retaliation to a tenant's complaint; whether it also covers organizing is not settled by the text, so treat any rent increase, service cut or eviction aimed at an organizing tenant as open to challenge. You may still evict a tenant who is behind on rent. The full retaliation rule is in edu-retaliation-az. Beyond that, we found no Arizona statute that gives tenants of apartments or houses a right to meet in common areas, to canvass or hand out literature in the building, or to have a tenant organization recognized or consulted. Mobile home parks and recreational vehicle parks are under separate acts that do give tenant associations meeting rights; they are not covered here. Apply any rule on common-area use, solicitation or postings evenly, and don't enforce it more strictly against tenants who are organizing.

title: The Tenant's Duties Under Arizona Law
Screening Applicants
bodyText: Arizona does not regulate tenant screening as a subject of its own. We found no Arizona statute that limits when or how far back you may look at an applicant's criminal history, requires a conditional offer before a criminal check, limits a minimum-income test, regulates tenant-screening companies or their reports, lets tax-credit properties set felony conditions, or shields a landlord from liability for renting to a person with a criminal record. These rules do apply. Fair housing: you may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability (edu-fair-housing-az), so apply the same written criteria to every applicant; Arizona's fair housing act does not bar refusing a person convicted under federal or state law of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. Children: knowingly refusing to rent because an applicant has children is a petty offense, but a reasonable occupancy standard that applies to all ages and was adopted and published in advance is allowed, and two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable. Sealed records: a person whose Arizona criminal record has been sealed may answer a housing application as if the arrest, charge or conviction never happened, unless a state or federal law requires disclosure or another listed exception applies; a sealed eviction case should not reach you either (edu-eviction-record-sealing-az). Certificate of second chance: if an applicant's conviction was set aside with this certificate, a person who provides housing to the applicant gets the same protection an employer gets that limits putting the conviction into evidence in a negligence suit; the certificate is not a recommendation of the applicant. Falsified applications: materially false information about occupants, pets, income, Social Security number, employment, criminal record, prior evictions or current criminal activity is a breach of the lease, and false criminal or eviction information can't be cured (rental-application-accuracy). Credit reports: if an applicant has frozen a credit report and won't lift it, you may treat the application as incomplete; a freeze does not reach a database used only for tenant screening, criminal records or fraud checks. Consumer reports you get on applicants, including adverse-action notices, are governed by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. § 1681 and following, FEDERAL, not read in this pass). Application fees are covered under the application-fees topic.

title: Changing Lease Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText: Arizona has only three statutory rules for changing lease terms during a tenancy. Rules: a rule or regulation you adopt after the tenant signs is enforceable if you give 30 days' notice of its adoption and it is not a substantial modification of the rental agreement. Changes in the law: if a state, county, city or other government adopts a new ordinance, rule or other legal provision affecting existing leases, you may amend leases immediately to comply, but you must give each tenant written notice that the lease has been amended, with a brief description of the amendment and its effective date. Utilities: after the lease is signed, you may not shift payment for a utility you provide under the lease to the tenant without the tenant's written consent. Beyond those, we found no Arizona statute that sets a notice period for changing another lease term, requires a longer notice for raising a fee than for raising rent, or treats a change of terms as a termination that offers a new tenancy. Rent, fees and other terms are what you and the tenant agree to in the lease. During a fixed term, a term changes only as the lease itself allows or with the tenant's agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy, the statutory tool is the termination notice: written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date it names (10 days before the termination date for week-to-week), with new terms offered for a new tenancy; put the new terms in writing and have the tenant sign them. Rent increases are covered in edu-rent-increases-az. A rent increase or service cut made in retaliation for a complaint or for organizing is prohibited (edu-retaliation-az).

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants that a rental is exempt from a statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law. Arizona has neither law for dwellings, and cities and towns may not control rents, so there is nothing for a property to be exempt from. We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease statement or notice that a rental is exempt from a rent cap, rent control, a just-cause rule or a tenant purchase right. Don't copy another state's exemption notice into an Arizona lease: it would cite law that doesn't apply here. Arizona rules that turn on the type of rental apply on their own terms, with no notice: for example, the Landlord and Tenant Act does not cover the arrangements it excludes (such as transient hotel or motel stays, an employee-manager's unit, or public housing), and the bedbug rules don't apply to a single family residence. See edu-no-tpa-notice-az for what Arizona does and doesn't have.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of November 5, 2026, none of Arizona's core landlord-tenant statutes is scheduled to expire. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act carries no repeal or expiration date, and no 2024-2026 session law sets one for it or for the eviction-action statutes. We found no Arizona statute or session law that puts a core tenant-protection rule on a repeal date. No 2024-2026 act amends any section of the Landlord and Tenant Act at all. Its rules change only when the Legislature amends them, so recheck the act after each legislative session.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Arizona has no statewide tenant protection act of the kind some states have. There is no cap on rent increases, no just-cause rule for ending a dwelling tenancy, and no right for tenants to buy, or to get the first offer on, a rental you plan to sell. So no notice telling tenants such protections apply is required, and none belongs in your lease. We found no Arizona statute that caps rent increases for dwellings, requires a reason to end or not renew a dwelling tenancy, gives tenants a purchase or first-refusal right when you sell, or requires a notice of any of these. Cities and towns may not control rents on private residential property; that preemption does not reach housing owned, financed, insured or subsidized by a state agency, city or town. You may end a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice before the rental date named, without giving a reason, unless the end is retaliatory or another rule applies (edu-periodic-tenancy-termination-az, edu-no-for-cause-eviction-az). Rent increases are covered in edu-rent-increases-az, and condominium conversions in edu-no-conversion-notice-az. Mobile home parks have their own good-cause and park-purchase rules under a separate act not covered here.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to translate a lease, to give a lease in the language you advertised or negotiated in, to print any lease text in a set type size, or to use prescribed lease wording. Arizona's constitution makes English the state's official language; that binds government, and also says no one may be penalized for using English in public or private communication. It doesn't stop you from offering a translated lease. If you do, say in the lease which version controls, give the tenant both versions, and make sure the translation says the same thing. Fair housing law bars treating applicants differently because of national origin (edu-fair-housing-az), so apply your language practices evenly. Some Arizona court forms carry required Spanish text (for example, garnishment notices); those are court forms, not leases.

title: Barring Non-Tenants and Trespass
bodyText:
Arizona's criminal trespass law lets the owner, or anyone else with lawful control of real property, ask a person to leave or give reasonable notice prohibiting entry. A person who knowingly enters or stays unlawfully after that commits criminal trespass in the third degree, a class 3 misdemeanor; a request to leave made by a police officer acting at your request counts the same as your own. Unlawfully entering or staying in a residential structure or a fenced residential yard is criminal trespass in the first degree.

Entry is unlawful only if it is not licensed, authorized or otherwise privileged.

We found no Arizona statute that says how a landlord may bar a non-tenant from a rental property's common areas, prescribes a trespass notice, or says whether a tenant's invitation makes a barred person's entry privileged.

The cautious course: give any trespass warning in writing, for specific conduct, and treat it as covering the common areas you control; deal with the unit itself through the lease.

The optional clause barred-person-covenant-ne lets you tell the tenant in writing that a named person is barred for conduct that threatened health or safety or damaged the property, and makes admitting that person a lease breach, which you may then address with a 10-day notice to remedy. Apply bans evenly and for conduct, not for who the person is.

After an eviction judgment, a former tenant who has been served with a writ of restitution and stays in or returns to the unit without your express permission commits third-degree criminal trespass.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Arizona has no truth-in-renting law. We found no Arizona statute that requires a lease notice saying it must comply with state law, requires you to give a state-published statement of tenant and landlord rights, or bars offering a lease with a clearly unenforceable clause as a separate violation. Arizona reaches the same ground in other ways. At or before the start of the tenancy you must tell the tenant in writing that the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website (the Arizona lease's landlord disclosure clause, landlord-disclosure-az, does this). A lease may not make the tenant waive rights under the act, pay your attorney fees except under a written prevailing-party clause, excuse or limit your legal liability, or limit or penalize calling the police or emergency help; such a clause is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease with clauses you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages and up to two months' rent (edu-prohibited-lease-terms-az). A written lease must have every blank filled in (edu-lease-completeness-az).

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires residential parking to be leased or priced separately from rent, or that bars including parking in the rent. You may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately; either way, say so in the lease. Under the Landlord and Tenant Act, the premises include grounds, areas and facilities held out for tenants' use or promised to the tenant, so a parking space the lease promises is part of what the tenant rents, and a parking charge the lease requires is a lease term. If you lease parking under a separate agreement, make clear whether it is part of the residential tenancy and what happens to it when the lease ends. The library's parking clauses (parking-ks-oh-ca, assigned-parking-space, parking-vehicle-rules) cover the usual terms. State zoning rules that limit what a city may require for parking at new multifamily or accessory-dwelling projects bind local governments, not your lease.

title: Interest on Amounts a Tenant Owes
bodyText:
Arizona's general interest statute covers money a tenant owes you, whether rent, damages beyond the deposit or another charge: for any loan, indebtedness or obligation other than medical debt, interest is 10% a year unless a different rate is agreed in writing, and a written agreement may set any rate.

So a written lease may set its own rate (the optional clause interest-on-unpaid-amounts-ca does this with a rate you choose), but a court may refuse to enforce a lease term that was unconscionable when made, so keep the rate reasonable.

When you sue, a judgment on a written lease with an agreed rate bears that rate, and the judgment must state it; otherwise judgment interest is the lesser of 10% a year or the federal prime rate plus 1%, fixed when the judgment is entered.

A court may not award interest before judgment on unliquidated damages, that is, amounts that aren't fixed until the court decides them, such as disputed repair costs.

Whether interest runs on an amount the lease doesn't mention, and from what date, rests on case law; stating a rate in the lease removes that question.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Arizona)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Arizona property law doesn't use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary doesn't arise here. The closest Arizona interest is a life estate (for example, a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder). We found no Arizona statute that says whether a lease signed by a life tenant or other owner of a limited interest survives the end of that interest, or what the lessor owes the tenant if it doesn't. Those questions are left to property case law, which we did not search. If you lease property in which you hold only a life estate or another limited interest, the cautious course is to tell the tenant in writing what interest you hold, and either keep the lease term within that interest or have the remainder owners sign the lease too. Whatever your interest, you must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the manager and of an owner or the owner's agent for notices and service of process (landlord-disclosure-az). Trusts that hold rental property have their own rent-apportionment rules when an income interest ends; those are in a title we hold as headings only and did not read.

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives landlords a tax credit, grant, vacancy payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans. The nearest state program helps tenants, not landlords: the military family relief fund, which runs through December 31, 2031, may pay widows, widowers or dependent children of service members who died in the line of duty in a combat zone a stipend for living expenses, including rent and utility payments, for up to six months. A veteran tenant may use that or other assistance to pay you; it doesn't change the lease. Military status is not a protected class under Arizona's fair housing act, but federal servicemember protections apply to tenants in service (edu-no-servicemember-lease-rule-az).

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets a maximum water heater temperature or requires you to reset a unit's water heater before a new tenant moves in. What Arizona does require is hot water: you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the unit's hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with a direct utility connection, and keep plumbing and appliances you supply in good and safe working order. Local building and plumbing codes, which the Landlord and Tenant Act incorporates for health and safety, may set temperature or safety-valve rules. Large boilers and commercial lined hot water heaters are regulated under the state boiler law, administered by the Industrial Commission; whether a building's equipment is covered depends on its size and on rules we did not read. As a practice, check the setting at each turnover and keep it at a safe level, especially where children or older adults will live.

title: No Waterbed Rule
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture: none requires you to allow one, lets you refuse one, sets a deposit or insurance requirement, or prescribes a notice.

Allowing, conditioning or banning a waterbed is a lease term you may set; the optional clause waterbed-mn requires your prior written consent. If you require money to cover the risk of water damage, it is security under the Landlord and Tenant Act and falls under the deposit rules, so don't label it a separate fee. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises and is responsible for damage the tenant causes.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires window guards or window-fall protection in rental units, regulates security or burglar bars, or requires a lease notice about window guards or bar release mechanisms. One window rule applies where a home's wall is part of a required pool enclosure and the owner relies on latched doors and windows instead of a separate barrier: emergency escape or rescue windows from sleeping rooms with access to the pool must have a latching device at least 54 inches above the floor, and other openable windows with similar access need a screwed-in wire mesh screen, a keyed lock that keeps the window from opening more than four inches, or a high latch (pool-safety-notice-az). That rule doesn't apply to pools built before the state pool-barrier law, to cities with their own pool ordinances, or to a home where all residents are at least six years old. Local building and fire codes may regulate bars on bedroom windows that must open for emergency escape. If you install security bars, make sure bedroom bars open from inside without a key or tool.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Many Arizona landlord-tenant notices must be in writing, and a lease can't downgrade them to verbal notice, because a lease term waiving a tenant's rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable.

Your notices that must be written include: the names and addresses of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices, and the notice that the act is on the Arizona Department of Housing's website, at or before move-in; the purpose of any nonrefundable fee or deposit; at move-in, notice that the tenant may attend the move-out inspection; the 5-day nonpayment notice; the 10-day (or 5-day health and safety) notice to remedy a breach, and the notice of a repeat breach; the 14-day notice before you make and bill a tenant repair; the 30-day (month-to-month) or 10-day (week-to-week) termination notice; notice of a lease amendment made to comply with a new law; notice of a pending foreclosure; and notice to the tenant when you sell or a manager leaves, which ends your or the manager's liability for later events.

The abandonment notice must be mailed by certified mail and posted.

The tenant's notices that must be written include: maintenance and repair requests; the 10-day or 5-day notice ending the lease for your breach; the repair-and-deduct notice; the notice of intent to pay your delinquent utility bill (other essential-service notices need only be reasonable notice, which the statute does not require to be written); a casualty termination within 14 days; a domestic-violence or sexual-assault termination; bedbug reports (written or electronic); and a submetering objection.

Two notices the act doesn't require in writing are the two days' notice before entry and the 30-day notice of a new rule, but give those in writing too so you can prove them.

A notice counts as received when delivered in hand or by registered or certified mail, and a notice sent by registered or certified mail is deemed received when it actually arrives or five days after mailing, whichever is first.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Private
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that generally bars a landlord from disclosing a tenant's information or sets a consent rule for sharing it. Several narrower rules apply. Associations: if the home is in a condominium or planned community, the association may not require you to disclose anything about a tenant beyond the names and contact information of adult occupants, the lease's beginning and ending dates, and a description and license plate numbers of the tenants' vehicles (plus photo identification showing age in an age-restricted community). It may not require a copy of the tenant's rental application, credit report, lease or other personal information. Social Security numbers: don't make a tenant's or applicant's number available to the public, don't require it to be sent over the internet unless the connection is secure or the number is encrypted, and don't print it on mailed materials except as the statute allows. Paper records: before you throw away paper records that pair a person's name with a full Social Security, card, bank or retirement account, or driver license number, redact or destroy them; violations carry civil penalties. Domestic-violence documents: see edu-dv-confidentiality-az. Breach notice: if you do business in Arizona and keep unencrypted computerized records that pair a person's name with a Social Security number, a driver license or state ID number, or a bank or card number with the code needed to use it (common in rental applications), Arizona's security-breach law applies to you. If you become aware of a security incident, investigate promptly to find out whether there was a breach. If there was, notify each affected person within 45 days after you determine it, by letter, email (if you have their addresses) or a live phone call, giving the approximate date, a brief description of the information involved, and contact details for the three largest consumer reporting agencies and the Federal Trade Commission. If more than 1,000 people must be notified, also notify those three agencies and the attorney general. You may delay while police say notice would impede a criminal investigation, and no notice is needed if a reasonable investigation finds the breach is not reasonably likely to cause the individuals substantial economic loss. The law has exceptions for businesses covered by the federal financial-privacy or health-privacy laws, and only the attorney general enforces it. Share tenant information only as the law requires or with the tenant's written consent.

title: Tenant Records and Rent Ledgers
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a landlord to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a copy of the payment history on request, or to attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice. Several record rules do apply. After the tenancy ends and the tenant has delivered possession and asked, you must give an itemized list of deposit deductions with any amount due within 14 days, excluding weekends and legal holidays. A licensed property management firm must keep each residential rental agreement, with its amendments, addenda and related documents such as rental applications, move-in forms and default notices, for one year after the agreement expires or until it hands them to the owner when the management agreement ends; it must keep client financial records, including ledgers, for at least three years. Those records are kept at the broker's office, electronically, or at an Arizona off-site location the department has been told about. When you sell an apartment community, you must give the buyer at closing the tenant security deposit records and a complete file for each tenant, with the rental agreements and the disclosures the Landlord and Tenant Act requires. Protect what you keep: before discarding paper records that pair a name with a full Social Security, card, bank or driver license number, redact or destroy them, and follow the Social Security number rules. If unencrypted computerized records that pair a name with a Social Security, driver license or financial account number are breached, you must investigate and, unless the breach is not reasonably likely to cause substantial economic loss, notify the affected people within 45 days (edu-tenant-confidential-information-az). Even without a ledger rule, keep a dated record of every charge and payment: you will need it to prove the rent due in an eviction.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that regulates smart locks, keypads, key fobs, app-based or biometric entry systems in residential rentals, or that lets a domestic-violence survivor have another person cut off from a connected device or its user account. Nothing requires you to offer a physical key instead of an app, to give tenants a privacy policy for the system, or to limit the entry data it records. The general rules apply whatever the technology. A remote unlock, or a code you give a vendor, is an entry: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice, enter only at reasonable times, and never use access to harass the tenant. A tenant's written maintenance request is permission to enter for that request only. Disabling or changing a tenant's code or credential to keep the tenant out is an unlawful exclusion: the tenant may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to two months' rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault may require a new lock at the tenant's cost, which you may meet by rekeying or replacing the locking mechanism; the statute does not mention electronic locks, so for one, reset the codes and revoke the old credentials. You may refuse a key to the person named in the protective order or police report, whatever the lease says. Say in the lease what system you use and how the tenant gets in if it fails, and restore a failed credential promptly. Arizona's breach-notice law covers computerized records that pair a person's name with certain data, including a Social Security, driver license or financial account number; we did not review the law's full list, so if the system stores tenants' identity or account data, check it. If covered data is breached, the notice rules in edu-tenant-confidential-information-az apply.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or a right to reinstatement in a nonpayment eviction because a Social Security check, other government benefit or housing-voucher payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply whatever the reason rent is late. A tenant may not withhold rent for a reason the Landlord and Tenant Act does not allow. If rent is unpaid, you may give the five-day written nonpayment notice. Before you file, the lease is reinstated if the tenant pays all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee set in a written lease; after you file, only if the tenant also pays attorney fees and court costs; after judgment, reinstatement is your choice. The court may postpone the trial only for good cause shown by affidavit, and then for no more than three days in justice court or five days in superior court. If you know a tenant's benefit is simply late, you may accept a partial payment and agree in writing, at the time of the payment, when the rest is due; that keeps your right to proceed. Accepting a housing-assistance payment is not accepting a partial payment and does not waive your right to terminate for the tenant's breach. For a tenant with a federal Housing Choice Voucher, the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing authority's payment covers, and the authority's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant: during the lease term you may not end the tenancy because the authority didn't pay. Take a missed or late authority payment up with the authority under your contract (edu-no-subsidy-late-fee-rule-az).

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early
bodyText:
Arizona lets a tenant end a lease early in these situations, whatever the lease says.

Domestic violence or sexual assault: a victim who gives written notice with a protective order or police report may leave within 30 days and owes no future rent and no early termination penalty or fee.

Law enforcement officers: an officer protected by an injunction against harassment issued in the 30 days before the notice may end the lease the same way, but must repay any lease concession actually received before moving out.

Fire or casualty: if damage substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out at once and give written notice within 14 days; the lease ends the day the tenant left.

Your material breach: the tenant may give written notice that the lease ends in 10 days unless you remedy the breach, or 5 days for a failure to maintain the premises that materially affects health and safety. A material breach includes materially false written information about the unit's availability, its condition, current or promised services, utility service and who pays for utilities.

Failure to deliver possession at the start of the term: rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on 5 days' written notice and get back all prepaid rent and security.

Lockout or wilful utility shutoff: the tenant may end the lease and recover statutory damages.

Unlawful or harassing entry: the tenant may end the lease and recover at least one month's rent.

Military service: under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, a tenant may end a residential lease after entering military service, if the lease was signed before that; or, if the tenant signed while in service, after receiving orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of at least 90 days, or a stop movement order of at least 30 days that keeps the tenant from moving in after signing on such orders. Ending the lease also ends the obligations of the servicemember's dependents under it. How the notice is given, when the termination takes effect and what happens to rent and the deposit are set by parts of the Act not reviewed here.

Arizona gives National Guard and armed forces reserve members ordered to active duty or training by any state or the United States the protections that federal servicemember civil-relief law gives people on federal active duty (A.R.S. 26-168(D)).

A lease can't waive these rights. We found no Arizona statute letting a tenant end a lease because of the tenant's death, or making you forfeit rent for leaving a prescribed statement out of the lease. Early-termination fees for a tenant who simply wants to leave are covered with the early termination clause.

title: Program Inspections in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute on refusing a subsidized tenancy because a housing program will inspect the unit, or on a subsidized tenant who refuses a program inspection. Arizona state law does not require you to accept a housing voucher, though some city ordinances may (edu-no-source-of-income-rule-az). If you take part in the federal Housing Choice Voucher program, the housing authority must inspect the unit before the lease term starts and at least every two years during assisted occupancy (every three years for a small rural housing authority), and also acts when the family or a government official reports a possible deficiency. The assisted family must let the housing authority inspect the unit at reasonable times after reasonable notice. Under Arizona law, the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for you to enter to inspect the premises, make repairs or show the unit to workmen or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice and enter at reasonable times. The statute does not mention program inspectors, so schedule a program inspection as your own entry, with that notice, and attend it. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may ask a court to order access or end the lease, and recover actual damages. Accepting a housing-assistance payment is not accepting a partial payment and does not waive your right to terminate for a tenant's breach. Public housing operated under the state housing-authority law or federal law is outside the Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: Subsidized Rent When Part of a Unit Is Unfit
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute on how a rent reduction is split between the tenant's share and the part a housing subsidy pays when part of a subsidized unit becomes unfit. The general remedies apply to every tenant. After fire or casualty, a tenant who lawfully stays may vacate the unusable part, and the tenant's liability for rent drops in proportion to the loss in the unit's fair rental value. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply water, gas, electricity, heat, cooling or other essential services, the tenant may recover damages based on the loss in fair rental value, among other remedies. For any other breach of your duties, the tenant may recover damages. These rules measure the loss against the unit's fair rental value and say nothing about who pays which share. Under the federal Housing Choice Voucher rules, you must keep a voucher unit up to the program's housing quality standards: correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours of notice and any other within 30 days (or an approved extension), or the housing authority must take enforcement action. If the authority finds the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the deficiency, beyond ordinary use, it may waive your responsibility to fix it, and then it may not withhold or reduce its payment to you; the family may be held responsible for breaches caused by unpaid tenant utilities, tenant-supplied appliances or damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. The federal text on how the authority reduces or withholds its payment was not reviewed here, so the split still depends on your contract and the program rules. Don't bill the tenant for a reduction or withholding the housing agency makes in its own payment unless the program rules allow it.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that bars or limits a late fee on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays. Arizona sets no late-fee cap; a late fee must be reasonable and stated in a written lease (edu-late-fee-limit-az). Even so, charge a late fee only on the tenant's own share, and only when the tenant's share is late. When a housing agency pays its share late, take it up with the agency under your assistance contract. Under the federal Housing Choice Voucher rules, the housing authority must pay its share promptly when due under the contract, and the contract must provide for penalties against the authority for late payment in the circumstances the rules list; and the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the authority's payment covers. So a charge for the authority's lateness belongs with the authority, not the tenant. Accepting the agency's payment is not accepting a partial payment of rent and does not waive your right to terminate for the tenant's own breach.

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that says whether you may enforce a writ of restitution after you learn a tenant has filed bankruptcy, or that governs a lease term triggered by a tenant's bankruptcy. The Landlord and Tenant Act says bankruptcy law supplements it, and federal bankruptcy law decides what you may do once a tenant files. A bankruptcy filing operates as an automatic stay of any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate. Two exceptions matter to landlords. The stay does not stop you continuing an eviction of a tenant from residential property the tenant lives in if you got a judgment for possession before the bankruptcy was filed. And it does not stop an eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal use of controlled substances on it, but only if you file with the bankruptcy court, and serve on the tenant, a certification under penalty of perjury that such an eviction has been filed or that the tenant endangered the property or illegally used or allowed the use of a controlled substance there in the previous 30 days. Both exceptions are subject to further conditions in the Bankruptcy Code that were not reviewed here. Once the case starts, a lease may not be terminated or modified solely because of a lease term conditioned on matters the Code lists; that list was not reviewed here, so don't rely on a lease clause that ends the lease because the tenant files bankruptcy. If you get notice of a filing, stop collection and eviction steps, including late notices, filings and writ enforcement, until you or your lawyer confirm which exception applies.

title: Arizona Lease Disclosure Checklist
bodyText:
What Arizona makes you disclose, and when.
- (1) At or before the start of the tenancy, in writing: the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices, kept current and given again on request, and a statement that the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website (landlord-disclosure-az). If you fail, the person who failed becomes your agent for service of notices and for performing your duties.
- (2) In the rental agreement, if you bill gas, water, wastewater, trash or electricity separately by submetering or ratio billing: the utilities billed and the amount of any administrative fee, and for ratio billing a description of the method (utility-billing-disclosure-az).
- (3) In writing: the purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit; anything not designated nonrefundable is refundable.
- (4) On move-in: a signed copy of the lease, a move-in form for noting existing damage, and written notice that the tenant may be present at the move-out inspection.
- (5) Bedbug educational materials to new and existing tenants, except for a single family residence (bedbug-obligations-az).
- (6) Notice of possible foreclosure, with the rental agreement if foreclosure has begun, or within five business days after you receive a first notice of trustee's sale; not for four or more connected units (foreclosure-notice-az).
- (7) If the dwelling has a swimming pool or similar body of water: the pool safety notice approved by the Department of Health Services (pool-safety-notice-az).
- (8) Your rules: they bind the tenant only if the tenant had notice of them on signing, and a later rule needs 30 days' notice.
- (9) On request: a written statement of the share of rent that goes to property tax.
- (10) For target housing, which federal law defines as housing built before 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and any 0-bedroom dwelling (unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there), federal law requires that, before the tenant is obligated under the lease, you give the tenant the federal lead hazard information pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint or known lead-based paint hazards, and provide any lead hazard evaluation report available to you; if you use an agent to lease the unit, the agent must ensure compliance (lead-based-paint). The federal regulations that carry this out were not read.

We found no Arizona statute that requires a notice of whether the unit is covered by a just-cause or rent law, a state form as the lease's first page, or a seller's disclosure because a lease includes an option to purchase. The military airport disclosure binds public reports and sellers of residential real estate, not landlords.

title: Renting to Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that makes it a crime or violation for a landlord to rent to a registered sex offender, to let two or more registered offenders live together, or to rent a unit near a school or child care facility to an offender, and none that offers a lease statement as a safe harbor. Arizona's residency limit binds the offender, not you: an offender convicted of a dangerous crime against children who must register may not, if classified level three, reside within 1,000 feet of a school or child care facility (with exceptions, such as a residence established before the school opened), and may not establish a residence within 1,000 feet of a former victim's home; a violation is the offender's misdemeanor or, for repeat victim-proximity violations, felony. Cities, towns and counties may not adopt greater distance restrictions. Two other rules can matter. If your rental is in a condominium or planned community, the association may enforce a provision in its documents restricting residency of level two or three offenders, so check them before leasing. And a city or town may limit or bar using a vacation or short-term rental to house sex offenders. On a rental application, untrue or misleading information about criminal records is a material falsification that the tenant cannot cure. Federally assisted housing is different: federal law requires an owner of federally assisted housing to refuse admission to any household that includes a person subject to a lifetime registration requirement under a state sex offender registration program. Federally assisted housing includes public housing, units with Section 8 tenant-based assistance (housing choice vouchers), housing with Section 8 project-based assistance, and housing assisted under 12 U.S.C. § 1701q; the definition may list other programs we did not review, so check your program rules. Apply any criminal-history screening policy the same way to every applicant.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText:
Arizona limits the total security you may demand or receive to one and one-half months' rent. The limit counts all security, whatever you call it (security deposit, pet deposit, cleaning or key deposit, or any other refundable deposit), and it includes prepaid rent, such as last month's rent collected at signing.

A tenant may choose on their own to pay more than one and one-half months' rent in advance; the limit stops you from requiring it. A reasonable charge for redecorating or cleaning is not security, but its purpose must be stated in writing if it is nonrefundable. Set the deposit, any pet deposit and any prepaid rent so that together they stay within the limit.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Arizona's main landlord-tenant law is the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (A.R.S. sections 33-1301 to 33-1381). A lease may not have the tenant agree to waive or give up any right or remedy the Act gives. A lease also may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees (a written lease may award fees to whichever party wins in court), excuse or limit your liability arising under law or have the tenant indemnify you for it, waive or limit anyone's right to call the police or other emergency help, or penalize the tenant for calling. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease with terms you know are prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages plus up to two months' periodic rent. Three more rules work the same way: a lease may not contain terms contrary to the essential-services section (A.R.S. 33-1364); no lease may let you collect rent free of your duty to keep the unit fit (A.R.S. 33-1316); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term. What the Act does allow: you and the tenant may settle a claim or right that is honestly disputed, and some sections let the lease or a separate writing set a different rule (for example the time and place of rent payment, and, for a single family residence or by separate signed writing, who does specified maintenance). A right outside the Act is waivable or not under its own statute.

title: Can a Lease Waive the Landlord's Repair Duties?
bodyText: No lease can remove your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable: a term waiving the tenant's rights under the Act is unenforceable, and no lease may let you collect rent free of your repair and maintenance duties. What Arizona allows is reassigning specified work, not removing the standard. For a single family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, supported by adequate consideration, that the tenant handles garbage removal facilities and the water, hot water, heat and cooling supply duties, and also specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling. For any other dwelling unit, the agreement for specified repairs or maintenance must be in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by adequate consideration, and must not reduce what you owe other tenants. Either way, the agreement must be made in good faith, not to evade your obligations, and can never cover work needed to bring the unit up to building codes affecting health and safety or to make it fit and habitable; that work stays yours. The Act has no rule letting a tenant accept a defect in exchange for lower rent.

title: When the Water, Heat and Cooling Duties Do Not Apply
bodyText: You must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat and air-conditioning or cooling where those units are installed and offered, when seasonal weather requires. The statute itself sets the only exceptions: the duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or where the unit is built so that the heat, air-conditioning, cooling or hot water comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection (for example a water heater on the tenant's own utility account). A lease cannot otherwise excuse these duties. For a single family residence only, a written agreement supported by adequate consideration may have the tenant take over these supply duties, subject to the good-faith limits in the statute. For a heating or cooling failure you cause deliberately or negligently, the tenant has special remedies (A.R.S. 33-1364).

title: A Lease Cannot Shorten or Waive Termination Notices
bodyText: Arizona's termination notices are rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a lease cannot waive or shorten them: a lease term in which the tenant gives up rights or remedies under the Act is unenforceable. The notices include the 5-day written notice before an action for unpaid rent, the 10-day notice to cure for a material breach, the 5-day notice for a health-and-safety breach, the written notice of immediate termination for a material and irreparable breach, and the 10-day (week-to-week) and 30-day (month-to-month) notices that end a periodic tenancy. You may give more notice than the statute requires. One built-in exception: if you served a 5-day nonpayment notice before you and the tenant signed a written partial-payment agreement, no new notice is needed if the tenant breaks that agreement.

title: Showing Notice Cannot Be Waived in the Lease
bodyText:
Arizona sets an entry-notice rule, and it covers showings: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to show the unit to prospective buyers, lenders or tenants, but except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times.

Because that notice is a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a lease term in which the tenant waives or shortens it is unenforceable.

The Act's only built-in waiver is narrow: when the tenant asks you for a repair or service, the request is permission to enter for that request alone, without separate notice. The Act says nothing about a tenant agreeing, at the time, to a specific showing on shorter notice; if you rely on that, get the tenant's agreement in writing for that showing only.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: The tenant's security-deposit rights (the one-and-one-half-months cap, the written statement of purpose for any nonrefundable fee, the move-in form and move-out inspection notice, the itemized list and refund within 14 business days, and double damages for wrongful withholding) are rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a lease term giving them up is unenforceable. The deposit rules bind whoever holds your interest in the property when the tenancy ends, and a landlord who sells remains liable to the tenant for deposit money owed. The only waiver the deposit statute itself creates runs the other way: if you mail the itemized list and any refund as the statute prescribes and the tenant does not dispute it within 60 days, the amount is final and the tenant's further claims are waived.

title: No Lease Clauses Excusing the Landlord
bodyText: An Arizona lease may not have the tenant excuse or limit your liability arising under law, or agree to indemnify you for that liability or its costs. A clause like "Landlord is not liable for any damage or injury" is unenforceable to that extent, and deliberately using a lease with terms you know are prohibited can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to two months' periodic rent. For this reason the Arizona lease uses clause versions that state who is responsible for what without disclaiming your liability (for example on storage, parking, renter's insurance and utility interruptions). Some protections come from statute rather than the lease: when you sell to a good-faith buyer and give the tenant written notice of the sale, you are relieved of liability for later events unless agreed otherwise (but stay liable for the deposit); a manager is relieved after written notice that the management has ended; you are not liable for good-faith actions under the domestic-violence termination section; and you are not liable for injuries or damage caused by a purported assistance or service animal allowed as a reasonable accommodation.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: If a court finds, as a matter of law, that a lease or any of its terms was unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the lease, enforce the rest without the unconscionable term, or limit the term to avoid an unconscionable result. The same applies to a settlement in which a party gave up a claim or right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the lease, if the settlement was unconscionable when made. When unconscionability is raised, by a party or by the court on its own, both sides get a reasonable chance to present evidence of the setting, purpose and effect of the lease or settlement. Arizona's statute names no particular term as unconscionable; draft every fee, damages and remedy clause so it is reasonable on its face.

title: Attorney Fees in Arizona Leases and Evictions
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees one-way. A written lease may say that the prevailing party in a court action may be awarded attorney fees, and the Arizona lease's default clause does exactly that. Even without such a clause, the winner of a contested eviction (forcible detainer) case is eligible for attorney fees under the general statute for contested contract actions; a fee award under that statute may not exceed what was actually paid or agreed to be paid. In the Act, you may recover reasonable attorney fees and court costs for a tenant's noncompliance, and after you file a nonpayment eviction the tenant can reinstate the lease only by paying the past-due rent, reasonable late fees set forth in the written lease, attorney fees and court costs. The eviction judgment covers attorney fees and costs as the law prescribes. A tenant who wins on an unlawful utility shutoff can also recover reasonable attorney fees. The Act has no special wording requirement for a fee clause. Court rules on eviction fee awards are not covered here; see Eviction Court Rules.

title: Jury Trials in Evictions and Lease Jury Waivers
bodyText: The Arizona Constitution says the right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate. In an eviction (forcible or special detainer), a jury is not automatic: the court tries the case unless a party demands a jury, and either side may request one (the tenant on appearing). We found no Arizona statute that allows, bars or sets a form for a jury waiver in a residential lease. Because the eviction jury right comes through the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's eviction section, and the Act voids a lease term waiving rights under it, the Arizona lease does not include a jury waiver. Don't add one without legal advice.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A lease clause authorizing someone to confess judgment against the tenant for rent or other money does not work in Arizona: judgment by confession on a written instrument for the payment of money, under a power of attorney to confess it, may not be entered unless the authority was signed and acknowledged on a day after the debt became due. A lease signed at move-in comes before any rent falls due, so it cannot supply that authority. Don't put a confession-of-judgment or warrant-of-attorney clause in a lease; to recover rent or possession, use the eviction process or a regular lawsuit.

title: Smoke-Free Common Areas and Smoke from Other Units
bodyText:
Arizona's Smoke-Free Arizona Act bans smoking tobacco in enclosed public places, and its definition of public place includes common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multifamily housing. A private residence is not covered unless it is used as licensed child care, adult day care or health care.

If you own or control an apartment building, you must clearly post "No smoking" signs (or the international no-smoking symbol) in the enclosed common areas where smoking is prohibited, saying where complaints can be made, put a no-smoking sign at every entrance, remove ashtrays from those areas, and ask anyone smoking there to stop.

You may also declare your whole property nonsmoking, and the Arizona lease's smoking policy does that. Cities may adopt stricter rules. No Arizona statute addresses smoke drifting between units or lets a lease make the tenant give up a claim about it; a lease term excusing your liability arising under law is unenforceable.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
No Arizona statute bars or caps a fee the lease charges for collecting unpaid rent or other lease charges. Two rules shape it.

First, a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees (only a prevailing-party fee clause is allowed), so a collection fee cannot include attorney fees.

Second, a licensed collection agency, and a licensed real estate broker such as a property management firm collecting for an owner, may not try to collect a collection fee, attorney fee, court cost or expense unless it is justly due and legally chargeable against the tenant or has been set by a court, and may not imply that fees can be added when they cannot.

In practice, a collection fee is chargeable only if the written lease authorizes it. If you use the optional collection-fee clause, set the fee at what the agency actually charges you, with a percentage ceiling, and don't charge it on amounts paid before referral. A fixed amount unrelated to cost may be attacked as a penalty. Federal debt-collection law may also apply to agencies.

title: No Statute on Fees for Notices or Eviction Filings
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that authorizes, caps or bars a lease fee for preparing or serving a notice (such as a 5-day nonpayment notice) or for filing an eviction. What the statutes do say limits such a fee's use: before an eviction is filed, a tenant reinstates the lease by paying all past-due rent and a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease, so you cannot demand a notice fee as a condition; after filing, reinstatement requires past-due rent, reasonable late fees, attorney fees and court costs. A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees except as a prevailing-party award, and court costs are what the court awards. The Arizona lease does not include a notice-service or eviction fee: no statute supports one, it could not be required for reinstatement, and a fixed charge unrelated to cost may be attacked as a penalty. A landlord who wants one should take legal advice first.

title: No Specific Ban on Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that specifically bans a lease clause charging the tenant a penalty or fee for being evicted. The general limits still apply: a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees except as a prevailing-party award; a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term; reinstatement cannot be conditioned on anything beyond rent, reasonable late fees in a written lease and, after filing, attorney fees and court costs; and a lease may not penalize a tenant for calling the police or other emergency help. Your recoverable losses are your actual damages for the breach, rent and the costs and fees a court awards. Whether a fixed eviction charge is an unenforceable penalty is a case-law question we did not search, so the Arizona lease does not include one.

title: No Statute on Liquidated Damages in Leases
bodyText:
We found no Arizona statute that permits, limits or voids a liquidated-damages clause (a damages amount fixed in advance) in a residential lease.

Whether a fixed amount is an enforceable estimate or an unenforceable penalty is decided by case law.

The statutes give you a claim for possession, rent, and actual damages for breach, require you to mitigate, and after an abandonment require reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental; a tenant ending the lease for domestic violence owes no early termination penalty or fee.

If you use a fixed early-termination or damages amount, keep it a reasonable estimate of your likely loss, and take legal advice before relying on it.

title: Accepting Rent Can Waive a Breach
bodyText: In Arizona, a statute decides this: if you accept rent, or any part of it, knowing the tenant is in default, or accept performance that differs from the lease or your rules, you waive the right to terminate the lease for that breach. Two exceptions: you keep your rights after accepting a partial payment only if the tenant signs, at the time, a written agreement on the terms of the partial payment that gives the date the balance is due; and accepting a housing assistance payment is never a partial payment or a waiver. A lease clause saying that accepting rent never waives a breach cannot override the statute. If you do not want to waive a breach, refuse or return payments for the period after your notice, in writing, or use the written partial-payment agreement.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic Violence or Sexual Assault Victims
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault may require you to install a new lock on the dwelling if the tenant pays the cost of installing it. You may do this either by rekeying the existing lock, if it is in good working condition, or by replacing the whole locking mechanism with one of equal or better quality. You may keep a copy of the new key. Whatever the lease says, you may refuse to give a key to the new lock to the person named in the order of protection or police report.
