If that person is a tenant who has been served with an order of protection naming them as the defendant, and you have received a copy, you must refuse them access to the dwelling to reclaim property unless a law enforcement officer escorts them in and out. You are not liable for actions taken in good faith under this section. The statute sets no deadline for the lock change and no separate penalty; a lease term that waives the right is unenforceable.

title: Documents a Domestic Violence Victim Must Give
bodyText: To end the lease early under Arizona's domestic violence and sexual assault section, the tenant gives you written notice that the tenant is a victim, a written notice requesting release with a mutually agreed release date within the next 30 days, and one of two documents: a copy of a protective order issued to the tenant under Arizona's order-of-protection statute (you may also ask for a receipt or signed statement that the order was submitted to a court officer for service), or a copy of a written law enforcement report stating that the tenant notified the agency that the tenant was a victim. The events must have happened within the 30 days before the tenant's written notice, unless you waive that limit; the limit runs from the events, not from the document's date. You may ask the victim in writing for the name and address of the person named in the order or report, if the victim knows it. A law enforcement officer may end the lease the same way with notice that the officer is protected by an injunction against harassment issued within the 30 days before the notice. The lock-change right lists no documents. In federally assisted housing, federal law sets its own document list and confidentiality rule.

title: Deposit After a Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: When a tenant lawfully ends the lease under Arizona's domestic violence and sexual assault section, you may not withhold the security deposit because of the early termination, but you may withhold for damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's maintenance duties. The tenant owes rent through the termination date plus earlier obligations, payable by the move-out date, and if the tenant prepaid rent for the month of termination you may keep it. The section sets no special refund deadline, so the general deposit rule applies: within 14 days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant asks for the deposit, you mail the itemized list and any refund. If several tenants are on the lease, the termination ends the tenancy for all of them; neither section says how the deposit is divided, or when the refund clock runs, if the other tenants stay on under a new lease, so settle that in writing with all the tenants.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Are Current in Arizona
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant domestic violence section points to the criminal code for its definitions and documents: domestic violence as defined in A.R.S. 13-3601, sexual assault under 13-1406, and protective orders issued under 13-3602; the law enforcement officer section points to injunctions against harassment under 12-1809. All of those sections are still in force at those numbers. The order-of-protection statute was amended in 2026 (a court may now, after a hearing, order the defendant to give identifying information to the plaintiff), but it was not moved or renumbered, so an Arizona order of protection still qualifies. Under that statute a court may give one party exclusive use of the residence and order the other party to stay away from it; if a tenant shows you such an order, follow it, and note that an emergency or protective order issued to a resident applies to the entire rental property.

title: Confidentiality of Domestic Violence Information
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that makes a private landlord keep confidential what a tenant tells or gives you about domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Arizona's Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Secretary of State, protects relocated victims' addresses: it binds the Secretary of State and government employees, not landlords, but anyone who knowingly tries to obtain a participant's actual address without authority commits a crime, and a participant may be served with any notice required or allowed by law by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, at the program's substitute address. If your property is in a federal covered housing program (for example Section 8 vouchers or tax-credit housing), federal law requires you to keep information a tenant submits to claim domestic violence protections confidential, with narrow exceptions. Good practice everywhere: keep these documents separate from the general tenant file and share them only as the law requires.

title: Evicting a Tenant Who Is a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that bars evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, or that stops you from counting abuse-related incidents against the victim. Related Arizona rules do apply: the domestic violence termination section says it does not limit your right to terminate the victim's lease for actions unrelated to the domestic violence or sexual assault; a lease may not waive or limit anyone's right to call the police or other emergency help, or penalize the tenant for calling; and an order of protection issued to a resident applies to the whole property. Federal law adds protection in federal covered housing programs: you may not deny or evict on the basis that the tenant is a victim, an incident is not a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim, and you may split the lease to remove the abuser. Federal fair housing law may also apply where a policy falls more heavily on one sex.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Prepaid rent, including last month's rent collected at signing, counts toward Arizona's limit on total security of one and one-half months' rent; the only exception is rent the tenant chooses on their own to pay in advance. At the end of the tenancy you may apply prepaid rent and security to all rent owed and, subject to your duty to mitigate, to charges stated in the signed lease and damages from the tenant's failure to meet maintenance duties. If a tenant ends the lease lawfully because of domestic violence or sexual assault, you may keep prepaid rent for the month of termination. Label money collected as last month's rent as prepaid rent in the lease, and apply it to the last month unless the tenant owes other rent first.

title: When the Deposit Refund Clock Starts
bodyText:
Your 14-day deadline (not counting Saturdays, Sundays or legal holidays) to give the tenant an itemized list of deductions and any refund starts only when three things have happened: the tenancy has ended, the tenant has delivered possession (returned the keys and vacated), and the tenant has demanded the deposit.

Unless the tenant arranges otherwise in writing, mail the list and any amount due by first class mail to the tenant's last known place of residence. Ask the tenant in writing at move-out for a forwarding address and a written demand; the Arizona lease's deposit clause does this. If the tenant does not dispute the list within 60 days after it is mailed as required, it becomes final.

title: Pre-Set Cleaning and Damage Charges
bodyText: Arizona has no statute on schedules of pre-set move-out charges. At the end of the tenancy you may apply the deposit to rent and, subject to your duty to mitigate, to charges stated in the signed lease and to the damages you suffered because the tenant did not meet the tenant's maintenance duties. A reasonable charge for redecorating or cleaning is not security, so it may be charged as a separate nonrefundable fee, but only if its purpose is stated in writing; otherwise it is refundable. Keep any schedule tied to your real costs: the statute lets you recover damages you actually suffered, the itemized list must show each deduction, and an unconscionable term can be refused enforcement. Whether a fixed charge above actual cost is enforceable is case law we did not search.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or that limits a landlord who agrees to installments. You may offer installments if you choose; put the amounts and due dates in writing, and keep the total of all security and prepaid rent within the one and one-half months' rent limit.

title: How Deposits Must Be Held
bodyText:
If you manage your own property, Arizona law does not require you to keep tenant deposits in a separate, escrow or interest-bearing account, or to pay interest on them. During the tenancy you may use refundable deposits as any applicable property management agreement allows; at the end of the tenancy all refundable deposits must be refunded as the deposit statute requires.

If a licensed property management firm handles the money, real estate law applies: the firm must deposit money it receives that is not in dispute within three banking days into the owner's own account or the firm's trust account for the owner's benefit, and every lease a property manager executes must include a provision clearly stating what happens to tenant deposits. The optional deposit-disposition clause is that provision.

title: Deposits When You Sell
bodyText: When the property changes hands, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules, so the buyer must refund and account for the deposit at move-out. You as seller are relieved of liability for later events once you sell in good faith to a bona fide purchaser and give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless agreed otherwise, but you remain liable to the tenant for any deposit money and property the tenant is entitled to. If you sell or transfer an apartment community (five or more units subject to the Act), you must give the buyer all records about tenant security deposits and the complete tenant files at closing. Transfer the deposits to the buyer at closing and tell the tenants in writing who now holds them.

title: Penalty for Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText:
If you don't give the itemized list and refund as the deposit statute requires (within 14 days, excluding weekends and legal holidays, after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and demands the deposit, by first class mail unless the tenant arranged otherwise in writing), the tenant may recover the property and money due plus damages equal to twice the amount wrongfully withheld. The multiple applies to the amount wrongfully withheld, not to the whole deposit. Either side may still recover other damages the Act allows.

Separately, a lease term giving up deposit rights is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with terms you know are prohibited adds actual damages and up to two months' periodic rent.

title: No Rule on Posted Deposit Standards
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires you to post or give applicants written standards for how you set security deposits, or that requires the same deposit for every unit. The limits that apply are the one and one-half months' rent cap on all security and fair housing law: apply your deposit standards consistently, and don't set a higher deposit because of a protected characteristic.

title: Stating Nonrefundable Fees in Writing
bodyText: Arizona requires you to state in writing the purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit; any fee or deposit not designated as nonrefundable is refundable. The statute does not require a separate document, so the statement may be in the lease itself, which is what the Arizona lease's nonrefundable fees clause does: it lists each nonrefundable fee, its amount and its purpose. A fee you forget to list there is refundable at move-out.

title: Deposit Alternatives
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that regulates a fee or insurance product offered in place of a security deposit. The deposit statute still reaches such a program: Arizona's cap covers security 'however denominated', and security means money or property given to assure payment or performance under the lease. So any part of a deposit-alternative payment that is refundable, or held to secure the tenant's performance, counts toward the one and one-half months' limit, and any part that is nonrefundable must have its purpose stated in writing. A program that bills the tenant later for damage is a claim against the tenant, not a deposit deduction. Offer an alternative only as an option, never as a requirement in place of the tenant's right to choose a lawful deposit.

title: Rental Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that caps, bans or regulates a rental application or screening fee, requires you to refund an unused fee, bars a fee for a minor, or requires a written notice of screening criteria before you take a fee. Arizona's rule that the purpose of every nonrefundable fee be stated in writing is written for landlords and tenants; it may not reach an applicant before a lease exists, but following it costs nothing. Say in writing before you take the fee what it covers (for example the actual cost of a credit or background check), whether any part is refundable, and how long the decision will take. Charge every applicant the same fee on the same terms, consistent with state and federal fair housing law. Condominium and planned-community associations may not demand a copy of your tenant's rental application.

title: Fees the Lease Must State
bodyText: Arizona has no general rule that every fee must be listed in the lease, but several rules make an unstated fee hard or impossible to collect. Utility charges you bill tenants need a lease disclosure listing the separately charged utilities and the amount of any administrative fee. A late fee counts toward reinstatement only if it is a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease, and an eviction judgment includes late charges only if the lease states them. In a forcible detainer judgment the court awards charges stated in the rental agreement. Nonrefundable fees need a written statement of purpose or they are refundable. A rule adopted after the tenant signs binds the tenant only after 30 days' notice and only if it is not a substantial change to the lease. The statute sets no cap on markups for third-party services, no ban on common-area fees, and no single "total monthly payment" figure. List every recurring and one-time fee, with its amount and purpose, in the lease.

title: No Rental Fee-Transparency Law
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute requiring all-in rent pricing, a fee disclosure on the lease's first page, or a single figure combining rent and mandatory fees, and no state list of fees a landlord may not charge. Two general rules still matter. Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act makes deception or misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise unlawful; whether it reaches a particular residential lease is a case-law question we did not search (see Consumer Fraud Act and Leases). And the landlord-tenant rules on late fees, utility charges and nonrefundable fees require those charges to be in writing. Advertise rent with every mandatory fee disclosed, and list each fee in the lease.

title: Don't Charge for Services You Don't Provide
bodyText: Arizona has no general statute barring a fee for a service you don't provide, but related rules do. If you bill utilities by submeter or ratio, you may recover only the utility provider's charges plus an administrative fee covering your actual administrative costs; you may not add other charges. You must provide all utilities and services the lease specifies, and the tenant has remedies if you don't. A fee or deposit not designated nonrefundable with a written purpose is refundable. Misrepresenting what a fee buys may also be a Consumer Fraud Act problem where that act applies. Tie each fee in the lease to a real service, amenity or cost.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText:
Arizona has no separate pet-deposit cap, but a refundable pet deposit is security under the deposit statute, so it counts toward the one and one-half months' rent limit on all security together with the regular deposit and any prepaid rent, and it is refunded and accounted for the same way. A nonrefundable pet fee is allowed only if its purpose is stated in writing; otherwise it is refundable. Monthly pet rent is not addressed by statute; state it in the lease.

Assistance animals are not pets: Arizona and federal fair housing law require reasonable accommodations in rules, policies and practices for a person with a disability, and charging pet fees or deposits for an assistance animal risks a refusal-to-accommodate claim, so don't. You may still recover actual damage the animal causes. The Arizona pet clause already reflects these rules.

title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText:
Arizona sets no dollar or percentage cap on late fees for apartments and houses. The limits are that the fee be reasonable and set forth in a written lease: only a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease must be paid to reinstate the lease before an eviction is filed, and an eviction judgment includes only late charges stated in the lease. An unconscionable fee can be refused enforcement.

Caps exist elsewhere in Arizona's landlord-tenant statutes but not for dwellings: a recreational vehicle long-term rental space lease may charge no more than $5 a day, counted from the rent due date until the rent is paid, and only if the rent is not paid by the sixth day after the due date. Mobile-home park spaces have their own act, not covered here.

title: No Rent Receipt Requirement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, including cash rent, or that gives a debtor a general right to demand a written receipt from a creditor. Receipt duties in Arizona statutes cover other transactions, such as cash payments on retail installment contracts and rental-purchase agreements for goods. Give a written or electronic receipt for every cash payment anyway, showing the date, amount, period covered and what it was applied to; it is your best evidence in a nonpayment dispute.

title: Rent Can't Be Collected Free of the Repair Duty
bodyText: No lease, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the landlord's duty to keep the premises fit (the building-code, repair, common-area, facilities, garbage, water, heat and cooling duties). So an assignment of rents to a lender, or a sale of the rental stream, does not split the right to collect rent from the duty to maintain, and a lease term trying to do so is not effective.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Arizona does not allow a self-help lockout for unpaid rent, even with notice. You may not take possession by removing the tenant or the tenant's belongings, or by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential services, except after abandonment, surrender or as the Act permits (an eviction judgment and writ). If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, or willfully interrupt essential services, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Apart from interruptions needed to make repairs, utilities you provide may be discontinued only on the day after a writ of restitution or execution is executed, and only by a person the utility authorizes. A lease clause allowing a lockout is unenforceable. Use the 5-day notice and the special detainer process.

title: Billing Tenants for Electricity
bodyText:
You may charge tenants separately for electricity (and gas, water, wastewater and solid waste removal) by submetering or by a ratio utility billing system. If you do, the lease must list the utilities charged separately and the amount of any administrative fee, you may recover only the provider's charges plus an administrative fee for your actual administrative costs, and each bill must show the period's charges with the opening and closing meter readings and their dates, and the administrative fee.

To start submetering during a lease, the lease must allow it and existing tenants need 90 days' notice.

Arizona's Constitution defines public service corporations as corporations furnishing electricity for light, fuel or power; whether a landlord that resells electricity by submeter falls under Corporation Commission regulation is not addressed by the landlord-tenant statute and depends on Commission rules and decisions we did not read. The Arizona lease's utility billing clause carries the required disclosure.

For a ratio utility billing system, the lease must give a specific description of the method: per tenant; proportionately by livable square footage; per type of unit; per number of water fixtures; for water and wastewater, by individually submetered hot water use; or another method that fairly allocates the charges. For submetering, the lease may simply say "submetering".

title: Required Utility Billing Disclosure
bodyText:
If you charge tenants separately for gas, water, wastewater, solid waste removal or electricity, Arizona requires the lease itself to contain a disclosure listing the utility services charged separately and the amount of any administrative fee for submetering or ratio billing. If you use a ratio method, the lease must also describe the method specifically.

The statute does not require a separate attachment; the disclosure may be a section of the lease, as in the Arizona lease's utility billing clause. Without the disclosure you are out of compliance with the statute: the tenant may object in writing and, if the dispute is not resolved, sue in justice court to enforce it.

title: Dividing Utility Costs Among Tenants
bodyText: Arizona lets you allocate gas, water, wastewater, solid waste or electricity costs that are not submetered by a ratio utility billing system, using one or more of these methods: per tenant, by livable square footage, by type of unit, by number of water fixtures, for water and wastewater by an individually submetered hot-water measure, or any other method that fairly allocates the charges and is described in the lease. The lease must specifically describe the method and list the separately charged utilities and any administrative fee, and you may recover only the provider's charges plus actual administrative costs. To start ratio billing for existing tenancies, give at least 90 days' notice, and during a lease term only if the lease provides for it. Arizona does not make a term charging for unmetered utilities unenforceable.

title: Limit on What You Can Charge for Utilities
bodyText: When you bill a tenant separately for gas, water, wastewater, solid waste removal or electricity, Arizona limits you to the charges the utility provider imposed on you plus an administrative fee covering only your actual administrative costs; no other charges are allowed. If you don't comply, the tenant must first object in writing, and if the dispute isn't resolved may sue in justice court to enforce the section. Arizona has no fixed-rent-only rule for master-metered electricity. Utility allowances in federally assisted housing follow the program's rules, not covered here.

title: No Shutoffs of Utilities You Bill
bodyText: Arizona gives you no right to interrupt utilities you provide or bill through a submeter or ratio system because the tenant hasn't paid. You may not terminate utility services provided as part of the lease except to make needed repairs or as the eviction section allows, and that section lets you discontinue utilities you provide only on the day after a writ of restitution or execution is executed, with the disconnection done by someone the utility authorizes. Outside those two exceptions, wilfully interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, whatever the reason (unpaid utility charges included), lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Unpaid utility charges billed under the lease are collected like other lease charges, through the lease remedies and the courts.

title: When the Landlord Holds the Utility Account
bodyText: If you fail to provide a utility the tenant is entitled to because you didn't pay your own utility bill, and the units are not separately metered so a tenant can't avoid the shutoff by putting service in the tenant's name, the tenants may, individually or together, after written notice to you of their intent, arrange with the utility company to pay your delinquent bill and deduct the actual cost from rent they owe you, with the utility's approval. They may keep paying the utility until you give adequate assurance that service will be maintained. More generally, if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, gas, electricity, hot water, heat, air-conditioning or other essential services, the tenant may buy them and deduct the cost, recover the lost rental value, or get substitute housing. Utility notice rules for master-metered buildings are Corporation Commission rules we did not read.

title: Utility Company Shutoff Rules
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets when a utility company may shut off a residential customer's service, such as notice periods or summer or weather moratoriums. Those rules are set by the Arizona Corporation Commission and by municipal and cooperative utilities, which we did not review. The landlord-tenant rules that do apply are in the Act: you may not cut off utilities you provide except for repairs or the day after an eviction writ is executed, and tenants may pay your delinquent utility bill and deduct it from rent when the building isn't separately metered.

title: No Statute on Copying Landlords on Shutoff Notices
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that lets a landlord authorize a utility, or a tenant designate a landlord, to receive notice of a tenant's pending utility disconnection. Some utilities offer third-party notification under their own rules or Corporation Commission rules, which we did not review. If you want notice, ask the tenant to name you as a third-party contact with the utility, in writing and voluntarily; don't make it a lease condition without checking the utility's program.

title: Moving Utilities into the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
If the lease makes the tenant responsible for a utility, have the tenant put the service in the tenant's name by the start date.

Arizona has two limits. Once the lease is signed, you may not shift payment of a utility the lease says you provide to the tenant without the tenant's written consent. And you may not terminate a utility you provide under the lease, or wilfully interrupt electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant for any reason, except to make needed repairs or on the day after an eviction writ is executed.

So the Arizona lease does not include a clause letting you cut off landlord-name service the tenant failed to transfer. If a tenant doesn't transfer service as the lease requires, treat it as a lease breach (written notice to cure), and bill the tenant for usage the lease makes theirs.

title: No Statute on Utility Deposit Refunds
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that governs a utility company's refund of a tenant's utility deposit, or a landlord's handling of a utility deposit. Utility deposits are governed by Corporation Commission rules and each utility's terms, which we did not review; the only statute found sends abandoned utility deposits to a fuel-assistance fund. If you collect money from a tenant toward utilities you provide, it is security under the deposit statute (counted in the cap and refunded the same way) unless its nonrefundable purpose is stated in writing.

title: No Meter or Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute that sets a meter conservation charge or energy-efficiency charge for tenants, or a special water-submetering regime like Kansas's. The general utility-billing rule controls: if you bill utilities by submeter or ratio, you may recover only the provider's charges plus an administrative fee for your actual administrative costs, with no other charges, and each bill must show opening and closing meter readings. Arizona also bars state environmental regulators from treating an apartment community as a regulated water system solely because it submeters or ratio-bills water.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Arizona does not require a residential lease to be recorded, and recording does not change any right under the landlord-tenant act. A lease for a term of more than one year must be in writing and signed by the landlord or an agent authorized in writing. Arizona's recording rule requiring real estate transfers to be recorded within 60 days expressly excludes leases. Recording matters only for priority against later buyers and lenders: an unrecorded conveyance of an estate for a term of years is void against later creditors and buyers who pay value without notice, and only a recorded instrument gives notice of its contents. Whether a tenant's possession of the unit gives a buyer notice anyway is case law we did not search. Arizona has no rule like Nebraska's for leases to relatives. Long leases are rarely recorded; if a tenant asks to record a memorandum of a lease longer than one year, it must be acknowledged before a notary to be recorded.

title: City and County Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: Arizona cities and counties may run rental inspection programs only under state limits, and before an inspector enters a rental the city must have the consent of the owner of record or a lawful tenant, or a warrant. Where the owner has not registered the property with the county assessor, the inspecting authority must ask an occupying tenant's consent before entering, and has other legal remedies if the tenant refuses. Nothing in the statutes makes a lease clause the tenant's consent to an inspector's entry, and your own right of entry is limited to the reasons and notice in the access statute: at least two days' notice of intent to enter, entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency. The Arizona lease therefore does not include an inspector-entry clause. When an inspection is scheduled, give the tenant the two days' notice, ask the tenant to be present or to consent, and accompany the inspector. Whether an owner's consent alone lets a city inspect an occupied unit over the tenant's objection is a constitutional question we did not research.

title: No State Tenant-Rights Statement
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute requiring a landlord to give tenants a state-agency statement of tenant rights, to attach one as the first page of the lease, to get a signed acknowledgment, or barring suit until one is provided. The nearest rule is a one-line notice: at or before the start of the tenancy you must tell the tenant in writing that the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website. The Arizona lease's landlord disclosure clause gives that notice.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: We found no Arizona statute requiring a landlord to give a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. Arizona requires only that you tell the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, that the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is available on the Arizona Department of Housing's website; the Arizona lease's landlord disclosure clause does this.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Arizona follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (A.R.S. § 47-3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (A.R.S. § 47-1308(B)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (A.R.S. § 33-1311). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
